questions.stem: Plaster of Paris is obtained by the calcination of:
questions.solution:
**Gypsum.**

Gypsum is **CaSO₄·2H₂O**. Heating it to about **150 °C** drives off three quarters of the combined water and leaves **plaster of Paris, CaSO₄·½H₂O**.

> **CaSO₄·2H₂O --(150 °C)--> CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O**

**Why the other options cannot be right:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Calcium oxide (CaO)** | **Quick lime** — the product of calcining limestone |
| **Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)** | **Limestone** — the raw material for lime and cement |
| **Quick lime** | The same as calcium oxide |

> Note that the last three are all part of the **lime** family, which is a completely separate material stream from gypsum. The chemistry settles it: plaster of Paris is a **SULPHATE**, and only gypsum is a sulphate.

**Properties and uses:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sets in 5–15 minutes** | Very rapid, which is why a retarder is often added |
| **EXPANDS slightly on setting** | Unusual — most binders shrink. This is why it takes a sharp impression of a mould |
| Low strength | Not a structural material |
| **Not water resistant** | Interior use only |

**Uses:** plaster of Paris cornices and mouldings, false ceilings, moulds and casts, orthopaedic bandages, and as a **retarder in cement** (as gypsum, before calcining).

**A related distinction worth holding**: **gypsum plaster** for walls is a different product again — it is plaster of Paris with retarders and aggregates added to give a workable setting time.

examTip.trap: All three wrong options belong to the **LIME** family — limestone, quick lime and calcium oxide. They are a completely different material stream, and offering three of them together is designed to make you second-guess a correct first instinct.
examTip.trick: Settle it by chemistry: plaster of Paris is a **SULPHATE** (CaSO₄·½H₂O). Only **gypsum** is a sulphate; the rest are carbonates or oxides.
examTip.mnemonic: **GYPSUM → POP, and it EXPANDS on setting** — almost uniquely among binders, which is why it takes a sharp impression from a mould. Uncalcined gypsum is also what **retards cement**.

questions.stem: The compressive strength of a 1st class brick should be:
questions.solution:
**Not less than 10.5 N/mm².**

**The brick class ladder:**

| Class | Minimum compressive strength | Water absorption (24 h) |
|---|---|---|
| **First class** | **10.5 N/mm²** | **≤ 20%** |
| **Second class** | **7.0 N/mm²** | ≤ 22% |
| **Third class** | **3.5 N/mm²** | ≤ 25% |

> Each step is roughly **two thirds** of the one above, which makes the ladder easy to hold.

**The other first-class requirements**, which are tested together:

| Requirement | First class brick |
|---|---|
| **Shape** | Sharp, straight edges; true right angles |
| **Colour** | Uniform deep red or cherry |
| **Sound** | A **clear metallic RING** when two are struck together |
| **Scratch** | No impression from a fingernail |
| **Fracture** | Uniform, compact, homogeneous |
| **Drop test** | Does not break when dropped flat from **about 1 m** |
| **Efflorescence** | Nil to slight |

**The compressive strength test procedure** matters for the number to mean anything:

> The **frog is filled with 1:1 cement mortar** and the brick cured for three days before testing. Without that, the load bears on a rim rather than a flat plane and the result is meaningless.

**Why the absorption limit accompanies the strength limit**: a brick that absorbs heavily is porous, and a porous brick is both weaker and more vulnerable to **frost damage and efflorescence**. The two properties measure the same underlying quality — the degree of vitrification achieved in firing.

examTip.trick: Learn the ladder as a falling sequence: **10.5 / 7 / 3.5** for first, second and third class — each about two thirds of the one above.
examTip.trap: The **water absorption** limits run the other way: **20 / 22 / 25%**, rising as the class falls. Strength down, absorption up — and questions often pair them to see whether you know which direction each runs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Strength 10.5, absorption 20 for a first class brick.** Both measure the same thing — how well the brick was vitrified in firing. And remember the test detail: **fill the frog with 1:1 mortar** first.

questions.stem: The Oedometer is used for:
questions.solution:
**Consolidation.**

The **oedometer (consolidometer)** confines a soil specimen laterally in a rigid ring and loads it vertically in increments, measuring the settlement against time for each increment.

**What it yields:**

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C_c** — compression index | Slope of the **virgin** e–log σ′ curve — governs **HOW MUCH** settlement |
| **C_r** — recompression index | Slope of the reloading curve, about **C_c/5 to C_c/10** |
| **σ′_c** — preconsolidation pressure | The maximum past effective stress; found by **Casagrande's construction** |
| **c_v** — coefficient of consolidation | Governs **HOW FAST**, from the time–settlement curve |
| **m_v** — coefficient of volume compressibility | — |
| **k** — permeability | Indirectly, from **k = c_v m_v γ_w** |

> **C_c says how much; c_v says how fast.** Keeping those two questions apart is the organising idea of consolidation — a clay may be highly compressible yet drain quickly, or barely compressible yet take decades.

**The lateral confinement is the essential feature**: it reproduces the **one-dimensional** condition of a wide loaded area on a clay layer, where the soil cannot spread sideways. That is exactly the field situation the test is meant to model.

**Note the spelling trap in the distractors**: an **ODOMETER** measures distance travelled by a vehicle; an **OEDOMETER** measures soil consolidation. The two words differ by one letter and the source paper flags the confusion explicitly.

**The other options and their proper tests:**

| Property | Test |
|---|---|
| **Compaction** | **Proctor** test (standard or modified) |
| **Permeability** | Constant head (coarse) or falling head (fine) permeameter |
| **Void ratio** | Computed from the phase relations, not measured directly |

examTip.trap: **ODOMETER (vehicle distance) versus OEDOMETER (soil consolidation)** — one letter apart. The source paper flags this confusion explicitly, which tells you it catches candidates every sitting.
examTip.trick: Also keep **compaction** and **consolidation** apart: compaction expels **AIR** in minutes by mechanical effort; consolidation expels **WATER** over years under sustained load. The oedometer does the second.
examTip.mnemonic: **C_c says HOW MUCH; c_v says HOW FAST.** One test yields both, plus the preconsolidation pressure that tells you whether the clay is normally or over-consolidated.

questions.stem: In which of the following do the centre of gravity and the geometric centre not coincide?
questions.solution:
**The right-angled triangle.**

**The principle:** for a **homogeneous lamina**, the centre of gravity coincides with the geometric centre **whenever the shape is symmetrical**. Symmetry guarantees that every element of area on one side is matched by one on the other.

| Shape | Symmetrical? | CG at geometric centre? |
|---|---|---|
| **Circle** | Yes — infinite axes | **Yes**, at the centre |
| **Equilateral triangle** | Yes — three axes | **Yes**, at the centroid |
| **Rectangle** | Yes — two axes | **Yes**, at the intersection of the diagonals |
| **Right-angled triangle** | **NO** | **No** |

**For a right-angled triangle** with base b and height h, measuring from the right-angle corner:

> **x̄ = b/3** and **ȳ = h/3**

> The centroid sits **one third of the way along each leg** — noticeably closer to the right angle than to the hypotenuse, because more of the area is concentrated there.

**Standard centroid positions** worth carrying:

| Shape | Centroid |
|---|---|
| **Triangle** (any) | **h/3 from the base** |
| **Semicircular area** | **4r/3π ≈ 0.424r** from the diameter |
| Semicircular arc | 2r/π |
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8** from the base |
| Hollow hemisphere | r/2 |
| Solid cone | h/4 from the base |

**A caution about the wording**: for a triangle the centroid is at h/3 from the base **whatever its shape** — so an equilateral triangle's centroid is also at h/3. The difference is that for an equilateral triangle that point **is** the geometric centre (the centre of symmetry), while for a right-angled triangle there is no centre of symmetry to coincide with.

**And for a composite shape** the centroid follows from **ȳ = Σ(A_i ȳ_i)/ΣA_i**, with the second moment of area then obtained by the **parallel axis theorem**.

examTip.trick: Ask one question: **is the shape symmetrical?** If it has an axis of symmetry the CG lies on it, and a shape with two or more axes has its CG at their intersection — the geometric centre. Only the right-angled triangle here has none.
examTip.trap: An **equilateral** triangle is symmetrical and a **right-angled** one is not — so the question is testing whether you noticed which triangle was offered.
examTip.mnemonic: **Right-angled triangle: x̄ = b/3, ȳ = h/3 from the right angle** — a third of the way along each leg, because the area bunches toward the corner.

questions.stem: Which of the following is important while designing a beam?
questions.solution:
**Bending moment at the centre.**

For a **simply supported** beam — the case a bare "beam" question implies — the two design quantities peak at **different** sections:

| Quantity | Maximum at | Value (UDL) | Governs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BENDING MOMENT** | **MIDSPAN** | **wL²/8** | **Main flexural steel and section depth** |
| **SHEAR FORCE** | **The SUPPORTS** | **wL/2** | Stirrups, web thickness |

> Bending moment is the **primary** design action for a beam — it sets the depth and the main reinforcement. Shear is checked afterwards and is usually satisfied by stirrups, which are cheap.

**Why the moment governs the section:**

> **σ = M/Z**, so the section modulus (and hence the depth) follows directly from the maximum moment. Shear is resisted by adding transverse steel, which does not change the section size — unless **τ_v exceeds τ_c,max**, at which point the section really is inadequate and must be enlarged.

**Note the distractors are not nonsense** — each is a real design quantity in a different situation:

| Option | When it governs |
|---|---|
| **SF at support** | Stirrup design; genuinely important, but secondary |
| **BM at support** | For a **CANTILEVER or a CONTINUOUS** beam — where the maximum moment is at the support |
| SF at centre | Zero for a symmetric UDL — never governs |

> **For a cantilever the answer would be BM at the support**, and for a continuous beam the support moment often exceeds the span moment. The question's implied simply supported beam is what makes midspan correct.

**The complementary detailing consequence**, which follows from the two peaks being at different sections: **stirrups closely spaced near the supports** and widely spaced at midspan; **main bars fully provided at midspan** and curtailed toward the ends. That is the whole logic of beam detailing in one sentence.

examTip.trap: **BM at support** is correct for a **CANTILEVER or CONTINUOUS** beam. The question implies a simply supported beam, where the moment peaks at midspan — so read which beam is meant before answering.
examTip.trick: Bending governs the **SECTION** (σ = M/Z sets the depth); shear is fixed afterwards by adding **stirrups**, which cost little and do not change the size.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment at midspan, shear at the supports** — the two peaks are at opposite ends, which is exactly why stirrups bunch near the supports and main bars are fullest at midspan.

questions.stem: What is the value of Lacey's silt factor f if the diameter of the particle is 2 mm?
questions.solution:
**About 2.5.**

> **f = 1.76 √d**, with **d in millimetres**
> **f = 1.76 × √2 = 1.76 × 1.414 = 2.49 ≈ 2.5** ✓

**What the silt factor represents**: it characterises the **coarseness of the bed material**, and through it the channel's resistance to scour. A coarser bed gives a larger f, a shallower regime channel and a steeper regime slope.

**Typical values:**

| Material | d (mm) | f |
|---|---|---|
| Fine silt | 0.05 | **0.4** |
| Medium silt | 0.16 | 0.7 |
| **Standard silt** | **0.32** | **1.0** |
| Coarse sand | 0.72 | 1.5 |
| **Fine gravel** | **2.0** | **2.5** |

> Note that **f = 1.0 corresponds to "standard silt"** of 0.32 mm — the reference against which Lacey calibrated the whole system.

**Where f is used — Lacey's regime equations:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75 √Q** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Velocity** | V = 0.4382 (f R)^{1/2} |
| **Bed slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| **Normal scour depth** | **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** |

**What "in regime" means** is worth stating, because it is a stricter criterion than hydraulic efficiency:

> A channel in regime carries **both its water AND its sediment load** without net scour or deposition. Its width, depth and slope have all adjusted to the discharge and the bed material.

> Lacey's advance over **Kennedy** was recognising that a regime channel adjusts **all three** dimensions, not merely its velocity. The modern successor is the **tractive force** method, checking the bed shear **τ₀ = γRS** against the critical value for the bed material.

**Note the scour application**: **R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}**, multiplied by a location factor (**2.0 at a bridge pier nose**), is what fixes foundation depths near a watercourse — usually deeper than bearing capacity alone would require.

examTip.trick: **f = 1.76√d with d in MILLIMETRES.** For d = 2, √2 ≈ 1.414 and 1.76 × 1.414 ≈ 2.5. Using metres instead of millimetres is the one way to get this badly wrong.
examTip.trap: Anchor on **f = 1.0 for "standard silt" of 0.32 mm** — check: 1.76 × √0.32 = 1.76 × 0.566 = 1.0 ✓. If your answer for a coarser material comes out below 1, the units are wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacey: P = 4.75√Q, R = 0.473(Q/f)⅓, S = f^{5/3}/(3340Q^{1/6}).** A channel "in regime" carries its **sediment** as well as its water — a stricter test than hydraulic efficiency.

questions.stem: What is the formula for the sequent depth of a hydraulic jump?
questions.solution:
**y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1].**

**Note carefully where the brackets fall.** The **½ multiplies the whole expression** including the −1, not just the square root. Option (a) is the same characters with the bracket closed in the wrong place, and it gives a materially different answer.

**Check at Fr₁ = 1** (the threshold of a jump), where y₂ must equal y₁:

| Option | Value at Fr = 1 |
|---|---|
| **(b) ½[√9 − 1] = ½(2)** | **= 1** ✓ |
| (a) ½√9 − 1 = 1.5 − 1 | = 0.5 ✗ |
| (c) √9 − 1 | = 2 ✗ |
| (d) √9 + 1 | = 4 ✗ |

> **Only option (b) gives y₂/y₁ = 1 at Fr = 1**, which it must — at critical flow there is no jump and the two depths coincide. That single check settles the question without any recall.

**Why the relation comes from MOMENTUM, not energy:**

> The energy loss in a jump is **large and unknown in advance**, so an energy balance has an unknown on both sides. But the **external forces are small** (the jump is short, so bed friction over its length is negligible), which makes the **momentum balance exact**.

> **Specific force M = Aȳ + Q²/(gA)** is the **same on both sides** of the jump, and equating it gives the conjugate depth relation.

**Conjugate versus alternate depths** — routinely confused:

| Pair | Conserved | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **CONJUGATE (sequent)** | **Specific FORCE (momentum)** | Across a **hydraulic jump** |
| **ALTERNATE** | **Specific ENERGY** | Two possible states at the same E |

**Energy loss** in the jump:

> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂)**

**Classification by Fr₁ (USBR):**

| Fr₁ | Type | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0–1.7 | Undular | Small waves |
| 1.7–2.5 | Weak | — |
| **2.5–4.5** | **OSCILLATING** | **AVOID** — throws waves far downstream |
| **4.5–9.0** | **STEADY** | **Best for a stilling basin** |
| > 9.0 | Strong | Effective but rough |

examTip.trick: **Test at Fr = 1**, where there is no jump and y₂ must equal y₁. Only option (b) gives ½[√9 − 1] = **1** ✓. That one substitution eliminates all three distractors without recalling the formula.
examTip.trap: Options (a) and (b) contain the **same characters with the bracket closed in a different place**. The ½ must multiply the **whole** expression including the −1.
examTip.mnemonic: **Momentum, not energy** — the jump's loss is large and unknown, but the forces are small. Design a stilling basin in the **steady range Fr 4.5–9** and avoid the **oscillating range 2.5–4.5**, which throws waves far downstream.

questions.stem: In which phase of the project are most of the money and manpower required?
questions.solution:
**The execution phase.**

**The project life cycle and its resource profile:**

| Phase | Activity | Resource level |
|---|---|---|
| **Initiation** | Concept, feasibility, charter | **Low** |
| **Planning** | Scope, schedule, budget, procurement | Moderate |
| **EXECUTION** | The work itself — construction, procurement, installation | **PEAK — the great majority** |
| Monitoring and control | Runs **in parallel** with execution | — |
| **Closing** | Handover, final accounts, lessons learned | Low |

> The resource curve is an **S-shape**: slow at first, steep through execution, tapering at the end. Typically **60–80% of the total cost** is spent in execution.

**But the phase that spends least DECIDES most**, and this is the point worth carrying:

> **The ability to INFLUENCE the outcome is highest at the start and falls steeply; the COST of making a change rises steeply.** The two curves cross early.

> So the **initiation and planning phases**, which consume little money, determine most of the eventual cost. A decision taken in a week of feasibility work can commit hundreds of times its own cost.

**The practical consequence:**

| Stage | Change |
|---|---|
| **Concept** | Costs almost nothing |
| Detailed design | Costs a redesign |
| **During construction** | Costs a **variation order**, delay and disruption |
| After completion | Costs demolition and rebuilding |

> That is why **risk analysis belongs in the feasibility phase** — by execution it is too late to act on what it finds.

**Monitoring and control is not a sequential phase** but a continuous process running alongside execution — comparing progress against the plan and correcting. **Earned value analysis** (BCWP, BCWS, ACWP) is its standard instrument.

examTip.trick: The resource curve is an **S-shape** — slow, steep, tapering. Execution takes **60–80%** of the cost, and it is where the physical work happens.
examTip.trap: **Monitoring and control is not a sequential phase** — it runs in **parallel** with execution throughout. Treating it as a fifth stage in sequence is a common error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Execution SPENDS the most; initiation and planning DECIDE the most.** The ability to influence falls as the cost of change rises, and the two curves cross early — which is why risk analysis belongs at feasibility.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a function of the Nepal Engineering Council?
options: Prepare and implement the policy, plan and programmes
To prescribe the basic conditions of student admission
questions.solution:
**Opening a college.**

The Council is a **REGULATOR**, not an operator. It sets standards, recognises institutions and registers engineers — but it does not **establish or run** educational institutions itself.

**What the NEC does (NEC Act 2055):**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Register engineers** and maintain the register | The core licensure function |
| **Recognise (accredit)** engineering academic institutions and their programmes | Approval, not ownership |
| **Prescribe minimum standards** for engineering education | Curriculum, staffing, facilities |
| Prescribe **conditions for student admission** | — |
| Prepare and implement **policy, plans and programmes** for the profession | — |
| **Regulate professional conduct** and take disciplinary action | — |
| Issue the **license to practise** | — |

**What it does NOT do:**

| Not a function | Who does it instead |
|---|---|
| **Open or run colleges** | Universities and their affiliating bodies; the Ministry of Education |
| **Fix fees or salaries** | The market; institutions themselves |
| **Represent** engineers' interests | The **Nepal Engineers' Association (NEA)** |
| Award degrees | Universities |

**The distinction that answers most institutional questions:**

> **The COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION represents.** Registration with the **NEC is a legal requirement to practise**; membership of the **NEA is voluntary**.

**Council composition (21 members)** — a recurring examination topic:

| Position | How appointed |
|---|---|
| **Chairman** | Government — bachelor's degree + **15 years** |
| **Vice-chairman** | Government — bachelor's degree + **10 years** |
| 7 members | Government, one per province, at least three women |
| President of the NEA | Ex officio |
| 5 members | **Elected from the NEA** |
| Campus chief, IOE and university representatives | Government |
| **2 members** | **Nominated by the COUNCIL itself** |
| **Member Secretary (Registrar)** | Bachelor's + 10 years |

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Three options are genuine Council functions and only one is not — and "recognising institutions" sounds close enough to "opening" one to catch a hurried reader.
examTip.trick: Ask whether the activity is **regulating** or **operating**. The Council **approves, prescribes, registers and disciplines**; it never **builds, runs or funds**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Council REGULATES, Association REPRESENTS.** NEC registration is a **legal requirement** to practise; NEA membership is voluntary. That one distinction answers most institutional questions on the paper.

questions.stem: What is the relation for active earth pressure in cohesive soil?
questions.solution:
**σ_a = K_a σ_z − 2c√K_a.**

**The cohesion term is SUBTRACTED** in the active case, because cohesion **helps the soil stand** and therefore **reduces** the pressure it exerts on the wall.

**The two Rankine expressions, side by side:**

| State | Expression | Cohesion term |
|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **σ_a = K_a σ_z − 2c√K_a** | **SUBTRACTED** — cohesion reduces the push |
| **PASSIVE** | **σ_p = K_p σ_z + 2c√K_p** | **ADDED** — cohesion adds to the resistance |

> **Active subtracts, passive adds.** The physical reading: in the active case the soil is trying to push the wall over and its cohesion holds it back; in the passive case the wall is pushing into the soil and its cohesion resists.

**The immediate consequence — the TENSION CRACK:**

> Setting **σ_a = 0** gives **z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a)** — the depth over which the computed active pressure is **negative**.

> Soil cannot pull, so that negative block is **ignored** in design. But the crack it represents is real, and it matters more than the pressure it removed:

> **The tension crack FILLS WITH WATER**, and the resulting hydrostatic thrust is often **larger than the earth pressure it replaced**. Ignoring the water is a real and dangerous omission.

**And the critical unsupported height:**

> **H_c = 4c/(γ√K_a)** — exactly **twice** the tension crack depth. For a purely cohesive soil (φ = 0, K_a = 1) that reduces to **H_c = 4c/γ**.

> In practice a factor of safety is applied, so an unsupported cut is limited to about **H_c/2**.

**A reminder about K_a itself:**

> **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45 − φ/2)**, and **K_a < 1 < K_p** with **K_p = 1/K_a**. For φ = 30°: **K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3**.

examTip.trick: Reason from the physics: **cohesion helps the soil stand up**, so it must **REDUCE** the active pressure — hence the minus sign. In the **passive** case the same cohesion **adds** to the resistance.
examTip.trap: The coefficient is **2c√K_a**, not c√K_a. Options with a single c are offered precisely because the 2 is easy to drop.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tension crack z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a); critical height H_c = 4c/(γ√K_a) — exactly twice.** And the crack **fills with water**, whose thrust often exceeds the earth pressure it replaced.

questions.stem: What would be the effect on effective stress if the water table is above the ground level?
questions.solution:
**It remains constant.**

**Why.** Consider a point at depth z below the ground surface, with the water table standing at a height h_w **above** ground level. Take **σ′ = σ − u**:

> **Total stress σ = γ_w h_w + γ_sat z** (the free water above contributes its own weight)
> **Pore pressure u = γ_w (h_w + z)**
> **σ′ = γ_w h_w + γ_sat z − γ_w h_w − γ_w z = (γ_sat − γ_w) z = γ′ z**

> **The h_w terms cancel exactly.** So the effective stress depends only on the depth below the **ground surface**, not on how much free water stands above it.

**The physical reading is worth having:**

> Water above the ground surface presses down on the soil **and** pushes up through the pore water by exactly the same amount. It adds to σ and to u equally, so it does nothing to σ′.

> **Which is why a submerged riverbed or lakebed is no stronger for the water above it** — and why raising a reservoir does not consolidate the soil beneath it.

**Contrast with the water table moving WITHIN the soil**, where the effect is quite different:

| Change | Effect on σ′ |
|---|---|
| Water table **rises within the soil** (from depth to ground level) | **DECREASES** — γ replaced by γ′, roughly halving it |
| Water table **falls below ground level** | **INCREASES** — which is why dewatering causes settlement |
| Free water rises **above** ground level | **NO CHANGE** |

> The middle row is the practically important one: **lowering the groundwater table increases effective stress throughout and causes settlement**, which is the mechanism behind the subsidence of cities that over-pump their aquifers.

**σ′ = σ − u is the most important equation in soil mechanics**, because **everything that matters — strength, stiffness, volume change — is a function of σ′ alone.** Total stress on its own governs nothing.

examTip.trick: Write out **σ′ = σ − u** and watch the free-water terms cancel: water above ground adds **γ_w h_w to BOTH σ and u**, so it contributes nothing to σ′.
examTip.trap: This is a different question from the water table rising **WITHIN** the soil, which **decreases** σ′ (γ replaced by γ′). Read where the water table is relative to the ground surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water ABOVE ground: no change. Water table rising WITHIN the soil: σ′ falls. Water table lowered: σ′ rises — which is why dewatering causes SETTLEMENT.**

questions.stem: What will be the effect on the probability of annual damage if the design flood is increased?
questions.solution:
**It decreases.**

**Why.** Designing for a **larger** flood means designing for a **rarer** event — one with a **longer return period** and therefore a **smaller annual probability of being exceeded**.

> **Annual probability of exceedance = 1/T**

| Design flood | Return period T | Annual probability of damage |
|---|---|---|
| 25-year | 25 | **4%** |
| 50-year | 50 | 2% |
| **100-year** | **100** | **1%** |
| 500-year | 500 | 0.2% |
| 1000-year | 1000 | 0.1% |

> Damage occurs when the actual flood **exceeds** what the structure was designed for. Raising the design flood raises that threshold, so the probability of exceeding it falls.

**The risk over a design LIFE compounds, and this is where the numbers become alarming:**

> **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ**

| Design | 50-year life | 100-year life |
|---|---|---|
| **T = 100** | **40%** | 63% |
| T = 500 | 10% | 18% |
| T = 1000 | 5% | 10% |

> **A structure designed for the 100-year flood with a 50-year life has a 40% chance of being overtopped at least once** — closer to a coin toss than to a rarity.

**Two rules of thumb:**

> When **n = T**, the risk is always about **63%**.
> To hold the risk at **10%** over n years, choose **T ≈ 10n**.

**The cost side of the trade-off:**

> A higher design flood means a **larger, costlier structure**. The economic optimum minimises the **sum of the capital cost and the expected annual damage** — which is why a culvert is designed for 25 years and a large dam for the **PMF**.

**And why a large dam abandons return periods entirely:**

> The consequences of failure are so catastrophic that **no annual probability is acceptable**, so the design flood becomes the **largest physically possible** — derived from the Probable Maximum Precipitation, not from statistics.

examTip.trick: **Annual probability = 1/T.** A bigger design flood means a bigger T, so 1/T falls. One line settles it.
examTip.trap: "Return period" is the most misread term in hydrology: a **100-year flood has a 1% chance in ANY year**, and one occurring this year does **nothing** to reduce next year's probability. The events are treated as independent.
examTip.mnemonic: **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ, and when n = T the risk is about 63%.** So a 100-year design over a 50-year life has a **40%** chance of being exceeded — which is why large dams are designed for the **PMF** instead.

questions.stem: In influence line diagrams (ILD):
options: Points remain fixed, position of load changes
Points change, position of loads remains fixed
questions.solution:
**The point remains fixed and the position of the load changes.**

**That single sentence is the definition of an influence line**, and it is what distinguishes it from every other structural diagram.

| | **Bending moment diagram** | **INFLUENCE LINE** |
|---|---|---|
| The **section** | **Varies** — every point on the beam | **FIXED** — one chosen section |
| The **load** | **FIXED** in position | **MOVES** across the structure |
| Horizontal axis | Position along the **beam** | Position of the **LOAD** |
| Answers | "How is this loading resisted?" | "Where should the load go to make this worst?" |

> They can share the **same triangular shape** for a simply supported span, which is exactly why the two are confused — but they answer entirely different questions.

**Standard influence lines for a simply supported span L**, section at a from the left (b = L − a):

| Quantity | Shape | Peak |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | Linear, 1 → 0 | **1** at A |
| **Moment at the section** | **Triangular** | **ab/L** |
| **Shear at the section** | Two parallel lines, **unit step** | +b/L and −a/L |

**Using one — two rules cover everything:**

| Load | Response |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × ORDINATE** at the load's position |
| **UDL w** | **w × AREA** under the line over the loaded length |

**And the placement rules follow at once:**

> **Point load → put it at the maximum ordinate. UDL → cover the whole region of ONE SIGN.**

> Because a **shear** influence line changes sign at the section, loading both sides partly cancels — so **maximum shear needs one side loaded only**. That is the pattern-loading principle in its simplest form.

**Why influence lines matter**: **bridges** (the vehicle must be positioned for the worst effect), **crane runway girders**, and **continuous beams** under pattern live load. For an indeterminate structure the influence line is a **curve** and cannot be obtained by statics — but **Müller-Breslau's principle** gives its shape from the deflected form when the corresponding restraint is released.

examTip.trick: Hold the one-line definition: **"One quantity, ONE fixed section, MOVING load."** Everything else about influence lines follows from it.
examTip.trap: Option (b) describes a **bending moment diagram** — fixed load, varying section. The two share a triangular shape on a simple span, which is why they are confused.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load → maximum ORDINATE; UDL → whole region of ONE SIGN.** Since a shear ILD changes sign at the section, maximum shear needs **one side loaded only**.

questions.stem: The shear strength of plastic undrained clay depends upon:
questions.solution:
**Cohesion alone.**

**Why.** For a **saturated clay tested under UNDRAINED conditions**, the angle of shearing resistance is **φ_u = 0**, so the Mohr–Coulomb equation reduces to:

> **τ = c + σ tan φ  →  τ = c_u**

> The strength is **independent of the confining pressure**, and the Mohr failure envelope is a **horizontal line**.

**The physical reason:**

> Under undrained loading a saturated clay **cannot change volume** — the water has nowhere to go. So any increase in cell pressure goes **entirely into pore pressure**, leaving the **effective stress unchanged**. Since strength depends on σ′, the strength is unchanged too.

> Every Mohr circle therefore has the **same diameter**, whatever the cell pressure, and their common tangent is horizontal.

**The crucial qualification** — and the point most often missed:

> **φ_u = 0 is a property of the TEST, not of the clay.** The same clay has a genuine **φ′ of 20–30°** in **drained** (effective stress) terms. It is the undrained condition that suppresses the frictional component, not any absence of friction in the soil.

**Which parameters to use, and when:**

| Condition | Parameters | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| **Short term** (end of construction) | **c_u, φ_u = 0** | Total stress analysis |
| **Long term** | **c′, φ′** | Effective stress analysis |

**And which is critical depends on the problem:**

> For an **EMBANKMENT** (loading), the **short term** is worse — the clay consolidates and gains strength afterwards.
> For a **CUTTING** (unloading), the **LONG term** is worse — pore pressures rise back to equilibrium and the clay softens.

> Getting that pairing the wrong way round is a genuine design error, and it is a favourite examination point.

**Measuring c_u:**

| Test | Note |
|---|---|
| **Unconfined compression** | **c_u = q_u/2** — quick, no cell needed, but only for a specimen that stands unsupported |
| **UU triaxial** | Controlled, works on any saturated clay |
| **VANE shear** | **In situ** — the clay is never sampled or trimmed, which matters for a sensitive clay |

**Consistency bands** by c_u: very soft < 25 kPa, soft 25–50, medium 50–100, stiff 100–200, very stiff > 200.

examTip.trick: The words **"undrained" and "saturated"** are the signal. No volume change means the extra cell pressure goes **entirely into pore pressure**, σ′ is unchanged, so the strength is unchanged and **φ_u = 0**.
examTip.trap: **φ_u = 0 is a property of the TEST, not of the clay** — the same soil has a real φ′ of 20–30° in drained terms. Saying "clay has no friction" is wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Embankment → SHORT term critical; CUTTING → LONG term critical.** Loading lets the clay consolidate and strengthen; unloading lets pore pressures recover and weaken it. Getting that pairing backwards is a real design error.

questions.stem: When two column loads are unequal, which of the possible footings can be provided?
questions.solution:
**A trapezoidal combined footing.**

**The governing principle** for any footing carrying more than one column:

> A footing bears **uniformly** only when its **CENTROID coincides with the RESULTANT of the column loads**. Otherwise the pressure is non-uniform and the footing **tilts**.

**Why a trapezoid rather than a rectangle:**

| Situation | Shape |
|---|---|
| Loads **equal**, or space available beyond the lighter column | **RECTANGULAR** combined footing — extend it until the centroid lines up |
| Loads **UNEQUAL** and **space constrained at both ends** | **TRAPEZOIDAL** — put the **wider end under the heavier column** |
| Columns **far apart** | **STRAP** footing — two pads linked by a beam |

> A trapezoid **puts more area under the heavier load** without extending further, achieving the correct centroid position within the available length. A rectangle long enough to do the same would have to project beyond the boundary.

**The geometry:**

> **A = (b₁ + b₂)L/2 = ΣP/q_allowable**
> **x̄ = (L/3)(2b₂ + b₁)/(b₁ + b₂)** from the b₁ end

> Set x̄ to place the centroid under the resultant, and solve for b₁ and b₂.

> **A trapezoid is only feasible if the resultant falls between L/3 and L/2 from the heavy end.** Outside that range a rectangle or a strap footing is needed — which is a real constraint, not a formality.

**Why the other options are wrong here:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strap footing** | For a **BOUNDARY** column whose footing cannot be centred, linked to an interior one — a different problem |
| **Raft / Mat** | The **same thing** under two names, and used when footings would cover **more than half the plan area** — a question of soil capacity, not of unequal loads |

> That **raft and mat are synonyms** is itself worth noticing: two of the four options describe the same foundation, which tells you neither is the intended answer.

**The structural surprise** in a combined footing: it spans as a **beam loaded UPWARD by the soil**, so it **hogs between the columns** and the **main steel goes in the TOP face** — the reverse of an isolated footing, and a classic detailing error.

examTip.trick: Notice that **raft and mat are the SAME foundation under two names** — two of the four options are identical, so neither can be the intended answer. That alone halves the field.
examTip.trap: A **STRAP** footing solves a different problem: a column at a **property boundary** whose footing cannot be centred. It is not about unequal loads.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wide end under the heavy column, so the centroid lands under the resultant.** And the structural surprise: a combined footing is loaded **upward by the soil**, so it **hogs** and the main steel goes in the **TOP**.

questions.stem: The weight of capillary water is held by:
questions.solution:
**Surface tension.**

**The mechanism.** At the top of a capillary column the water surface forms a **concave meniscus**. Surface tension acting around the circumference of that meniscus pulls **upward**, and it is this force that supports the weight of the water column below.

> Equating the vertical component of the surface tension force to the weight of the column:
> **σ cos θ × πd = γ × (πd²/4) × h**
> **h = 4σ cos θ/(γ d)** ✓

**The key relation:**

> **h ∝ 1/d** — the rise is **inversely proportional to the pore diameter**. A ten-times finer pore gives ten times the rise.

**Capillary rise in soils:**

| Soil | Capillary rise |
|---|---|
| Coarse sand | 0.1 – 0.15 m |
| Fine sand | 0.3 – 2 m |
| **Silt** | **1 – 10 m** |
| **Clay** | **10 m and more** |

**The three consequences that matter in soil mechanics:**

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **NEGATIVE pore pressure** above the water table | The water hangs in tension, so **u is negative** |
| **INCREASED effective stress** | **σ′ = σ − u**, and a negative u makes σ′ **exceed** σ |
| **APPARENT COHESION** in moist sand | The menisci bind the grains — the sandcastle effect |

**Apparent cohesion deserves emphasis because it is dangerous:**

> **Moist sand appears to have cohesion and will stand in a vertical cut** — but that cohesion comes **entirely from the capillary menisci between grains**. **Saturate it or dry it completely and the cohesion vanishes.**

> That is why trench collapses in sand so often follow rain, or the drying of a previously damp face.

**And frost susceptibility:**

> **SILT is the most frost-susceptible soil** — it has both a large capillary rise **and** enough permeability to feed water fast to a growing ice lens. Clay has the rise but is too impermeable; sand is permeable but has too little rise.

**Note why the distractors fail**: **cohesion** is a property of clay particles, not of water; **shear force** does not act in a static fluid at all; and while intermolecular forces underlie surface tension, the mechanism being asked for is surface tension itself.

examTip.trick: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd), so h ∝ 1/d** — fine pores, big rise. That relation explains soil capillary heights, frost susceptibility and the manometer correction all at once.
examTip.trap: "Cohesion" is tempting because capillary water produces **apparent cohesion** in sand — but that is the *effect*, not the mechanism holding the water up. The holding force is **surface tension**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Damp sand stands; saturated or bone-dry sand collapses.** The menisci are doing the work, which is why trench faces in sand fail after rain — and why **SILT** is the most frost-susceptible soil, having both the rise and the permeability.

questions.stem: What would be the effect on pH if bleaching powder is added to water?
questions.solution:
**The pH increases** — the water becomes more alkaline.

**Why.** Bleaching powder is **calcium hypochlorite, Ca(OCl)₂** (with calcium hydroxide and calcium chloride present in the commercial product). In water it hydrolyses and **releases hydroxide ions**, raising the pH.

> The calcium base content is what does it: the product is manufactured by chlorinating **slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂**, and the residual alkalinity carries into the solution.

**The disinfection chemistry, and why the pH rise matters:**

> Chlorine in water forms **HOCl (hypochlorous acid)** and **OCl⁻ (hypochlorite ion)**:

> **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**

| Species | Disinfecting power |
|---|---|
| **HOCl** | **Strong — about 80 times more effective** |
| **OCl⁻** | Much weaker |

> **Raising the pH shifts the balance toward OCl⁻**, so the disinfection becomes **less effective**. That is the practical consequence of the alkalinity.

**Hence the operating rule:**

> **Chlorinate at pH below about 7.5** where possible. Above pH 8 the required dose rises sharply for the same kill.

**Contrast with chlorine GAS**, which behaves oppositely:

| Chlorinating agent | Effect on pH |
|---|---|
| **Bleaching powder / hypochlorite** | **RAISES** pH (alkaline) |
| **Chlorine gas (Cl₂)** | **LOWERS** pH — it forms HOCl **and HCl** |

> So the two common chlorinating agents pull the pH in **opposite directions**, and the choice affects whether pH correction is needed.

**Other requirements for effective chlorination:**

| Factor | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Contact time** | At least **30 minutes** |
| **Residual** | **0.2 mg/l** free chlorine after contact |
| **Turbidity** | Must be **low** — suspended particles **shield pathogens** from the chlorine |
| Ammonia present | Forms **chloramines** — weaker but longer-lasting (combined residual) |

**The drawback of chlorination** is worth knowing: reacting with natural organic matter it forms **trihalomethanes (THMs)**, which are themselves regulated — so the dose is balanced between adequate residual and minimising by-products.

examTip.trick: Bleaching powder is made by chlorinating **slaked lime**, so it carries residual **alkalinity** into the water — hence the pH rise. Chlorine **gas** does the opposite, forming HCl as well as HOCl.
examTip.trap: The pH rise is not harmless: **HOCl is about 80× more effective than OCl⁻**, and raising the pH shifts the balance toward the weaker species. So the alkalinity **reduces** disinfection efficiency.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chlorinate below pH 7.5, 30 minutes contact, 0.2 mg/l residual — and filter FIRST**, because turbidity shields pathogens from the chlorine however large the dose.

questions.stem: The maximum permissible moisture content in bitumen is:
questions.solution:
**0.2% by weight.**

**Why the limit is so tight.** Bitumen is applied **hot** — mixing temperatures are around **150 °C**, well above the boiling point of water. Any moisture present:

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **FLASHES INTO STEAM** on heating | Violent **foaming and frothing** in the boiler |
| **Safety hazard** | Hot bitumen can boil over — a serious burn risk |
| **Poor adhesion** to aggregate | Water at the interface prevents the bond forming |
| **STRIPPING** in service | The binder peels off the aggregate under traffic and water |

> The **safety** consequence is the immediate one: a small amount of water in a hot bitumen boiler causes it to froth over, and 150 °C bitumen is extremely dangerous.

**The bitumen specification tests**, of which this is one:

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Penetration** | Hardness — in **tenths of a millimetre** (grade 60/70, 80/100) |
| **Softening point** | Temperature susceptibility — **ring and ball** test |
| **Ductility** | Ability to stretch without cracking — **minimum 50 cm** |
| **Flash and fire point** | Safety in handling |
| **Viscosity** | Mixing and laying temperatures |
| **Specific gravity** | ~0.97–1.02 |
| **Water content** | **Maximum 0.2%** |
| **Loss on heating** | Volatility |

> **No single test characterises bitumen** — a binder can pass penetration and still be unsuitable, which is why the specification lists all of them.

**STRIPPING** deserves a note because it is the failure the moisture limit ultimately guards against:

> **Stripping** is the loss of adhesion between the binder and the aggregate in the presence of water. The bitumen peels away, the mix loses cohesion, and the pavement ravels and forms potholes.

> It is worse with **hydrophilic (acidic, siliceous) aggregates** such as quartzite and granite, and better with **basic** aggregates such as limestone and basalt. Where a susceptible aggregate must be used, an **anti-stripping agent** (usually an amine) is added — or hydrated lime, which is cheaper and works well.

examTip.trick: Reason from the temperature: bitumen is handled at about **150 °C**, far above water's boiling point. Even a little water **flashes to steam** and the boiler froths over — which is why the limit is a fraction of a percent, not a percent.
examTip.trap: The values 1% and 2% look like plausible "small" numbers, but they are an order of magnitude too generous for a material heated past 100 °C.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.2% water; ductility ≥ 50 cm; penetration in TENTHS of a millimetre.** The failure the water limit guards against is **STRIPPING** — loss of binder–aggregate adhesion, worst with siliceous aggregates, cured by hydrated lime or an amine.

questions.stem: If the level is located at the mid-point between two staff stations, which error is eliminated?
questions.solution:
**Both** — curvature and refraction, and the collimation error with them.

**Why.** Each of these errors is **proportional to the sighting distance**. Setting the instrument **midway** makes the backsight and foresight distances **equal**, so the error is **identical in both readings** — and since a level reading is a **difference**, the identical parts cancel exactly.

**The three errors eliminated by balancing the sights:**

| Error | Cause | Magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| **CURVATURE** | The earth curves away from the horizontal line of sight | **+0.0785 d²** m (d in km) |
| **REFRACTION** | The line of sight bends **downward** through the atmosphere | **−0.0112 d²** m — about **1/7** of curvature, opposite sign |
| **COLLIMATION** | The line of sight is not truly horizontal | Proportional to distance |

> **Combined curvature and refraction correction = −0.0673 d²** metres, with d in kilometres.

> Note that the two act in **opposite directions** and refraction partly offsets curvature — but only partly, so a net correction remains if the sights are unbalanced.

**The rule that follows:**

> **Keep the backsight and foresight distances equal.** It is the single most effective precaution in levelling, and it costs nothing but a little care in positioning the instrument.

**What balancing does NOT remove:**

| Error | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **Staff not vertical** | Use a staff bubble; or **wave the staff** and take the minimum reading |
| **Staff graduation errors** | Calibrate the staff |
| **Settlement** of the instrument or turning point | Firm ground, change points on solid objects |
| **Bubble not centred** when reading | Check before every reading |
| Parallax | Focus the crosshairs, then the object |

**RECIPROCAL LEVELLING** is the technique for when balancing is impossible:

> Across a **river or ravine** the instrument cannot be set midway. So a reading is taken from **each bank in turn**, and the two sets are **averaged** — the errors being equal and of opposite sign in the two positions, they cancel in the mean.

**Arithmetic checks on the field book:**

| Method | Check |
|---|---|
| **Height of instrument** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** (two-part) |
| **RISE AND FALL** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** (three-part) |

> The rise-and-fall method's **extra leg** checks the intermediate sights as well, which is why it is preferred where accuracy matters despite being slower.

examTip.trick: All three errors are **proportional to sighting distance**, and a level reading is a **difference**. Equal distances mean equal errors, which cancel — so balancing the sights removes curvature, refraction **and collimation** at once.
examTip.trap: It does **not** remove staff verticality, graduation errors, instrument settlement or an off-centre bubble. Those need separate precautions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Combined correction −0.0673 d² metres (d in km)**; refraction is about **1/7 of curvature and opposite in sign**. When you cannot set up midway — across a river — use **RECIPROCAL levelling** and average both banks.

questions.stem: Any gradient on a road is said to be an exceptional gradient if it is:
options: Less than the minimum gradient or more than the maximum gradient
questions.solution:
**Outside the permitted range — less than the minimum or more than the maximum gradient.**

**The gradient hierarchy in highway design:**

| Gradient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **RULING (design) gradient** | The **normal maximum** used in design — the target for the whole alignment |
| **LIMITING gradient** | Steeper, permitted **for short stretches** where topography demands it |
| **EXCEPTIONAL gradient** | Steeper still, permitted only in **unavoidable** situations and for **very short lengths** |
| **MINIMUM gradient** | Needed for **DRAINAGE** — a road too flat does not shed water along its side drains |
| Floating gradient | The gradient on which a vehicle coasts at constant speed |

> The question defines exceptional as **outside the acceptable band at either end** — too flat to drain, or too steep to climb.

**Typical values (Nepal Road Standard / IRC), plain and rolling terrain:**

| Gradient | Value |
|---|---|
| Ruling | **3.3%** (1 in 30) |
| Limiting | 5% (1 in 20) |
| Exceptional | **6.7%** (1 in 15) |

**In mountainous and steep terrain** the values are relaxed — ruling **5%**, limiting **6%**, exceptional **7%** — reflecting what the topography actually permits.

**The minimum gradient** is easy to overlook and matters greatly:

> **1 in 200 (0.5%)** on a lined side drain and **1 in 100 (1%)** on an unlined one. Below that, water stands in the drain, infiltrates the formation, and softens the subgrade.

> **On a hill road, water does more damage than traffic** — which is why drainage governs so much of the geometry.

**GRADE COMPENSATION on curves** is the companion provision:

> A vehicle on a curve already faces **curve resistance** from tyre scrub. Adding a steep gradient makes the total resistance excessive, so the gradient is **eased**:

> **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R percent, subject to a maximum of 75/R**

> and it is **not applied on gradients flatter than 4%**, where the total resistance is not a problem.

> **Failing to compensate is why trucks stall on tight hairpin bends** — the combination of a sharp curve and a steep grade exceeds what the vehicle can pull.

**Exceptional gradients also require** a **minimum length of gentler grade** between successive steep stretches, so that a heavy vehicle can recover speed.

examTip.trick: The word **"exceptional"** means outside the acceptable band — and the band has **two ends**. Options naming only a maximum miss the drainage requirement at the flat end.
examTip.trap: The **MINIMUM** gradient is real and often forgotten: **1 in 200 lined, 1 in 100 unlined**, needed so the side drains actually flow. A road too flat is as defective as one too steep.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ruling 3.3% → limiting 5% → exceptional 6.7%** in plain terrain, relaxed in the hills. And on curves apply **grade compensation (30+R)/R, max 75/R** — its absence is why trucks stall on hairpins.

questions.stem: The design speed for a 1st class road in plain terrain is:
questions.solution:
**120 km/h.**

**The design speed table**, which is the source of the answer:

| Road class | Plain | Rolling | Mountainous | Steep |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | **120** | **100** | **80** | **60** |
| **II** | **100** | 80 | 60 | 40 |
| **III** | 80 | 60 | 40 | 30 |
| **IV** | 60 | 40 | 30 | 20 |

> The pattern is regular and worth noticing: **each step down in class, or each step up in terrain difficulty, drops the design speed by one band.** Reading the table diagonally, Class I steep (60) equals Class IV plain (60).

**What terrain class means**, defined by the **cross slope** of the ground:

| Terrain | Cross slope |
|---|---|
| **Plain** | **0 – 10%** |
| **Rolling** | 10 – 25% |
| **Mountainous** | 25 – 60% |
| **Steep** | **> 60%** |

**Why design speed matters so much**: it is the **single parameter from which almost all the geometry follows**.

| Element | Dependence on speed V |
|---|---|
| **Minimum radius** | **R = V²/(127(e + f))** — **V²** |
| **Superelevation** | e = V²/(225R) using 75% of design speed |
| **Stopping sight distance** | **vt + v²/(2gf)** — the braking term goes as **V²** |
| Overtaking sight distance | Much longer |
| **Transition curve length** | From rate of change of radial acceleration |
| Summit curve length | From sight distance, so **V²** |
| **Extra widening** (psychological term) | V/(9.5√R) |

> **Nearly every geometric element scales with V or V².** So raising the design speed by 25% roughly **halves** the permissible curvature and lengthens every sight distance — which is why design speed is chosen carefully and not optimistically.

**A practical caution**: the **design speed is not the speed limit**. The design speed is what the geometry is built to accommodate safely; the **speed limit** is set operationally from the **85th percentile** observed speed. The two are chosen by different bodies for different purposes and need not agree.

examTip.trick: The table is regular: **each step down in class OR up in terrain difficulty drops the speed one band.** Class I plain is the top of the table at 120, and Class IV steep the bottom at 20.
examTip.trap: **Design speed is not the speed limit.** The geometry is built for the design speed; the limit is set from the **85th percentile** observed speed, by a different authority for a different purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Terrain by CROSS SLOPE: plain 0–10%, rolling 10–25%, mountainous 25–60%, steep >60%.** And nearly every geometric element scales with **V or V²** — which is why design speed drives the whole alignment.

questions.stem: A sinking fund is:
options: The fund for rebuilding a structure when its economic life is over
The total sum to be paid to the municipal authorities by the tenants
A part of the money kept in reserve for providing additional structures and structural modifications
questions.solution:
**A fund accumulated to rebuild or replace a structure when its economic life is over.**

**How it works.** A **uniform annual amount** is set aside, and it **accumulates at compound interest** so that the total at the end of the asset's life equals the replacement cost.

> **A = (F × i)/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]**

where A is the annual deposit, F the amount required, i the interest rate and n the life in years.

> The **sinking fund factor** is the bracketed expression, and it is one of the standard compound interest factors.

**The three depreciation methods compared:**

| Method | How it writes off value |
|---|---|
| **Straight line** | An **equal AMOUNT** each year: **(C − S)/n** — simplest |
| **Declining balance** | A fixed **PERCENTAGE** each year — depreciates **faster early on**, which is closest to how plant actually loses value |
| **SINKING FUND** | A uniform annual deposit **accumulating at interest** to the replacement cost |

> The sinking fund method is the only one that explicitly **provides the money** rather than merely recording the loss of value — which is why it is used in valuation and in lease agreements.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| "To meet maintenance costs" | **Maintenance** is a recurring annual expense, funded from income — not a sinking fund |
| "Paid to municipal authorities" | That is **rates or taxes** |
| "Reserve for additional structures" | That is a **capital reserve** or contingency, for expansion rather than replacement |

> The discriminator is **replacement at end of life**, not upkeep during it.

**Related valuation terms** worth holding together:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Scrap value** | Value of the **dismantled materials** — about 10% of cost |
| **Salvage value** | Value of the asset **still standing and usable** |
| **Book value** | Original cost less accumulated depreciation |
| **Year's purchase (YP)** | **100/rate of interest** — the multiplier on net annual income |
| **Capitalised value** | **Net annual income × YP** |

> **A lower interest rate gives a HIGHER year's purchase and a higher valuation** — which is why property values rise when interest rates fall.

examTip.trap: "To meet maintenance costs" is the natural wrong answer. **Maintenance is a recurring expense funded from income**; a sinking fund is for **REPLACEMENT at the end of life**. That distinction is the whole question.
examTip.trick: The sinking fund is unique among the depreciation methods in that it **actually provides the money**, rather than merely recording the loss of value on paper.
examTip.mnemonic: **A = Fi/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1].** Keep the family straight: **straight line** (equal amount), **declining balance** (fixed percentage, faster early), **sinking fund** (deposits accumulating at interest).

questions.stem: In Bernoulli's equation, each term represents:
options: Total energy per unit flow area
questions.solution:
**Energy per unit WEIGHT** — which is why every term has the dimensions of a **length**.

> **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant**

| Term | Name | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **p/γ** | **Pressure head** | metres |
| **V²/2g** | **Velocity (kinetic) head** | metres |
| **z** | **Elevation (potential) head** | metres |

**Check the dimensions:** **p/γ = (N/m²)/(N/m³) = m** ✓, and **V²/2g = (m²/s²)/(m/s²) = m** ✓

**The three forms of the same equation:**

| Divided by | Form | Units of each term |
|---|---|---|
| **Weight** | **p/γ + V²/2g + z** | **metres (HEAD)** |
| Mass | p/ρ + V²/2 + gz | J/kg |
| Volume | p + ρV²/2 + ρgz | Pa (pressure) |

> The **head** form is used almost universally in civil engineering, because every term becomes a **length that can be DRAWN** — which gives the **hydraulic grade line (HGL)** and the **energy grade line (EGL)**.

**HGL and EGL properties:**

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **EGL is always ABOVE the HGL** by **V²/2g** | The gap is the velocity head |
| **EGL always FALLS** in the direction of flow | Friction — unless a pump adds energy |
| **HGL may RISE** where the pipe expands | Velocity head converts back to pressure |
| HGL **coincides with the water surface** in an open channel | Since p = 0 there |
| **HGL below the pipe** | **NEGATIVE pressure** — risk of air ingress and contamination |

**Bernoulli's assumptions**, all of which matter:

> **Steady, incompressible, frictionless (inviscid) flow along a streamline**, with no energy added or removed.

**The extended form** is what is actually used:

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L**

**And the caution about where it fails:**

> Bernoulli must **not** be applied across a region of **large, unknown loss** — a sudden expansion, or a **hydraulic jump**. There the **MOMENTUM** equation is used instead, precisely because it does not require the losses to be quantified.

examTip.trick: **Every term is a LENGTH**, so the equation must be energy per unit **weight** (energy ÷ force = length). Checking the units of p/γ settles it in one step.
examTip.trap: All four options are grammatically plausible and three describe real normalisations — per mass gives J/kg, per volume gives pascals. Only **per weight** gives metres.
examTip.mnemonic: **Head form because it can be DRAWN** — the HGL and EGL. **EGL always falls; HGL may rise where the pipe expands; HGL below the pipe means negative pressure** and the risk of drawing contamination in.

questions.stem: Variability in the rate of return is known as:
questions.solution:
**Risk.**

**In financial and engineering economics, risk is defined as the VARIABILITY of the outcome** — the extent to which the actual return may differ from the expected one. It is measured by the **standard deviation** or **variance** of the returns.

> **Risk is not "the chance of losing money"** but the **dispersion** of possible outcomes, in both directions.

**The terms distinguished:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Return** | The **gain** itself — the expected or realised value |
| **RISK** | The **VARIABILITY** of that return |
| **Interest** | The **price of money** over time |
| **Volatility** | A **measure** of risk (usually the standard deviation) — closely related, but it is the metric rather than the concept |

> Option (d), volatility, is the near-miss: it is how risk is **quantified**, not what the variability **is called**. In a strict reading the concept is risk and the measure is volatility.

**The fundamental relationship:**

> **Higher risk demands higher expected return.** No rational investor accepts more variability without compensation.

| Investment | Risk | Expected return |
|---|---|---|
| Government bonds | **Lowest** | Lowest |
| Debentures / secured debt | Low | Low |
| **Preference shares** | Medium | Medium |
| **Ordinary (equity) shares** | **HIGHEST** | Highest |

> The ordering follows the **claim priority in a liquidation**: debt is paid first, preference shares next, and **equity last** — which is precisely why equity carries the most risk and commands the highest return.

**How risk enters an engineering economic decision:**

| Method | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Risk-adjusted discount rate** | Add a **risk premium** to the MARR |
| **Sensitivity analysis** | Vary one input at a time and see how the NPV moves |
| **Scenario analysis** | Best case, expected case, worst case |
| **Expected value** | Σ(probability × outcome) |
| **Monte Carlo simulation** | Sample the input distributions repeatedly |

> **Sensitivity analysis is the most used in practice**, because it identifies **which assumption the decision actually turns on** — and that is usually more valuable than a single probability-weighted number.

**Risk versus uncertainty** is a distinction worth knowing: **RISK** is where the probabilities are **known or estimable**; **UNCERTAINTY** is where they are not. Most large infrastructure decisions involve genuine uncertainty rather than measurable risk, which is why judgement remains essential.

examTip.trap: **Volatility** is the near-miss — it is the **MEASURE** of risk (the standard deviation), not the name of the concept. The question asks what the variability *is called*.
examTip.trick: Risk is **dispersion in BOTH directions**, not just the chance of loss. That is why it is measured by a standard deviation rather than a probability of failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Higher risk demands higher return**, and the ordering follows **claim priority in liquidation**: debt → preference shares → equity last, which is why equity is riskiest. And keep **RISK (probabilities known)** apart from **UNCERTAINTY (they are not)**.

questions.stem: The applicability of the middle third rule, used in the design of structures under combined direct and bending stresses, is:
options: Feasible to circular cross sections only
Feasible to square and circular cross sections only
questions.solution:
**Feasible to rectangular cross-sections only.**

**Why.** The "middle third" is a result **specific to the rectangle**. It comes from:

> **σ = (P/A)(1 ± 6e/d)**, and setting the minimum stress to zero gives **e ≤ d/6**

> The **6** in that expression is a property of the rectangular section's geometry (Z = bd²/6). A different shape gives a different fraction.

**The general concept is the KERN (or core)** — the region within which the load must act for the **whole section to remain in compression**. Its shape and size depend on the section:

| Section | Kern | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × d** | A **RHOMBUS** with diagonals **b/3 and d/3** | **e ≤ d/6** — the middle **third** |
| **Circle diameter D** | A **CIRCLE** of diameter **D/4** | **e ≤ D/8** — the middle **quarter** |
| Hollow circular | A larger circle | Bigger kern |
| I-section | A complex shape | — |

> **So for a circle it is the middle QUARTER, not the middle third.** The rule as stated — "middle third" — belongs to the rectangle alone, which is what makes option (c) correct and (d) wrong.

**Note that hollow sections have a LARGER kern** relative to their size, because their material is further from the centroid — a genuinely useful property for chimneys and hollow piers, which can tolerate more eccentricity than a solid section of the same outside dimension.

**The stress states for a rectangle:**

| Eccentricity | Distribution | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **e = 0** | Uniform P/A | Full |
| **0 < e < d/6** | **Trapezoidal**, all compression | Full |
| **e = d/6** | **Triangular**, zero at one edge | Full, just |
| **e > d/6** | **TENSION develops; the section lifts off** | **Partial** |

> Beyond the limit the contact width reduces to **x = 3(d/2 − e)** and the maximum stress becomes **2P/(3bx)**.

**Why the limit is enforced rather than merely advised:**

> Once part of the base lifts off, the **contact area shrinks**, so the **resultant moves further toward the edge**, which **reduces the contact further**. The process is **PROGRESSIVE**, and progressive instability is a different matter from a section merely being overstressed.

**Where it governs:** **masonry** columns and walls, **GRAVITY DAMS** (where a crack at the heel would admit full reservoir pressure and propagate), retaining wall bases, and footings on soil. It does **not** apply to **reinforced** sections, where the steel carries the tension.

examTip.trap: "Feasible to all cross sections" is the tempting generalisation. It is wrong: for a **CIRCLE the limit is the middle QUARTER (e ≤ D/8)**, not the middle third. The "third" belongs to the rectangle alone.
examTip.trick: The **6** in σ = (P/A)(1 ± 6e/d) comes from the rectangle's **Z = bd²/6**. A different section has a different Z and therefore a different fraction.
examTip.mnemonic: **The general concept is the KERN: a RHOMBUS for a rectangle, a CIRCLE of D/4 for a circle.** Hollow sections have a **larger** kern — useful for chimneys and hollow piers. And it does not apply to **reinforced** sections at all.

questions.stem: What is the main function of a weir and barrage?
questions.solution:
**To raise the water level upstream**, so that water can be diverted into a canal by gravity.

**The purpose in full:**

> A river's natural water level is usually **too low** to command the land to be irrigated. A weir or barrage **raises the upstream level (the pond level)** so that water flows into the offtaking canal under gravity — with no pumping.

> **It is a DIVERSION structure, not a storage structure.** It creates a small pond, not a reservoir.

**Weir versus barrage** — the distinction the examiner usually wants:

| | **WEIR** | **BARRAGE** |
|---|---|---|
| Crest | **Mostly solid**, raised | **Low**, with **gates over most of its length** |
| Pond level controlled by | The **crest height** — fixed | **GATE OPERATION** — adjustable |
| Afflux and upstream submergence | **Fixed**, and higher | **Controlled**; gates can be opened in a flood |
| Cost | Lower | Higher |
| Operating staff | Not needed | Required |
| Silt control | Poorer | Better — gates can flush |
| Road across | Difficult | Usually incorporated |

> **Barrages are almost always preferred on large alluvial rivers**, because the gates let the flood pass with far less upstream flooding, and because they permit silt to be flushed.

**The components of a diversion headworks:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Weir or barrage** | Raises the level |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | Separates the under-sluice pocket from the weir bays |
| **Under-sluices** | Flush accumulated silt; pass low flows |
| **Head regulator** | Controls flow **into the canal** |
| **SILT EXCLUDER** | Stops silt **entering** the canal |
| **Fish ladder** | Allows fish migration |
| **Guide banks** | Confine the river; prevent outflanking |
| Launching apron | Protects against scour |

> **Silt excluder and silt ejector are different structures** and are constantly swapped: the **excluder** sits at the head regulator and stops silt **entering**; the **ejector** sits **inside the canal** and removes silt that has **already entered**. Prevention versus cure.

**Design of the floor** against seepage is the other major consideration: **Bligh's creep theory** (which wrongly weighted vertical and horizontal creep equally), **Lane's weighted creep** (vertical counted three times), and **KHOSLA's theory**, which solved the actual potential flow and showed that safety depends on the **EXIT GRADIENT** and on a **downstream cut-off** rather than on total creep length.

examTip.trick: A weir or barrage is a **DIVERSION** structure, not a storage one — it raises the level so a canal can draw by gravity. It creates a pond, never a reservoir.
examTip.trap: **Weir versus barrage**: a weir's pond level is fixed by its **crest**; a barrage's is controlled by **GATES**, so its upstream flooding can be released in a flood. That is why barrages dominate on large alluvial rivers.
examTip.mnemonic: **Silt EXCLUDER excludes at the entrance; silt EJECTOR ejects from within the canal.** Prevention versus cure — and the two are swapped constantly.

questions.stem: Cross regulators are provided:
options: To raise the water level to its upstream during periods of low discharge in the parent channel
To help in closing the supply to the downstream of the parent channel
To absorb fluctuations in various sections of the channel systems
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — a cross regulator serves all three purposes.

**What it is.** A cross regulator is a gated structure built **ACROSS the parent canal**, just **downstream of an offtake**. By closing its gates it **raises the water level upstream of itself**, which is exactly what the offtaking channel needs in order to draw its full supply.

**Its three functions:**

| Function | How |
|---|---|
| **Raise the upstream level** during low discharge | Partly closing the gates ponds the water so the offtake can draw |
| **Close the supply downstream** | Fully closing the gates isolates the reach for maintenance |
| **Absorb fluctuations** in the system | The gates are adjusted to balance the distribution between reaches |

> A fourth, incidental benefit: it usually carries a **road bridge** across the canal.

**Cross regulator versus HEAD regulator** — the pairing that must be kept apart:

| | **CROSS regulator** | **HEAD regulator** |
|---|---|---|
| Located | **ACROSS the parent canal** | At the **head of the offtaking canal** |
| Controls | The **parent** canal's level and flow | The flow **INTO the distributary** |
| Purpose | Raise the level so the offtake can draw | Regulate and measure what the offtake takes |

> **They work as a pair**, built together at every major offtake: the cross regulator provides the head, and the head regulator controls how much is taken.

**The other canal structures**, for contrast:

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Escape** | Discharge **surplus water OUT** of the canal — protects the banks when demand drops suddenly |
| **Fall** | Take the bed down a step where the **ground falls faster than the canal's design slope** |
| **Outlet** | Deliver water from a minor to a watercourse |
| **Cross-drainage works** | Carry the canal past a natural drain |

**The four cross-drainage works** are worth holding since they are easily scrambled — name them by **which one goes over**:

| Structure | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **Canal over drain**; drain flows free |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | Canal over drain; **drain runs under pressure** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **Drain over canal**; canal free |
| **CANAL SYPHON** | Drain over canal; **canal under pressure** |

> **"Aqueduct" always means the CANAL is on top; add "syphon" when the thing underneath is pressurised.**

examTip.trap: **Cross regulator and head regulator** are constantly swapped. The **cross** regulator sits **ACROSS the parent canal**; the **head** regulator sits at the **head of the offtake**. They are built as a pair at every major offtake.
examTip.trick: On an "all of the above" question, read every option — here all three are genuine functions, and stopping at the first plausible one loses the mark.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cross regulator holds the LEVEL UP so the offtake can draw.** And for cross-drainage works: **"aqueduct" always means the CANAL is on top; add "syphon" when the thing underneath is pressurised.**

questions.stem: The Froude number value for a steady hydraulic jump is:
questions.solution:
**4.5 to 9.**

**The USBR classification of hydraulic jumps by approach Froude number:**

| Fr₁ | Type | Character | Energy loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1.0 – 1.7** | **Undular** | A train of small surface waves | < 5% |
| **1.7 – 2.5** | **Weak** | Smooth surface rollers | 5 – 15% |
| **2.5 – 4.5** | **OSCILLATING** | An **unstable jet oscillating** between bed and surface — **generates waves that travel far downstream** | 15 – 45% |
| **4.5 – 9.0** | **STEADY** | **Well balanced and stable — the BEST for a stilling basin** | **45 – 70%** |
| **> 9.0** | **Strong** | Very effective but the surface is rough and choppy | 70 – 85% |

**Why the steady range is the design target:**

> It gives **good energy dissipation (45–70%)** in a **stable, predictable** jump whose position can be relied on — which is exactly what a stilling basin needs.

**And why the OSCILLATING range must be avoided:**

> Its **unstable jet oscillates between the bed and the surface**, generating **surface waves that propagate a long way downstream**, eroding banks and damaging structures. A basin designed to operate in this range performs badly **however well it is built**.

> Where the Froude number cannot be raised out of that band, **baffle blocks** are used to force the jump to stabilise.

**The jump relations:**

> **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]** — the conjugate (sequent) depths, from **MOMENTUM**
> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂)** — the energy loss
> **Length ≈ 5 to 7 × y₂** (commonly 6y₂) — **empirical**, since no theory predicts it

**The design risk that governs a stilling basin:**

| Tailwater | Jump behaviour | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Too LOW** | The jump **SWEEPS OUT** downstream | High-velocity flow escapes onto **erodible bed** — the apron is undermined |
| **Correct** | Forms within the basin | Energy dissipated where intended |
| **Too HIGH** | The jump is **DROWNED** | Poor dissipation; the fast jet dives along the bed |

> **Sweep-out is what destroys spillway aprons**, and it typically occurs not at the design flood but at some **intermediate discharge**, where the tailwater rating curve and the required conjugate depth diverge most. The basin must therefore be checked **across the full range** of operating discharges.

**The remedies**: a **depressed basin floor** (creating the required tailwater locally), an **end sill**, **baffle blocks**, and **chute blocks** at the entrance. The USBR Types I–IV and IS 4997 codify these arrangements for different Froude ranges.

examTip.trick: Remember the two that matter and the rest follow: **4.5–9 is STEADY (the design target)** and **2.5–4.5 is OSCILLATING (to be avoided)**. Undular and weak are below, strong is above.
examTip.trap: The oscillating range is not merely "less good" — its **unstable jet throws waves far downstream**, eroding banks. A basin designed in that band fails however well it is built.
examTip.mnemonic: **Length ≈ 6 y₂, and the TAILWATER must actually supply y₂.** If it does not, the jump **sweeps out** of the paved basin and undermines it — usually at an intermediate discharge, not at the design flood.

questions.stem: The lowest edge of the sloping surface of a roof is called the:
questions.solution:
**The eaves.**

**The parts of a pitched roof, by position:**

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **RIDGE** | The **highest** point — the horizontal line where two slopes meet |
| **EAVES** | The **LOWEST edge** of the slope, usually overhanging the wall |
| **Rafters** | The **inclined members** running from ridge down to eaves |
| **Pitch** | The **slope** of the roof — a ratio (1:4) or an angle |
| Purlins | Horizontal members spanning between trusses, supporting the rafters |
| Hip | An external sloping intersection of two roof surfaces |
| Valley | An internal intersection — where water collects |
| Verge | The edge at a gable |
| Fascia | The board fixed at the eaves, carrying the gutter |

> **Ridge at the top, eaves at the bottom** — the two extremes of the slope, and the pair the question turns on.

**What the eaves do:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Throw rainwater CLEAR of the wall** | The overhang is the point |
| Carry the **gutter** | Fixed to the fascia board |
| **Shade** the wall and windows | Significant in a warm climate |
| Protect the wall head from driving rain | — |

> **The overhang is not decoration.** Water running down a wall is the commonest cause of damp in a building, and a generous eaves overhang is the cheapest defence against it — particularly in Nepal's monsoon.

**Roof pitch and its consequences:**

| Pitch | Note |
|---|---|
| **Steep** | Sheds water and snow well; needs more material; **snow load reduced** (above about 60° it is taken as zero) |
| **Flat** | Less material; needs a reliable membrane; **ponding risk** |

**Truss spans** are the companion fact:

| Truss | Economical span |
|---|---|
| **King post** | up to **8 m** — one central vertical |
| **Queen post** | **8 – 12 m** — two verticals |
| Mansard, truncated | Greater |

> **One king to 8, two queens to 12.** The queen post spans further precisely because its two verticals divide the span.

**A caution on truss members**: in a **PRATT** truss the long **diagonals are in TENSION** and the short verticals take the compression — putting the buckling problem in the shortest members, which is why Pratt suits steel. The **HOWE** is the reverse and suited timber, which is strong in compression along the grain.

examTip.trick: **Ridge at the top, EAVES at the bottom.** The other two options are not positions at all — **rafters** are members and **pitch** is a slope, so they can be eliminated on category alone.
examTip.trap: "Eves" is often mis-spelled in papers (as in this source). It is **eaves**, and the overhang is functional — throwing water clear of the wall is the cheapest damp defence there is.
examTip.mnemonic: **King post to 8 m, queen post to 12 m.** And **PRATT puts the long diagonals in TENSION** (good for steel); **HOWE** is the reverse and suited timber.
