questions.stem: The locus of the reaction of a two-hinged semi-circular arch is:
questions.solution:
**A straight line**, parallel to the line joining the abutments and at a height of **πR/2** above it.

**What the "locus of reaction" means.** As a unit load moves across the arch, the **line of action of the support reaction** changes direction. The **locus** is the curve traced by the point where those successive reaction lines intersect a fixed reference — and for a two-hinged **semicircular** arch that locus is a **straight horizontal line**.

> **Height of the locus above the springing line = πR/2 ≈ 1.571 R**

**The comparison worth holding:**

| Arch | Locus of reaction |
|---|---|
| **Two-hinged SEMICIRCULAR** | **Straight line** at πR/2 |
| **Two-hinged PARABOLIC** | A **curve** |

> That the semicircular case gives a straight line is a genuinely useful simplification — it makes the graphical determination of reactions straightforward for that geometry.

**The wider arch context**, which is what the question is really testing:

| Arch | D_s | Horizontal thrust from |
|---|---|---|
| **Three-hinged** | **0 — determinate** | **Statics: H = M_crown/rise** |
| **Two-hinged** | **1** | **Strain energy: H = ∫My ds/EI ÷ ∫y² ds/EI** |
| **Fixed** | **3** | Full indeterminate analysis |

**The arch equation that governs all three:**

> **M_arch = M_beam − H y**

> The horizontal thrust **subtracts** from what the bending moment would otherwise be — and that subtraction is the whole structural virtue of an arch.

**For the FUNICULAR shape the subtraction is exact:**

| Loading | Ideal shape | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **UDL on the horizontal projection** | **PARABOLA** | **M = 0 everywhere** |
| **Self-weight along the arch** | **CATENARY** | M = 0 everywhere |

> Which is why **masonry**, unable to carry tension, spans so far as an arch and not at all as a beam.

**The two-hinged arch's sensitivities** are worth knowing, since they are what distinguishes it from the three-hinged form:

| Effect | Direction |
|---|---|
| **Temperature RISE** | **Increases** H |
| **Rib shortening** | Decreases H |
| **Abutment yielding (spread)** | **Decreases** H substantially |

> A **three-hinged** arch is **immune to all of them**, being determinate — which is the real reason for the third hinge, not the easier arithmetic.

examTip.trick: The **semicircular** arch is the special case that gives a **straight** locus, at height **πR/2**. A two-hinged **parabolic** arch gives a curve — so the shape named in the question is doing real work.
examTip.trap: "Circle" is offered because the arch itself is semicircular. The locus of the **reaction** is a different curve from the arch's own geometry.
examTip.mnemonic: **M_arch = M_beam − Hy** — the thrust subtracts the beam moment away. And a **three-hinged** arch is immune to temperature, rib shortening and abutment spread; a **two-hinged** one is not.

questions.stem: The capacity of an irrigation channel is fixed based on:
options: Cultivable command area and water transmission losses
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

**The design capacity of a canal:**

> **Q = (Duty of water at the canal outlet, including all losses) × CCA ÷ (time factor × capacity factor)**

**Each term explained:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CCA** — culturable command area | The area that **can actually be irrigated** — gross command area less unculturable land |
| **Duty** | Area irrigated **per cumec** of discharge over the base period. A **HIGHER duty means LESS water per hectare** |
| **Time factor** | Actual operating period of the canal ÷ crop period |
| **Capacity factor** | Mean supply discharge ÷ designed full capacity |
| **Transmission losses** | Seepage and evaporation between the headworks and the field |

**The relation between duty, delta and base period:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B/D** metres, with B in days and D in hectares per cumec

> The **8.64** comes from **86 400 seconds per day ÷ 10 000 m² per hectare**.

> **Note the inverse relation: a HIGHER duty means LESS water per hectare**, so a high duty signals an **efficient** system, not a thirsty one. That reads backwards to many candidates.

**The critical design point — GROSS versus NET:**

> The canal must be sized for the **GROSS** irrigation requirement, which is the net crop requirement **divided by the efficiencies**:

> **η_overall = η_conveyance × η_application**

> Efficiencies **MULTIPLY**, never average. Two stages at 70% give **49%**, not 70% — so the gross requirement can be **1.5 to 2 times** the net. Sizing on the net figure guarantees a scheme that cannot deliver.

**And the peak, not the average, governs:**

> The canal must carry the **maximum peak demand of all the crops** requiring water at any one time — which is what the **kor depth and kor period** describe. **Outlet discharge factor = 8.64B/Δ** using the kor values gives the peak capacity directly.

**Lining the canal** improves the conveyance efficiency, and its benefits compound: less seepage (so more command area from the same headworks), a **higher permissible velocity** (so a smaller section), **no weed growth**, and **no waterlogging** of adjacent land from seepage.

examTip.trick: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY, never average.** Two stages at 70% give **49%** overall — which is why the gross requirement can be twice the net, and why sizing on the net figure guarantees a scheme that cannot deliver.
examTip.trap: **A HIGHER duty means LESS water per hectare** — the relation is inverse, and it reads backwards to most candidates. A high duty is a sign of efficiency, not of thirst.
examTip.mnemonic: **Δ = 8.64 B/D**, where 8.64 = 86 400 s/day ÷ 10 000 m²/ha. And size the canal for the **PEAK** demand (kor depth over the kor period), not the seasonal average.

questions.stem: The Vice President of the Nepal Engineering Council is:
options: Nominated by the Government of Nepal
questions.solution:
**Nominated by the Government of Nepal.**

**The Council's composition (21 members) under the NEC Act 2055:**

| Position | Number | How appointed | Qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chairman / President** | 1 | **Nominated by GoN** | Bachelor's + **15 years** |
| **Vice-Chairman / VP** | 1 | **Nominated by GoN** | Bachelor's + **10 years** |
| Members | 7 | **Nominated by GoN** — one from each province, **at least three women** | Bachelor's + 7 years |
| President of the NEA | 1 | **Ex officio** | — |
| Members | 5 | **ELECTED from the NEA** | — |
| Campus chief of an engineering campus | 1 | Nominated by GoN | — |
| Representative, Institute of Engineering (TU) | 1 | Nominated by GoN | — |
| Representative of universities teaching engineering | 1 | Nominated by GoN | — |
| **Members** | **2** | **NOMINATED BY THE COUNCIL ITSELF** — at least one woman | Bachelor's + 7 years |
| **Member Secretary (Registrar)** | 1 | — | Bachelor's + **10 years** |

**The four numbers most often asked:**

> **Chairman 15 years, Vice-Chairman 10 years, Registrar 10 years — and TWO members nominated by the Council itself.**

**The three appointment routes** are the discriminator in this question:

| Route | Who |
|---|---|
| **Nominated by the Government** | Chairman, VP, 7 provincial members, the three academic representatives |
| **ELECTED from the NEA** | **5 members** |
| **Nominated by the Council itself** | **2 members** |

> Only **five** members are elected, and the VP is not among them.

**Other Act facts worth carrying:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulations** | **2057 BS** |
| First Registrar | Er. Bindeshwar Yadav |
| Minimum average for institutional affiliation | **70%** |

**And the standing distinction** that answers most institutional questions:

> **The COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION represents.** Registration with the **NEC is a legal requirement to practise**; membership of the **NEA is voluntary**.

examTip.trick: Learn the **three appointment routes**: nominated by **GoN** (chairman, VP, provincial and academic members), **ELECTED from the NEA** (5 only), and nominated by the **Council itself** (2 only). The VP is a government nomination.
examTip.trap: "Elected" is tempting because five members genuinely are elected — but they are the **NEA representatives**, not the office-holders.
examTip.mnemonic: **Chairman 15 years, VP 10 years, Registrar 10 years, and TWO nominated by the Council itself.** Act **2055**, Regulations **2057** — the numbers that recur every sitting.

questions.stem: Which type of canal does not need cross drainage structures?
questions.solution:
**Both the side slope canal and the watershed canal.**

**The three canal alignments:**

| Alignment | Runs along | Cross-drainage works |
|---|---|---|
| **WATERSHED (ridge) canal** | The **ridge line** — the high ground between two drainage basins | **NONE** — every stream flows **away** on either side |
| **SIDE SLOPE canal** | **Parallel to the natural drainage**, along the slope | **NONE** — it runs with the drainage, not across it |
| **CONTOUR canal** | Along a **contour**, across the fall of the land | **MANY** — it crosses every natural drain |

> Both the ridge canal and the side slope canal avoid cross-drainage works, for different geometric reasons — which is why the answer is "both".

**The watershed canal is the preferred alignment** wherever the topography permits:

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No cross-drainage works** | A very large saving — aqueducts and syphons are expensive |
| **Commands land on BOTH sides** | Twice the command from one canal |
| No drainage crosses it | Nothing to interrupt supply |

> Its cost is a **long lead** — the canal must first climb from the headworks to the ridge, and that reach commands nothing.

**The contour canal reaches its command quickly** but pays for it with a cross-drainage structure at every stream — and it commands land on **one side only**, since the ground rises on the other.

**The four cross-drainage works**, named by **which one goes over**:

| Structure | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **Canal over drain**; drain flows free |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | Canal over drain; **drain under pressure** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **Drain over canal**; canal free |
| **CANAL SYPHON** | Drain over canal; **canal under pressure** |

> **"Aqueduct" always means the CANAL is on top. Add "syphon" when the thing underneath runs under pressure.**

> A **level crossing** (both at the same level, with regulators) is the fifth arrangement, used where the drain is large and the canal small — but it mixes drainage water with irrigation supply and is avoided where possible.

**Choosing the alignment** is one of the first decisions in canal design, and it sets the cost of the whole scheme. In Nepal's Terai the ridge alignment is often achievable; in the hills a contour canal with numerous crossings is usually unavoidable.

examTip.trick: Ask **which way the streams run relative to the canal**. Along a **ridge** they flow away on both sides; along a **side slope** the canal runs with them. Only a **contour** canal cuts across them.
examTip.trap: "Watershed canal" alone is the tempting single answer — but the **side slope** canal also avoids cross-drainage works, which is why the correct option is "both".
examTip.mnemonic: **Ridge canal: no CD works AND commands both sides — but a long lead to reach the ridge.** For the crossings: **"aqueduct" means the CANAL is on top; add "syphon" when the thing underneath is pressurised.**

questions.stem: A submerged intake is located at:
questions.solution:
**At the bottom of the river** — the whole structure lies **below the water surface**.

**What a submerged intake is.** A structure built **entirely under water**, on the bed, drawing water through a screened opening into a conduit. Nothing projects above the surface.

**Its advantages:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No obstruction to navigation or to floating debris** | Nothing projects into the flow |
| **Not damaged by floods, ice or floating timber** | It is out of the way of everything the river carries on its surface |
| No superstructure to build or maintain | Cheaper |
| Unobtrusive | — |

**Its disadvantages, which are serious:**

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Draws from the BED, where the sediment concentration is HIGHEST** | The fundamental objection |
| **Cannot be inspected or cleaned** without dewatering or diving | Maintenance is difficult |
| Screens clog and cannot be seen to clog | — |
| No control over the draw-off level | Cannot select the cleanest layer |

> **The sediment problem is the decisive one for a hydropower or water supply intake**, because sediment concentration **increases sharply toward the bed**.

**Which is why an exposed SIDE intake is generally preferred where it is feasible:**

> A side intake **draws from the upper layer**, which carries the **least sediment** — and it can be placed on the **OUTSIDE of a river bend**, where the **secondary (helical) current sweeps the bed load toward the inside** and leaves the cleaner water at the outer bank.

> **That single siting decision removes more sediment than any downstream structure**, and it costs nothing.

**Why sediment matters so much in a Nepali context:**

> Himalayan rivers carry very heavy sediment loads, and **quartz sand ERODES turbine runners fast** — a Pelton needle or a Francis runner can lose its profile in a single monsoon.

**The sediment defences, in order along the water's path:**

| Structure | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Intake siting** (outer bank, surface draw) | The most, for free |
| **Trash rack** | Floating debris, branches |
| **GRAVEL TRAP** | Coarse **bed load** — rolling stones |
| **SETTLING (desilting) BASIN** | Finer **suspended** sand |
| Flushing arrangements | Removes what has settled |

> **Coarse first, fine second** — a settling basin cannot handle boulders, which is why the gravel trap comes before it.

examTip.trick: The name says it: **submerged** means the whole structure sits below water — on the **bed**. Its advantage is being out of the way of floods and debris; its cost is drawing from where the **sediment is worst**.
examTip.trap: Being unobtrusive and flood-proof sounds ideal, but a submerged intake **cannot be inspected or cleaned** without dewatering, and its screens clog unseen.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sediment concentration is HIGHEST at the bed.** So a side intake drawing from the **surface**, on the **OUTSIDE of a bend** (where the helical current sweeps bed load to the inside), removes more sediment than any structure downstream.

questions.stem: An abrupt change in the bending moment diagram occurs if ……… is applied.
questions.solution:
**A couple** — an applied moment produces a **step (jump) in the bending moment diagram**.

**Why.** Consider a short element containing the applied couple:

> **Vertical equilibrium**: a couple applies **no net vertical force**, so the **shear is unchanged** across it.
> **Moment equilibrium**: the couple must be balanced, so the **bending moment steps by exactly its magnitude**.

**The contrast with a point load** is the whole point, and it is a standard examination discriminator:

| Applied | Shear force diagram | Bending moment diagram |
|---|---|---|
| **POINT LOAD W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** — the slope changes, but the value is continuous |
| **COUPLE M** | **NO change** | **JUMPS by M** |

> **A point load jumps the shear and kinks the moment; a couple does nothing to the shear and jumps the moment.** They are exact opposites.

**The complete table of diagram behaviour:**

| Feature | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| Free end | V = 0 | M = 0 |
| **Simply supported end** | V = reaction | **M = 0** |
| **Fixed end** | V = reaction | **M = fixing moment** |
| **Internal hinge** | — | **M = 0** |
| Point load | **Jump** | Kink |
| **Couple** | **Nothing** | **Jump** |
| UDL | Linear | Parabolic |
| Unloaded span | Constant | Linear |

**Where applied couples actually arise:**

| Situation | Source |
|---|---|
| A **BRACKET or corbel** framing into a beam | The eccentric load resolves into a **force PLUS a couple** |
| A column framing eccentrically | Eccentric axial load |
| Torsion transferred from a secondary beam | — |
| A crane bracket on a column | The classic case |

**The bracket case is the everyday one, and getting it right matters:**

> A load **P at eccentricity e** is statically equivalent to **P acting on the axis PLUS a couple Pe**. **Both must be applied.** Analysing only the transferred force understates the moment — a genuine and common error in the design of brackets, corbels and eccentric connections.

**The governing relations** behind the whole table:

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx** — so the shear is the **slope** of the moment diagram, and **V = 0 marks a moment peak**. The **change in M equals the AREA of the shear diagram**, which is the fastest way to draw a BMD by hand.

examTip.trick: Reason from equilibrium: a couple has **no net vertical force**, so the shear cannot change — but the moment must step to balance it. A point load is the exact reverse.
examTip.trap: "Shear force" is offered because a point load **does** jump the shear diagram. But a jump in the **BMD** needs a moment, not a force.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load: jumps V, kinks M. Couple: nothing to V, jumps M.** And remember where couples come from in practice — a **bracket** load P at eccentricity e is **P plus a couple Pe**, and both must be applied.

questions.stem: Prandtl's mixing length is:
options: Independent of radial distance from the pipe axis
questions.solution:
**Zero at the pipe wall.**

**What the mixing length is.** Prandtl modelled turbulent momentum transfer by analogy with the mean free path of a gas: a **mixing length ℓ** is the distance a fluid parcel travels before it loses its identity and mixes with its surroundings.

> **τ_turbulent = ρ ℓ² (du/dy)²**

**Why it is zero at the wall:**

> The **NO-SLIP** condition fixes the fluid at the wall, so there is **no room for a parcel to move and mix**. The mixing length must therefore vanish there.

> Prandtl took **ℓ = k y**, where y is the distance **from the wall** and **k ≈ 0.4** is von Kármán's constant. At y = 0, ℓ = 0 ✓

**Why each other option fails:**

| Option | Why wrong |
|---|---|
| "A universal constant" | It **varies with position** — that is its whole character. **k = 0.4 is the universal constant**, not ℓ |
| "Independent of shear stress" | The shear stress is **defined through** it: τ = ρℓ²(du/dy)² |
| "Independent of radial distance" | It depends **directly** on distance from the wall (ℓ = ky) |

> Option (a) is the closest trap, because **von Kármán's constant k IS universal** — but k is the coefficient, not the mixing length.

**What the model produces** — integrating with ℓ = ky gives the **logarithmic velocity profile**:

> **u/u* = (1/k) ln(y) + C**, where **u* = √(τ₀/ρ)** is the **shear velocity**

> That logarithmic law is the foundation of turbulent boundary layer theory and of the **Colebrook–White** friction relation.

**The regions of a turbulent pipe flow:**

| Region | Character |
|---|---|
| **Viscous (laminar) sublayer** | Very thin, at the wall; **viscous stress dominates** |
| Buffer layer | Transition |
| **Turbulent core** | **Turbulent (Reynolds) stresses dominate**; logarithmic profile |

**The viscous sublayer is what makes the smooth/rough distinction:**

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Roughness **buried within** the sublayer | **Hydrodynamically SMOOTH** — f depends on **Re only** |
| Roughness **projecting through** it | **Fully ROUGH** — f depends on **k/D only** |

> As Re rises the **sublayer thins**, so the same pipe moves from smooth toward rough behaviour. **"Smooth" and "rough" describe the FLOW as much as the PIPE** — which is why the Moody curves go horizontal at high Reynolds number.

**Contrast with laminar flow**, where the profile is **parabolic**, **V_mean = V_max/2** exactly, and **f = 64/Re** with the **roughness irrelevant**.

examTip.trick: Reason from **no-slip**: the fluid at the wall cannot move, so it cannot mix — the mixing length must be **zero** there. Prandtl took **ℓ = ky** with **k ≈ 0.4**.
examTip.trap: "A universal constant" is the near-miss: **von Kármán's k = 0.4 IS universal**, but ℓ itself varies with distance from the wall. The option confuses the coefficient with the quantity.
examTip.mnemonic: **ℓ = ky gives the LOGARITHMIC velocity profile** — the foundation of turbulent boundary layer theory. And the **viscous sublayer** is what makes a pipe hydrodynamically smooth or rough, depending on the Reynolds number.

questions.stem: What is the inclination of inclined lettering?
questions.solution:
**75° to the horizontal**, sloping to the right.

**The two lettering styles in engineering drawing:**

| Style | Inclination |
|---|---|
| **Vertical (upright)** | **90°** |
| **INCLINED (italic)** | **75° to the horizontal**, sloping right |

> Both are acceptable, but **only one style may be used on a single drawing** — mixing them is a drafting fault.

**Lettering standards (IS 9609 / ISO 3098):**

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Standard heights** | **2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm** |
| Ratio between successive heights | **√2** — matching the A-series paper progression |
| Stroke thickness (type B) | **h/10** |
| Spacing between characters | About 2/10 h |
| Minimum spacing between lines | 14/10 h |

> The **√2 progression** is why a drawing reduced from A1 to A2 keeps its lettering exactly one standard size smaller and remains legible — the same reasoning that governs the paper sizes.

**Why lettering is specified by HEIGHT**: height is what determines legibility at a given reduction. The width follows from the height by a fixed proportion.

**Other drawing conventions** that appear alongside in examinations:

| Convention | Value |
|---|---|
| **Line types** | Continuous **thick** = visible outline; **dashed** = hidden; **thin chain** = centre line; **thick chain** = cutting plane |
| **Hatching** | Thin lines at **45°**, only on material the section plane **cuts** |
| **Isometric axes** | **120°** apart; isometric scale ≈ **0.816** |
| **Sheet sizes** | A0 = **1 m²**, 841 × 1189; each size halves the longer dimension |
| **First angle** | Top view **BELOW** the front view |
| **Third angle** | Top view **ABOVE** the front view |

> **Ribs, webs, shafts, bolts and fasteners are NOT hatched** even when the section plane passes through them — hatching them would misrepresent the shape.

> And every drawing must carry the **projection symbol** in its title block, because **a drawing read in the wrong system is a mirror image of the intended part**.

examTip.trick: Only two styles exist: **vertical at 90°** and **inclined at 75°**. Since 90° is not offered, 75° is the only candidate that is actually a standard — the others are simply plausible-looking angles.
examTip.trap: **Only ONE lettering style may be used on a single drawing.** Mixing vertical and inclined is a drafting fault, and questions sometimes test that rather than the angle.
examTip.mnemonic: **Heights 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 — each √2 times the last**, matching the A-series paper progression. That is why a reduced drawing keeps legible lettering one size down.

questions.stem: The coefficient of subgrade reaction does not depend upon:
questions.solution:
**The water table** — at least not directly.

**What the coefficient of subgrade reaction is:**

> **k = pressure ÷ settlement**, with units of **kN/m³** (a pressure per unit length).

> It treats the soil as a **bed of independent springs** — the **Winkler** model — and it is the parameter used in the **flexible** method of raft and pavement design.

**What it does depend on:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Soil type and density** | The dominant factor |
| **SIZE of the loaded area** | Larger area → **lower k**, because the stress bulb reaches deeper |
| **SHAPE** of the loaded area | Square, rectangular and strip all differ |
| **DEPTH** of the footing | Confinement increases with depth |
| Rate and duration of loading | Creep in clay |

> The **water table** affects the soil's properties **indirectly** — a saturated soil is weaker and more compressible — but it is **not a direct term** in the calculation of k. That indirect route is what the source explanation identifies, and it is the basis of the answer.

**The size correction is the important one in practice**, because k is measured by a **plate load test** on a small plate and then applied to a full-size foundation:

| Soil | Correction from a 300 mm plate to a footing of width B |
|---|---|
| **Clay** | **k_footing = k_plate × (0.3/B)** |
| **Sand** | **k_footing = k_plate × [(B + 0.3)/(2B)]²** |

> **Ignoring the size correction is a serious error** — for a 3 m footing on clay it overstates k by a factor of ten.

**The plate load test's deeper limitation** is worth stating alongside:

> A **300–750 mm plate** stresses only about a metre of soil. A **real footing** stresses several metres. **A soft layer below the plate's bulb but within the footing's is completely invisible to the test.**

**Where k is used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Flexible raft design** | Beam or plate on an elastic foundation |
| **Rigid pavement design** | **Westergaard's** analysis of slab stresses |
| Laterally loaded piles | Subgrade reaction along the shaft |
| Sheet pile walls | — |

**The Winkler model's weakness**, which is worth knowing: the springs are **independent**, so the model cannot represent the fact that loading one point actually depresses the soil around it too. It is a convenient idealisation, not a physical truth — and for a large raft on clay it can mislead badly.

> **The rigid (conventional) method** — assuming a stiff raft and a **linear** pressure distribution — remains the safer choice for a thick raft on soft soil, precisely because it avoids depending on k.

examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. Three options are genuine direct dependencies (size, shape, depth) and only the water table acts **indirectly**, through the soil's properties rather than as a term in the calculation.
examTip.trick: **k is measured on a small plate and MUST be size-corrected**: **× (0.3/B) for clay**, **× [(B+0.3)/2B]² for sand**. For a 3 m footing on clay, skipping that correction overstates k **tenfold**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Winkler treats the soil as INDEPENDENT springs** — convenient but not physical, since loading one point really does depress its neighbours. For a thick raft on soft soil the **rigid method** is safer, because it does not depend on k at all.

questions.stem: Resource smoothing is:
options: An optimization and economical utilization of resources
An adjustment of resources without affecting project duration
questions.solution:
**An adjustment of resources that does not affect the project duration.**

**The two resource techniques**, which are constantly confused:

| | **RESOURCE SMOOTHING (levelling)** | **RESOURCE ALLOCATION (constrained levelling)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed** | The **project DURATION** | The **RESOURCE limit** |
| **Varies** | The resource profile — smoothed | The **project duration** — extended |
| Uses | **FLOAT** on non-critical activities | Reschedules regardless of float |
| Critical path | **Unchanged** | **May change** |

> **Smoothing: fixed time, smoother resources. Allocation: fixed resources, longer time.**

**How smoothing works:**

> Non-critical activities are **shifted within their FLOAT** so that the resource histogram's peaks are cut and its troughs filled. Because only float is consumed, **the completion date does not move**.

**Why an even resource profile is worth having:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Avoids hiring and firing** | A peak means recruiting for a few weeks and dismissing after |
| **Better plant utilisation** | Equipment stands idle in the troughs |
| **Steadier supervision and quality** | A team that stays together works better |
| **Lower cost** | Peaks are expensive to service |
| More realistic and achievable | — |

> **The histogram's shape matters as much as its total.** Two schedules with the same total man-days can differ greatly in cost if one is even and the other spiky.

**Where the float comes from:**

| Float | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Total float** | Delay possible **without affecting project completion** = **LST − EST** |
| **Free float** | Delay possible **without delaying the NEXT activity** |
| Independent float | Without affecting either neighbour |

> **A critical activity has ZERO total float** — which is precisely how the critical path is identified, and why smoothing can only work on **non-critical** activities.

**And the forward/backward pass that produces it:**

> **Forward pass takes the MAXIMUM** (an activity cannot start until all predecessors finish); **backward pass takes the MINIMUM** (it must not delay the earliest successor).

**Compare CRASHING**, which is a different tool again: it **shortens** the critical path by **adding resources at extra cost**, and it is worth doing only on critical activities — with the critical path **re-identified after every step**, because it can shift.

examTip.trick: The discriminator is **what is held fixed**. **Smoothing fixes the DURATION** and uses float to even the resources; **allocation fixes the RESOURCES** and accepts a longer duration.
examTip.trap: Option (a) is true of both techniques and of good planning generally — it is too vague to be the definition. The defining phrase is **"without affecting project duration"**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Smoothing consumes FLOAT, so it can only touch NON-CRITICAL activities** — a critical activity has zero total float by definition. **Crashing** is the opposite tool: it shortens the critical path by spending money.

questions.stem: The shear stress at the edge (outer surface) of a shaft under torsion is:
questions.solution:
**Maximum** at the outer surface.

**Why.** The torsion formula gives:

> **τ/r = T/J = Gθ/L**

> so **τ = Tr/J** — the shear stress is **directly proportional to the radius**.

| Position | Shear stress |
|---|---|
| **Centre (r = 0)** | **ZERO** |
| Mid-radius | Half the maximum |
| **Outer surface (r = R)** | **MAXIMUM** |

> The distribution is **LINEAR** from zero at the axis to maximum at the surface.

**For a solid circular shaft:**

> **J = πd⁴/32** and **τ_max = Tr/J = T(d/2)/(πd⁴/32) = 16T/πd³**

**The structural consequence is the reason hollow shafts are used:**

> Material near the **centre** carries **almost no stress** — it is nearly dead weight. **Removing it costs very little strength and saves a great deal of material.**

> A hollow shaft of the same outside diameter with an inner diameter of half the outer loses only **1/16 of its polar moment** (since J ∝ d⁴) while removing **1/4 of the area**.

**Note the parallel with bending**, and the contrast:

| Action | Distribution | Maximum at | Zero at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Torsion** | **Linear** | **Outer surface** | **Centre** |
| **Bending** | **Linear** | **Extreme fibres** | **Neutral axis** |
| **Transverse shear in a beam** | **Parabolic** | **Neutral axis** | Extreme fibres |

> Torsion and bending both put the work in the **outermost material**, which is why hollow tubes are efficient for both — and why the transverse shear, peaking at the neutral axis, is the odd one out.

**Torsional rigidity GJ** and the angle of twist:

> **θ = TL/(GJ)**

**And the difference between section types is dramatic:**

| Section | Torsional constant |
|---|---|
| **Solid circular** | **J = πd⁴/32** |
| **CLOSED thin tube** | **J = 4A²t/s** (Bredt) — **very stiff** |
| **OPEN section (I, channel, angle)** | **J = Σ(bt³/3)** — **extremely flexible** |

> **A closed section is hundreds of times stiffer in torsion than an open one of the same weight.** An I-beam is a poor torsion member; a box section is an excellent one — which is why **box girders** are used for curved bridges and any deck carrying eccentric load.

examTip.trick: **τ = Tr/J**, so the stress is **proportional to r** — zero at the centre, maximum at the surface. One formula settles it.
examTip.trap: Do not confuse it with **transverse shear in a beam**, which is **parabolic** and **maximum at the NEUTRAL AXIS**. Torsional shear and beam shear have opposite distributions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Material at the centre does almost nothing — hence HOLLOW shafts.** And a **CLOSED** section is hundreds of times stiffer in torsion than an **OPEN** one of the same weight, which is why curved bridges use box girders.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a dead load?
questions.solution:
**Students in a class** — people are a **live (imposed)** load.

**The distinction:**

| | **DEAD LOAD** | **LIVE (IMPOSED) LOAD** |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | **Permanent** and **fixed** in position | **Variable** in magnitude or position |
| Examples | Self weight, floor finishes, **permanent partitions**, fixed services, cladding | **People**, furniture that moves, stored goods, snow |
| Can be patterned? | **NO** — it acts everywhere always | **YES** — positioned adversely |
| Load factor when adverse | **1.5** | 1.5 |
| **Load factor when STABILISING** | **0.9** | Taken as zero |

**Why "furniture" is dead load here but people are not** — the distinction is **permanence and fixity**, and the source paper treats fixed classroom furniture as part of the permanent fit-out. **Movable** furniture would be a live load, and codes generally treat it so.

> The unambiguous case is the one the question turns on: **people are never a dead load.** Their number and position vary continuously.

**The critical practical point about dead load:**

> **Dead load DOMINATES in concrete construction.** For a typical floor beam, self weight plus slab often exceeds the imposed load before any finishes are counted — which is why a preliminary design must include the structure's **own weight from the outset**, not add it later.

**Typical values:**

| Item | Load |
|---|---|
| **Reinforced concrete** | **25 kN/m³** |
| Plain concrete | 24 kN/m³ |
| Brick masonry | 19–20 kN/m³ |
| **Floor finish** | **1 – 1.5 kN/m²** |
| Imposed load, residential | 2 kN/m² |
| **Imposed load, classroom** | **3 kN/m²** |
| Imposed load, assembly | 4–5 kN/m² |

**The 0.9 DL combination** is the one most often omitted, and omitting it hides real problems:

> Where the **dead load is STABILISING** — resisting **overturning, sliding or uplift** — it is factored **DOWN to 0.9**, because relying on a load that might be less than estimated is unsafe.

> Applying 1.5 to a stabilising dead load conceals **overturning and uplift** failures entirely. Cantilever canopies, retaining walls, light roofs under wind uplift and empty basements are all cases where the 0.9 combination governs.

**Seismic weight** is a related distinction: earthquake force is an **inertia** force, so it is proportional to **mass**. Seismic weight = **full dead load + a fraction (25–50%) of the imposed load** — because only part of the live load is likely to be present, and it may not be rigidly attached.

examTip.trick: Ask whether the item is **permanent and fixed**. **People are never dead load** — that is the unambiguous case, whatever view is taken of fixed furniture.
examTip.trap: The **0.9 DL** combination is the one most often forgotten: where dead load **STABILISES** (against overturning, sliding or uplift), it is factored **DOWN**, not up. Using 1.5 there hides the failure entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead load DOMINATES in concrete** — self weight plus slab often exceeds the imposed load, so include it from the first sketch. **Seismic weight = full DL + 25–50% of LL**, because earthquake force follows mass.

questions.stem: The rise of a liquid in a capillary tube depends on:
options: The inner radius of the tube
questions.solution:
**The INNER radius of the tube.**

> **h = 4σ cos θ/(γ d) = 2σ cos θ/(γ r)**, where **d and r are the INTERNAL diameter and radius**

> **h ∝ 1/r** — the rise is **inversely proportional to the internal radius**.

**Why each other option fails:**

| Option | Why wrong |
|---|---|
| **The material** | The **contact angle θ** depends on the liquid–solid pair, so the material does matter — but the question asks what the rise **depends on** quantitatively, and the dominant geometric variable is the bore |
| **The length** | Irrelevant — the water rises to h whatever the tube's total length (provided it is longer than h) |
| **The outer radius** | The water has no contact with the outside of the tube at all |

> **The outer radius is the deliberate trap**, and it is a good one: only the **wetted internal surface** takes part in the capillary action. A thick-walled tube and a thin-walled one of the same bore behave identically.

**Worked magnitudes for water (σ = 0.073 N/m, θ ≈ 0):**

| Internal diameter | Rise |
|---|---|
| **1 mm** | **30 mm** |
| 0.1 mm | 300 mm |
| 0.01 mm | **3 m** |

> Which is why capillary effects are **negligible in a pipe and dominant in a fine-grained soil**.

**The contact angle decides the direction:**

| Liquid on glass | θ | Meniscus | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Water** | **≈ 0°** — wetting | **Concave** up | **RISES** |
| **Mercury** | **≈ 130°** — non-wetting | **Convex** up | **DEPRESSES** |

> **cos 130° is negative**, so h comes out negative — a depression. Mercury's cohesion exceeds its adhesion to glass.

**In soil mechanics** the same relation governs three important effects:

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Capillary fringe** above the water table | Soil saturated but under **NEGATIVE** pore pressure |
| **Increased effective stress** | **σ′ = σ − u**, and negative u makes σ′ **exceed** σ |
| **APPARENT COHESION** in moist sand | Menisci bind the grains — the sandcastle effect, which **vanishes on saturation or drying** |

**And frost susceptibility:**

> **SILT is the most frost-susceptible soil** — enough capillary rise (1–10 m) **and** enough permeability to feed water fast to a growing ice lens. Clay has the rise but is too impermeable; sand is permeable but has too little rise.

**A practical note for laboratory work**: manometer tubes are specified at **6 mm bore or more** precisely to keep the capillary correction negligible, since h ∝ 1/r.

examTip.trap: **"Outer radius"** is the deliberate trap — the water never touches the outside of the tube. Only the **wetted internal bore** takes part, so wall thickness is irrelevant.
examTip.trick: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd), so h ∝ 1/d.** A 1 mm tube gives 30 mm of rise; a 0.01 mm pore gives 3 m — which is why capillarity is negligible in pipes and dominant in soils.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water wets and rises (θ ≈ 0); mercury does not wet and is depressed (θ ≈ 130°, cos negative).** In soil this gives **apparent cohesion** — which vanishes the moment the sand is saturated or fully dried.

questions.stem: The relationship between the flexural strength and the characteristic compressive strength of concrete is:
questions.solution:
**f_cr = 0.7 √f_ck** (IS 456 cl. 6.2.2), both in N/mm².

**What it represents.** The **flexural strength (modulus of rupture)** is concrete's apparent **tensile** strength in bending — the stress at which a plain concrete beam cracks.

**Typical values:**

| Grade | f_ck | **f_cr = 0.7√f_ck** |
|---|---|---|
| M20 | 20 | **3.13 N/mm²** |
| **M25** | **25** | **3.50 N/mm²** |
| M30 | 30 | 3.83 |
| M40 | 40 | 4.43 |

> **Note that flexural strength is only about 10–15% of the compressive strength** — which is the single most important fact about concrete as a material, and the reason reinforcement exists.

**The √ relationship matters:** because strength enters as a **square root**, **doubling the compressive strength increases the tensile strength by only about 40%**. Concrete's tensile weakness cannot be engineered away by using a richer mix.

**The three related strengths, and their companion formulae:**

| Property | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Flexural strength (modulus of rupture)** | **f_cr = 0.7√f_ck** |
| **Modulus of elasticity** | **E_c = 5000√f_ck** |
| Split tensile strength | ≈ 0.66 f_cr, or about 0.5√f_ck |
| **Direct tensile strength** | Lowest of the three |

> **Both of the main ones go as √f_ck** — flexural strength with 0.7 and elastic modulus with 5000. Confusing the two coefficients is the commonest error here.

**Why three different "tensile" strengths?** Because each is measured differently and gives a different number:

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Flexural (modulus of rupture)** — third-point loading on a beam | Highest, because it assumes a linear stress block that does not really exist |
| **Split cylinder (Brazilian)** | Intermediate; the usual practical test |
| **Direct tension** | Lowest and hardest to perform |

**Where f_cr is used in design:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cracking moment** and deflection calculations | **M_cr = f_cr I_gr/y_t** |
| **Rigid pavement** design | The slab is designed in **flexure**, so f_cr governs directly |
| Minimum reinforcement | To ensure the section does not fail on first cracking |
| Shrinkage and temperature crack assessment | — |

> **For a rigid pavement f_cr is the governing strength**, not the compressive strength — because the slab bridges over the subgrade in **bending** rather than crushing.

**The design assumption that follows** from concrete's tensile weakness: **reinforced concrete design ASSUMES the concrete is cracked in tension** and that the **steel carries all of it**. The design question is therefore not whether it cracks, but whether the **crack WIDTH** stays within limits — 0.3 mm normally, 0.2 mm in aggressive exposure.

examTip.trick: Two IS 456 relations both go as **√f_ck** — **f_cr = 0.7√f_ck** and **E_c = 5000√f_ck**. Keep the coefficients apart; confusing them is the commonest error in this topic.
examTip.trap: Because strength enters as a **square root**, doubling f_ck raises the tensile strength by only about **40%**. Concrete's tensile weakness cannot be designed away with a richer mix.
examTip.mnemonic: **Flexural strength is only 10–15% of compressive** — which is the entire reason reinforcement exists. For a **RIGID PAVEMENT** f_cr is the governing strength, since the slab works in bending.

questions.stem: What is the use of a governor?
questions.solution:
**It controls the mean speed** of the machine, holding it constant as the load varies.

**Why speed control matters in a power plant:**

> The **generator frequency is tied directly to its rotational speed**: **N = 120f/P**. Nepal's grid runs at **50 Hz**, so the turbine speed must be held constant within very tight limits — otherwise the frequency drifts.

**How it works:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | The governor **senses the speed** (mechanically by flyballs, or electronically) |
| **2** | A speed change indicates a **load change** — more load slows the machine |
| **3** | The governor **adjusts the FLOW** to restore the speed |

**What it moves depends on the turbine:**

| Turbine | Control element |
|---|---|
| **Pelton** | The **SPEAR (needle) valve** in the nozzle, plus a **deflector** for rapid response |
| **Francis** | The **guide vanes (wicket gates)** |
| **Kaplan** | Guide vanes **and** the adjustable **runner blades** |

> The **deflector** on a Pelton is worth knowing: it swings across the jet to divert it from the buckets **instantly**, while the spear valve closes slowly. That combination gives fast load rejection **without** the water hammer a rapid valve closure would cause.

**Which brings the governor's connection to WATER HAMMER:**

> A sudden **load rejection** makes the governor close the gates. If it closes them **fast**, the decelerating water column generates a large pressure surge — **Δp = ρcΔV**, potentially hundreds of metres of head.

> So the **governor timing and the surge protection are designed together**. The closure time must be compared against **2L/c**, the wave's round trip: closure **slower** than that greatly reduces the rise; closure **faster** gives the full Joukowsky value however fast it actually is.

**The competing requirements** the governor must balance:

| Requirement | Pulls toward |
|---|---|
| **Fast response** to hold the frequency | **Rapid** gate closure |
| **Limiting water hammer** | **Slow** gate closure |
| Limiting speed rise on load rejection | Rapid closure |

> The **deflector, the surge tank and the machine's flywheel effect (GD²)** are the devices that let both requirements be met — which is why a hydropower governing system is designed as a whole rather than as an isolated component.

**Note the other options** are all real control problems in a hydropower plant — temperature (of bearings and windings), sediment (by traps and settling basins) — but none is the governor's function.

examTip.trick: **Speed control IS frequency control** — **N = 120f/P**, and the grid needs 50 Hz. That is why a hydro machine's speed must be held so tightly.
examTip.trap: The governor adjusts the **FLOW**, not the load. It responds to a speed change by opening or closing the gates — spear valve on a Pelton, guide vanes on a Francis.
examTip.mnemonic: **The governor is the ORIGIN of the water hammer problem** — a load rejection makes it close the gates, and Δp = ρcΔV follows. Which is why the **deflector, surge tank and governor timing** are designed together, against the **2L/c** criterion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following methods of tunnelling is used in hard rocks?
questions.solution:
**The heading and benching method.**

**How it works.** The tunnel face is excavated in two stages:

> The **HEADING** is the upper portion, driven first as a smaller advance excavation. The **BENCH** is the lower portion, excavated afterwards.

> The heading provides a **working face and ventilation**, and it allows the ground to be **assessed and supported** before the full section is opened. In hard rock the two are usually drilled and blasted separately, with the bench blasted to the already-free heading face — which improves fragmentation.

**Why it suits HARD rock:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| The rock **stands unsupported** long enough to work in stages | Soft ground would collapse |
| **Smaller rounds** are easier to drill and blast accurately | Better control of overbreak |
| The heading acts as a **pilot** — it reveals the ground ahead | Geological risk reduced |
| Suits a **large section** that cannot be taken in one round | — |

**The other methods are all for SOFT ground**, which is what makes the question a clean discrimination:

| Method | Ground | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Fore poling** | **Soft, loose ground** | Poles or spiles driven **ahead** of the face to hold the roof while excavating beneath |
| **Needle beam** | **Soft ground** | A beam supported at the face and behind, carrying the roof supports |
| **Shield tunnelling** | **Soft, water-bearing ground** | A steel shield advanced by jacks, with segmental lining erected **inside its tail** |

> **All three of the wrong options are soft-ground techniques.** Recognising that immediately isolates the hard-rock method.

**Hard rock tunnelling methods more generally:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Drill and blast** | The traditional approach; flexible, suits variable rock and any shape |
| **Heading and benching** | A drill-and-blast sequence for a large section |
| **Full face** | For smaller sections in good rock |
| **TBM (tunnel boring machine)** | Fast and produces a smooth bore, but **inflexible** and very costly to mobilise |
| **NATM** | Uses the rock's own **arching capacity**, supported by **shotcrete, rock bolts and mesh**, with convergence monitored |

**NATM's principle** is worth stating because it is the modern standard in rock:

> The rock is allowed to **deform slightly** and is then supported **flexibly and promptly**. The support works **WITH the ground**, mobilising its self-supporting arch, rather than resisting it with a rigid lining. **Monitoring convergence is integral, not optional.**

**And the practical constraint that governs progress in any tunnel:**

> The cycle time is set by the **slowest of drill – blast – MUCK – support**. **Muck removal frequently controls the advance rate**, along with ventilation — which is why the heading's role in providing working space and airflow matters so much.

examTip.trick: **All three wrong options are SOFT-ground methods** — fore poling, needle beam and shield tunnelling all exist because the ground will not stand on its own. Recognising that isolates the hard-rock answer immediately.
examTip.trap: **Shield tunnelling** sounds robust and modern, but the shield exists precisely because the ground is **soft and water-bearing**. It would be pointless in competent rock.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rock stands up for a time → NATM with shotcrete and rock bolts. Soft ground does not → shield with segmental lining.** The ground condition, not the diameter, chooses the method. And **muck removal usually controls the advance rate**.

questions.stem: If a circular sewer is partially full and the depth is increased, then:
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — though the third statement is only true over part of the range, which is what makes this question worth working carefully.

**What happens as the depth rises in a circular sewer:**

| Quantity | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter P** | **Always INCREASES** with depth ✓ |
| **Area A** | Always increases |
| **Hydraulic radius R = A/P** | Rises to a **maximum at about 0.81D**, then **falls** |
| **Velocity** (∝ R^{2/3}) | **Maximum at 0.81D**, then **DECREASES** ✓ |
| **Discharge** (∝ AR^{2/3}) | **Maximum at 0.94D**, then decreases |

> So **velocity decreases** above **0.81D** and **discharge decreases** above **0.94D**. Over most of the upper range all three statements hold.

**The two counter-intuitive maxima:**

| Quantity | Maximum at | Value relative to full |
|---|---|---|
| **VELOCITY** | **≈ 0.81 D** | **1.14 × V_full** |
| **DISCHARGE** | **≈ 0.94 D** | **1.07 × Q_full** |

> **A pipe running just below full carries MORE than the same pipe running full** — about 7% more. Beyond 0.94D the section is closing over, so the **wetted perimeter grows faster than the area**, R falls, and the discharge with it.

**The half-full result** is the one worth memorising:

> At **half full**, a circular pipe has **half the area**, the **SAME hydraulic radius (D/4)**, the **same velocity**, and therefore **exactly half the discharge**.

> R = D/4 for **both** the full and half-full conditions — a neat coincidence of the circular geometry.

**Why sewers are designed to run PART FULL:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTILATION** | Sewer gases must escape — a full sewer cannot ventilate |
| **Reserve capacity** for peak and storm flows | — |
| **Free-surface (gravity) flow** maintained | Pressurising a gravity sewer surcharges the manholes |
| **Corrosion control** | H₂S in a sealed sewer oxidises to sulphuric acid on the crown |

**Design practice (CPHEEO):** small sewers **half full**, medium **two-thirds**, large **three-quarters** at peak flow.

**The two velocity limits** that set the gradient:

| Limit | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum (SELF-CLEANSING)** | **0.6 – 0.75 m/s at MINIMUM flow** | Below it, silt deposits and the sewer blocks |
| **Maximum** | **3.0 m/s** | Erosion of the invert |

> **The self-cleansing requirement at MINIMUM flow is the binding one**, and it is what makes sewer design harder than water main design — a new development's early flows are a small fraction of the ultimate design flow, so the gradient must suit both.

**CROWN CORROSION** is the failure the ventilation guards against: **H₂S** from septic sewage is oxidised by bacteria on the moist crown to **sulphuric acid**, which destroys concrete sewers within decades.

examTip.trick: Track **R = A/P**. Above **0.81D** the perimeter grows faster than the area, so R falls and the **velocity** falls with it; above **0.94D** the **discharge** falls too.
examTip.trap: "A full pipe carries the most" is the intuitive and **wrong** answer — maximum discharge is at **0.94D**, about **7% more** than running full.
examTip.mnemonic: **Half full: same R (D/4), same velocity, exactly half the discharge.** Sewers run part full for **VENTILATION** — a sealed sewer breeds H₂S, which becomes sulphuric acid and destroys the crown.

questions.stem: Pot hole maintenance in the case of a bituminous road is:
questions.solution:
**Recurrent maintenance.**

**The maintenance categories:**

| Category | Frequency | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **ROUTINE** | **Continuous or annual**, regardless of condition | Drain clearing, vegetation control, sign cleaning, minor shoulder repair |
| **RECURRENT** | **As the defect appears** — several times a year | **POTHOLE patching**, crack sealing, edge repair, local patching |
| **PERIODIC** | At **intervals of years** | Resurfacing, overlay, surface dressing, renewal of markings |
| **SPECIAL / emergency** | **Unpredictable** | Landslide clearance, flood damage, accident repair |
| Rehabilitation | Once in the life | Reconstruction of the pavement |

> **The discriminator is the trigger**: routine work is done on a **schedule**; recurrent work is done **when the defect appears** and recurs through the year; periodic work is done at **multi-year** intervals.

**Why potholes are recurrent rather than routine**: they appear unpredictably through the monsoon and must be patched **as they form**, several times in a season — not on an annual schedule.

**Why prompt patching matters far more than its cost suggests:**

> A pothole admits water directly into the **base and subgrade**. The water **softens the layers, strips the binder, and the hole enlarges rapidly under traffic**. What begins as a repair costing a few rupees becomes a failed section costing a thousand times as much.

> **The economics of maintenance are steeply non-linear: work deferred does not merely wait, it multiplies.** That is the argument for **preventive** maintenance, and it is why a road authority that spends its budget on emergencies is permanently short of money.

**Pavement distresses and what they indicate:**

| Distress | Cause | Family |
|---|---|---|
| **Potholes** | Water ingress plus traffic | Disintegration |
| **RUTTING** | Inadequate compaction, excess bitumen, weak mix or subgrade | **DEFORMATION** |
| **Alligator (fatigue) cracking** | Repeated loading; structural inadequacy | **CRACKING** |
| Ravelling | Loss of binder; ageing | Disintegration |
| Bleeding | Excess bitumen | Deformation |
| Corrugation | Unstable mix | Deformation |

> **Rutting and cracking need OPPOSITE remedies** — one indicates a mix too soft or under-compacted, the other one too brittle or structurally inadequate. Diagnosing which family the distress belongs to is the first step in any pavement investigation.

**Proper pothole repair** is worth stating, since a poor patch fails within weeks: **cut back to sound material with vertical faces**, clean and dry the hole, apply a **tack coat**, fill in **layers**, and **compact each layer** properly. Throwing loose premix into a wet hole is not a repair.

examTip.trick: The discriminator is the **trigger**: **routine** is on a schedule, **recurrent** is when the defect appears (and it recurs through the year), **periodic** is at multi-year intervals.
examTip.trap: "Routine" is tempting because patching feels like everyday work — but routine maintenance is **scheduled regardless of condition** (drain clearing, vegetation), while potholes appear unpredictably.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deferred maintenance multiplies, it does not wait.** A pothole admits water to the base, which softens and enlarges the failure — turning a cheap patch into a failed section costing a thousand times more.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most efficient weir?
questions.solution:
**The parabolic (ogee) profile.**

**Why it is the most efficient.** The **ogee crest is shaped to follow the LOWER NAPPE of a freely falling jet** at the design head. The water therefore just maintains contact with the crest, the pressure on it stays close to atmospheric, and **almost no energy is wasted** in separation or turbulence.

> **The ogee achieves the highest discharge coefficient of any weir shape** — around **2.2 in SI terms** against roughly 1.7–1.8 for a broad-crested weir.

**The behaviour at different heads is the key design consideration:**

| Head | Flow behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Below** the design head | Water **presses on the crest** — safe, but slightly less efficient |
| **AT** the design head | Atmospheric pressure on the crest — **maximum efficiency** |
| **ABOVE** the design head | Flow tends to **LIFT OFF**, creating **sub-atmospheric pressure** and a **CAVITATION** risk |

> That asymmetry is why the design head is chosen carefully and why **crest profiles are built to tight tolerances** — a surface irregularity of a few millimetres in a 30 m/s flow is enough to initiate cavitation damage.

**The weir types compared:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Ogee (parabolic)** | **Most efficient**; the standard for concrete dams |
| **Sloping** | Simpler to build; lower coefficient |
| **Vertical drop** | Simplest; energy dissipated by the fall; lowest efficiency |
| **Barrage** | Not a weir profile at all — a **gated** structure |

> **"Barrage" is the odd one out on category**: it is a **type of diversion structure** (low crest with gates over most of its length), not a **crest profile**. Recognising that removes it immediately.

**The distinction between weir and barrage** is worth carrying:

| | **WEIR** | **BARRAGE** |
|---|---|---|
| Pond level controlled by | The **crest height** — fixed | **GATES** — adjustable |
| Upstream flooding in a flood | Fixed and higher | **Controlled** — gates opened |
| Cost, staffing | Lower, none | Higher, operators needed |

**Other efficient-discharge structures**, for contrast:

| Structure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Siphon spillway** | Runs **full bore** once primed — a very high discharge per unit width, but sudden onset and debris-prone |
| **Shaft (morning glory)** | Compact, but **CHOKES** once the shaft runs full, giving a flat rating curve |
| **Labyrinth weir** | A zig-zag plan that greatly increases the crest **length** in a given width |

> The **labyrinth** is the modern answer where a long crest is needed in a narrow site — it achieves by **plan geometry** what the ogee achieves by **profile**.

examTip.trick: **"Barrage" is the odd one out on category** — it is a gated diversion structure, not a crest profile. Removing it on those grounds leaves three genuine profiles, of which the ogee is clearly the most refined.
examTip.trap: The ogee is efficient **at its design head**. **Above** it the nappe tends to lift off, creating sub-atmospheric pressure and a **CAVITATION** risk — which is why crest tolerances are so tight.
examTip.mnemonic: **The ogee follows the LOWER NAPPE of a free jet**, so the water just stays in contact and almost no energy is wasted. Discharge coefficient about **2.2**, against 1.7–1.8 for a broad-crested weir.

questions.stem: What is the dead storage of a storage reservoir?
options: Level between bed level and full reservoir level
Level between bed level and minimum pool level
Level between bed level and maximum water level
Level between minimum pool level and full reservoir level
questions.solution:
**The volume between the bed level and the minimum pool level.**

**The reservoir storage zones, from the bottom up:**

| Zone | Between | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **DEAD storage** | **Bed level and MINIMUM POOL LEVEL** | **Sediment accumulation**; keeps the intake submerged |
| **LIVE (useful) storage** | **Minimum pool level and FULL RESERVOIR LEVEL** | The **usable** water — what the scheme actually delivers |
| **Flood (surcharge) storage** | Full reservoir level and **maximum water level** | Temporary, during a flood |
| Freeboard | Above maximum water level | Waves, settlement, safety |

> **Option (d) describes the LIVE storage**, which is the deliberate near-miss and the one candidates most often pick.

**Why dead storage exists — three reasons, and sediment is the main one:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **SEDIMENT accumulation** | Reserved so that silting does not eat into the useful storage |
| **Keeps the intake SUBMERGED** | The outlet must always draw water, not air |
| Provides a minimum depth for aquatic life and for navigation | — |

**Sediment is the reason a reservoir has a finite life:**

> **The dead storage is sized for the sediment expected over the DESIGN LIFE** — commonly 50 or 100 years. Once it fills, sediment begins to consume the live storage and the scheme's yield falls.

**Which matters greatly in Nepal:**

> Himalayan rivers carry **very heavy sediment loads**, so reservoirs here silt up far faster than the international norms assume. Several schemes have lost storage much sooner than designed.

**Sediment management options:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adequate dead storage** | The passive approach |
| **Sluicing and flushing** | Drawing the reservoir down and letting the river scour its deposits out |
| **Density current venting** | Passing the turbid underflow through low-level outlets |
| **Catchment management** | Reafforestation and check dams — treats the cause, but slow |
| Dredging | Very expensive |

> **Flushing is the most effective active measure**, but it requires the reservoir to be drawn down — which means giving up water and generation, so it is scheduled for the end of the monsoon when inflows will refill it.

**The related levels** worth holding together:

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **MDDL** — minimum draw-down level | The lowest operating level, top of dead storage |
| **FRL** — full reservoir level | Top of live storage; the normal maximum |
| **MWL** — maximum water level | Reached only during the design flood |

**Sizing the live storage** is done from a **MASS CURVE** (Rippl's method): the **largest vertical gap** between the cumulative inflow curve and the demand line is the storage required.

examTip.trap: Option (d) — between minimum pool and full reservoir level — is the **LIVE storage**, and it is the answer most often picked. Dead storage is **below** the minimum pool level.
examTip.trick: Work up from the bed: **dead → live → flood → freeboard.** Dead storage is the bottom zone, and the minimum pool level is the boundary.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dead storage is reserved for SEDIMENT and to keep the intake submerged.** In Nepal it fills far faster than the design assumes — which is why **flushing** at the end of the monsoon is the active remedy.

questions.stem: Under what strata should tile drainage not be placed?
questions.solution:
**Below a less pervious stratum.**

**Why.** If the drain is placed **beneath an impervious or low-permeability layer**, the waterlogged water sitting **above** that layer **cannot reach the drain** — the layer blocks it. The drain then runs dry while the land above it stays waterlogged.

> **The drain must be in hydraulic contact with the water it is meant to remove.** Placing it below a barrier defeats the entire installation.

**Correct placement:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Within a PERVIOUS stratum** | So water can flow to it |
| **Below the root zone** | Typically 1–2 m deep |
| **Above any impervious layer**, not below it | The critical point of this question |
| Surrounded by a **graded filter or gravel envelope** | To stop soil piping into the drain |

**Spacing** follows from the soil's permeability:

> **Spacing is directly proportional to the coefficient of permeability k.** A more permeable soil transmits water to the drain more readily, so the drains can be further apart.

> **Hooghoudt's equation** relates spacing, permeability, drain depth, the impermeable layer depth and the drainage coefficient.

**Surface versus subsurface drainage:**

| Type | Removes | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **SURFACE** (bedding, open ditches, land grading) | **Ponded** water from the surface | Flat, slowly permeable land |
| **SUBSURFACE (tile) drainage** | Lowers the **WATER TABLE** | **Waterlogging and salinity** |

> **Waterlogging and salinity are WATER TABLE problems**, so they require **subsurface** drainage. Surface drainage removes standing water but does nothing to the water table beneath.

**Why waterlogging and salinity travel together:**

| Step | Effect |
|---|---|
| Water table rises into the root zone | **Waterlogging** — roots suffocate |
| **Capillary rise** brings water to the surface | Carrying dissolved salts with it |
| **Evaporation** removes the water | **Concentrating the salts at the surface** |

> **The remedy for both is DRAINAGE** — and for a **sodic (alkali)** soil, **gypsum first, then leaching**, because leaching alone would make a sodic soil worse by removing the calcium that holds its structure together.

**Leaching requires drainage to work:**

> Flooding a saline soil with good water dissolves the salts — but they must have somewhere to **go**. Without adequate drainage the water table simply rises and the salts return by capillary action. **Leaching without drainage is futile.**

**The causes of waterlogging**, all of which involve water arriving faster than it leaves: over-irrigation, **canal seepage** (which is why lining pays), poor natural drainage, an impervious subsoil, and flat topography.

examTip.trick: The drain must be in **hydraulic contact** with the water it is removing. Put it **below** a low-permeability layer and the water simply cannot reach it — the drain runs dry while the land stays waterlogged.
examTip.trap: Note that **spacing is proportional to permeability**: a more permeable soil transmits water readily, so the drains can be **further apart**. That relation reads backwards to many candidates.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging and salinity are WATER TABLE problems** — they need **subsurface**, not surface, drainage. And **leaching without drainage is futile**: the salts must have somewhere to go, or they return by capillary rise.

questions.stem: Which method of population forecasting is used for a large and old town?
questions.solution:
**The arithmetical increase method.**

**Why.** A **large, old, established town** has reached a stage where its growth has **slowed and steadied** — it adds roughly the **same number of people each decade** rather than a constant percentage. That constant *increment* is exactly what the arithmetic method assumes.

> **P_n = P₀ + n x̄**, where **x̄** is the average increment per decade.

**Matching the method to the stage of growth:**

| Method | Assumes | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETICAL increase** | **Constant INCREMENT** each decade | **Large, old, saturating** towns |
| **GEOMETRIC progression** | **Constant PERCENTAGE** growth | **Young, rapidly growing** towns — it gives the **highest** forecast |
| **INCREMENTAL increase** | The increment itself changes by a constant amount | **Maturing** towns — between the two |
| **Decreasing rate of growth** | The percentage falls as saturation nears | Towns approaching a limit |
| **Graphical / comparison** | Extrapolate by analogy with similar towns | Where local data is poor |
| **LOGISTIC curve** | An **S-shape with a saturation limit** | Long-term forecasts where a physical limit exists |

> **Geometric gives the highest forecast and arithmetic the lowest**, with incremental increase between them. Choosing the wrong one over a 30-year design period gives wildly different works — which is why the choice matters more than the arithmetic.

**Why the forecast matters so much:**

> **Population forecasting is the FIRST step in every water supply and sewerage design.** Everything downstream — the source yield, the treatment capacity, the main sizes, the reservoir volume — follows from it.

> **Over-forecast** and the works stand idle, with capital wasted and (for sewers) too little flow to be self-cleansing. **Under-forecast** and the scheme fails within its design life.

**The design period** is chosen alongside:

| Component | Design period |
|---|---|
| **Storage reservoirs, dams** | **50 years** — hard to extend later |
| Treatment works | 15–20 years (built in stages) |
| **Distribution mains** | **30 years or more** — buried, so expensive to replace |
| Pumps | 10 years — easily replaced |

> **Components that are hard to enlarge later get a longer design period.** A buried main is sized generously because digging it up again costs far more than the extra diameter; a pump is sized tightly because replacing it is routine.

**Then the demand follows:**

> **135 lpcd** domestic (IS 1172, full flushing systems), plus industrial, commercial, public and fire demand, plus losses. Peak factors: **maximum daily 1.8 × average**, **maximum hourly 1.5 × maximum daily** — so the peak hour is about **2.7 × average**, and that is what sizes the distribution mains.

examTip.trick: Match the method to the **stage of growth**: **arithmetic = old and slow** (constant increment), **geometric = young and fast** (constant percentage), **incremental = maturing**, **logistic = approaching a saturation limit**.
examTip.trap: **Geometric gives the HIGHEST forecast and arithmetic the LOWEST.** Over a 30-year design period the two differ enormously, so the choice matters far more than the arithmetic does.
examTip.mnemonic: **Components hard to enlarge later get LONGER design periods** — dams 50 years, buried mains 30+, pumps only 10. And the peak hour is about **2.7 × average**, which is what sizes the distribution mains.

questions.stem: Bacteria that grow more at high temperature (40 to 70 °C) are called:
questions.solution:
**Thermophilic.**

**The temperature classification of micro-organisms:**

| Class | Optimum range | Where found |
|---|---|---|
| **PSYCHROPHILIC** | **0 – 20 °C** | Polar regions, glaciers, cold ocean water |
| **MESOPHILIC** | **20 – 45 °C** | **Most common bacteria** — including those in the human body and in ordinary wastewater treatment |
| **THERMOPHILIC** | **45 – 70 °C** | Hot springs, **compost heaps**, thermophilic digesters |
| Hyperthermophilic | **> 70 °C** | Deep-sea hydrothermal vents, volcanic areas |

> The prefixes are Greek and carry the meaning: **psychro-** cold, **meso-** middle, **thermo-** heat, **hyper-** beyond.

**Where the distinction matters in engineering — SLUDGE DIGESTION:**

| | **MESOPHILIC digestion** | **THERMOPHILIC digestion** |
|---|---|---|
| Temperature | **30 – 38 °C** | **50 – 60 °C** |
| Detention time | **20 – 30 days** | **10 – 15 days** — much faster |
| **Pathogen kill** | Partial | **Excellent** — the heat itself sterilises |
| Heating energy required | Moderate | **High** |
| Process stability | **More stable** | **More sensitive** to temperature shocks |
| Gas production | Good | Slightly higher |

> **Thermophilic digestion is faster and produces a far cleaner sludge**, but it costs more energy to heat and is less forgiving of upsets. **Mesophilic is the usual choice** unless pathogen destruction is the priority — for instance where the digested sludge is to be applied to land.

**COMPOSTING** is the other application, and the same thermophilic phase is what makes it work:

> A compost heap self-heats to **55–65 °C** through microbial activity. That temperature, held for several days, **destroys pathogens and weed seeds** — which is why properly managed compost is safe and a cold heap is not.

**Anaerobic digestion chemistry**, for completeness:

| Stage | Process |
|---|---|
| **Hydrolysis** | Complex organics broken to simpler compounds |
| **Acidogenesis** | To volatile fatty acids |
| **Acetogenesis** | To acetic acid, H₂, CO₂ |
| **METHANOGENESIS** | To **CH₄ (60–70%) and CO₂** — the biogas |

> The **methanogens are the slowest and most sensitive** organisms in the chain, so they govern the process. They are inhibited by low pH, so a digester that turns acidic **stalls** — and the standard operating check is the **volatile acids to alkalinity ratio**.

examTip.trick: The Greek prefixes give it away: **psychro-** cold, **meso-** middle, **thermo-** heat, **hyper-** beyond. The bands run **0–20, 20–45, 45–70, above 70 °C**.
examTip.trap: **Hyperthermophilic** is offered as a near-miss but starts **above 70 °C**. The stated range 40–70 °C sits squarely in the thermophilic band.
examTip.mnemonic: **Thermophilic digestion: 50–60 °C, 10–15 days, excellent pathogen kill — but energy-hungry and less stable.** Mesophilic (30–38 °C, 20–30 days) is the usual choice. The same thermophilic phase is what makes **composting** safe.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct order of steps in the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process?
options: Scoping, Screening, Public Hearing, EIA, Issue of Environmental Clearance
Screening, Public Hearing, Scoping, EIA, Issue of Environmental Clearance
Screening, Scoping, EIA, Public Hearing, Issue of Environmental Clearance
Screening, EIA, Scoping, Public Hearing, Issue of Environmental Clearance
questions.solution:
**Screening → Scoping → EIA study → Public Hearing → Issue of Environmental Clearance.**

**What each step does, and why the order is forced:**

| Step | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **1. SCREENING** | Decides **whether** an assessment is needed at all, and **which level** — IEE or full EIA |
| **2. SCOPING** | Decides **what** the study must cover — which impacts, which alternatives, over what area. Produces the **Terms of Reference** |
| **3. EIA STUDY** | The assessment itself — baseline data, impact prediction, mitigation measures, monitoring plan |
| **4. PUBLIC HEARING** | Affected people comment on the **findings** |
| **5. Review and CLEARANCE** | The authority approves, with conditions |
| **6. Monitoring** | Verifies that the mitigation is actually implemented |

**Why the order cannot be otherwise:**

> **Screening must come first** — you cannot scope a study you have not yet decided to do.
> **Scoping must precede the study** — otherwise there is no basis for deciding what to investigate.
> **The public hearing must follow the study** — people can only comment meaningfully on **findings**, not on a blank page.

> Every wrong option violates one of these: (a) scopes before screening, (b) holds the hearing before scoping, (d) studies before scoping.

**IEE versus EIA:**

| | **IEE** | **EIA** |
|---|---|---|
| For | **Smaller** projects | **Large or sensitive** projects |
| Depth | Preliminary | Full |
| **Scoping required?** | **No** | **YES** |
| Public hearing | Usually not | **Required** |

> A project in a **protected area** requires an **EIA regardless of size**.

**The step most often neglected is the last one:**

> **MONITORING.** An EIA that is not followed by monitoring and enforcement is a document, not a safeguard. The mitigation measures it promises have to be built, operated and checked — and that is where environmental assessment most often fails in practice.

**What an EIA report contains:**

| Section | Content |
|---|---|
| Project description | — |
| **Baseline environment** | Physical, biological, socio-economic — the pre-project state |
| **Impact prediction** | Magnitude, extent, duration, reversibility |
| **Alternatives** | Including the **"no project"** option |
| **Mitigation measures** | — |
| **Environmental Management Plan** | Who does what, when, and at what cost |
| Monitoring programme | — |

> **The "no project" alternative is a required part of the analysis**, and it is the benchmark against which every impact is measured.

examTip.trick: Reason the order out rather than memorising it: **you cannot scope a study you have not decided to do**, and **the public cannot comment on findings that do not yet exist**. Those two constraints fix the sequence completely.
examTip.trap: **Screening and scoping** are the pair that gets swapped. **Screening decides WHETHER; scoping decides WHAT.** Screening always comes first.
examTip.mnemonic: **Screening → Scoping → Study → Hearing → Clearance → MONITORING.** The last step is the most often neglected — an EIA without monitoring is a document, not a safeguard.

questions.stem: The design canal discharge is based on:
questions.solution:
**The maximum irrigation water requirement.**

**Why not the river's maximum discharge**: the canal takes only what the **command area needs**. The river's flood discharge is irrelevant to the canal's size — indeed the headworks are designed to keep most of it **out**.

**And why "irrigation water requirement" rather than "crop water requirement":**

> The **CROP water requirement** is what the plants need in the field. The **IRRIGATION water requirement** is what must be **delivered at the canal head** — the crop requirement **plus all the losses** along the way.

> **Irrigation requirement = crop requirement ÷ overall efficiency**

**Efficiencies MULTIPLY along the chain:**

> **η_overall = η_conveyance × η_application**

> Two stages at 70% give **49%**, not 70%. So the gross requirement at the head can be **1.5 to 2 times** the net crop requirement — and sizing on the crop figure guarantees a scheme that cannot deliver.

> **That compounding is why canal LINING is often the cheapest single improvement available**: it raises the conveyance efficiency directly, and every percentage point recovered serves more land from the same headworks.

**The PEAK, not the average, governs:**

> The canal must carry the **maximum demand occurring at any one time** across all the crops in the command — not the seasonal total divided by the days.

> That peak is described by the **kor depth** (the water needed at the crop's critical growth stage) delivered over the **kor period**:

> **Outlet discharge factor = 8.64 B/Δ** hectares per cumec, using the kor values.

**The design chain in order:**

| Step | Quantity |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Crop water requirement** — ET_crop = K_c × PET |
| **2** | Less effective rainfall | 
| **3** | Plus leaching requirement | 
| **4** | ÷ **application efficiency** → field irrigation requirement |
| **5** | ÷ **conveyance efficiency** → **canal head discharge** |
| **6** | Take the **PEAK** of that across the season |

**And the capacity formula that assembles it:**

> **Q = (Duty at the canal outlet, including all losses) × CCA ÷ (time factor × capacity factor)**

> where the **time factor** is the actual operating period ÷ crop period, and the **capacity factor** is the mean supply ÷ full designed capacity. Both are less than 1, and both **increase** the required capacity.

examTip.trap: **"Crop water requirement"** is the near-miss and it is the most-picked wrong answer. The crop requirement is what the **plants** need; the **irrigation** requirement is what must be delivered at the **head**, after all the losses.
examTip.trick: **Efficiencies MULTIPLY** — two 70% stages give 49%. So the head discharge can be **twice** the crop requirement, and sizing on the crop figure guarantees failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design for the PEAK, not the seasonal average** — the kor depth over the kor period. And the river's flood discharge is irrelevant: the headworks exist to keep most of it **out**.

questions.stem: The maximum permissible eccentricity of a retaining wall of base width 'B' to avoid failure in tension is:
questions.solution:
**B/6** — the **middle third rule**.

**Derivation.** The base pressure under combined direct load and moment is:

> **p = (ΣV/B)(1 ± 6e/B)** per unit length of wall
