> For **no tension**, the minimum pressure must be **≥ 0**:
> **1 − 6e/B ≥ 0**, so **e ≤ B/6** ✓

> Since the load may be eccentric either way, the resultant must lie within the **middle third** — a band of width **B/3** centred on the base.

**The pressure states:**

| Eccentricity | Distribution | Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **e = 0** | **Uniform** ΣV/B | Full |
| **0 < e < B/6** | **Trapezoidal**, all compression | Full |
| **e = B/6** | **Triangular**, zero at the heel | Full, just |
| **e > B/6** | **TENSION at the heel; the base LIFTS OFF** | **Partial** |

> Beyond the limit the contact width reduces to **x = 3(B/2 − e)** and the maximum toe pressure becomes **2ΣV/(3x)** per unit length.

**Why the limit is enforced rather than merely advised:**

> Once part of the base lifts off, the **contact area shrinks**, so the **resultant moves further toward the toe**, which **reduces the contact further**. The process is **PROGRESSIVE** — and progressive instability is a different matter from a section merely being overstressed.

> **Soil cannot pull.** Neither can the interface between a concrete base and the ground beneath it.

**The retaining wall's four stability checks:**

| Check | Factor of safety |
|---|---|
| **Overturning** | **2.0** |
| **Sliding** | **1.5** |
| **Bearing pressure** | **3.0** |
| **OVERALL (deep-seated) slope stability** | **1.5** |

> **The fourth is the one most often skipped**, and on a Nepali hillside it frequently governs — a wall can pass every internal check and still ride down the slope on a deeper failure surface passing beneath it.

**But the commonest actual cause of failure is none of these:**

> **Inadequate DRAINAGE behind the wall.** Water adds a **full hydrostatic thrust** (γ_w = 9.81 kN/m³, against an effective soil thrust often around 6) **and** reduces the soil's own strength. The design load can easily **double**.

> **Weep holes and a granular filter drain are not a detail — they are the design.** Blocked weep holes have brought down more walls than any calculation error.

**A note on the tension crack**: in a cohesive backfill the active pressure is negative over a depth **z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a)**. That negative block is ignored — but the **crack fills with water**, and the resulting thrust often exceeds the earth pressure it replaced.

examTip.trap: **B/3 is the WIDTH of the middle-third band**; the **eccentricity limit is half of it, B/6**, measured from the centre. Confusing the band with the limit is the standard slip.
examTip.trick: Derive it in one line: **p = (ΣV/B)(1 ± 6e/B)**, and set the bracket to zero. The **6** in the formula is where the /6 comes from.
examTip.mnemonic: **Four checks: overturning 2.0, sliding 1.5, bearing 3.0, OVERALL SLOPE 1.5** — the last is most often skipped and often governs on a hillside. But the commonest real cause of failure is **blocked drainage**.

questions.stem: Which intersection has no conflict?
questions.solution:
**The clover leaf** — a full grade-separated interchange in which every turning movement is made by a ramp, so **no two traffic streams cross at grade**.

**Types of traffic conflict:**

| Conflict | Description | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **CROSSING** | Two streams cut across each other | **Most dangerous** — head-on or right-angle collision |
| **MERGING** | Two streams join | Moderate |
| **DIVERGING** | One stream splits | Least |
| Weaving | Merging and diverging in sequence over a length | Moderate |

> A simple four-arm at-grade crossroads has **32 conflict points**, of which **16 are crossings** — which is why it is the most hazardous common junction layout.

**How each solution deals with conflict:**

| Solution | Effect |
|---|---|
| **GRADE SEPARATION (clover leaf)** | **ELIMINATES crossing conflicts** — streams pass over or under one another |
| **ROUNDABOUT** | **Converts crossings into WEAVING** — all traffic circulates one way |
| **SIGNALS** | **Separates conflicts in TIME** rather than in space |
| **CHANNELIZATION** | **Guides and reduces** conflicts with islands and markings, but does not eliminate them |

> **Three different answers to the same problem, at three very different costs** — and channelization, being the cheapest, only manages the conflicts rather than removing them.

**The interchange types:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **CLOVER LEAF** | Four indirect loop ramps; **all movements grade-separated**; needs a **lot of land** |
| **DIAMOND** | Simpler, less land; but the ramp terminals are **at-grade junctions** on the minor road |
| **TRUMPET** | For a **T-junction** (three arms) |
| Directional | High-speed direct ramps; most expensive |

> A **diamond** is only partially conflict-free — its ramp terminals still have at-grade conflicts, which is why it is not the answer here. A **trumpet** serves only three arms.

**The clover leaf's own weakness** is worth knowing: the **WEAVING sections** between successive loop ramps are short, and at high volumes they become the capacity constraint. That, plus its large land take, is why **directional and partial-cloverleaf** designs are now more common.

**Roundabout design criteria**, since it is the common alternative:

| Criterion | Value |
|---|---|
| **Weaving angle** | **15 – 40°** — smaller is better |
| **Weaving length** | At least **4 × the entry width** |
| Entry and exit radii | Large enough to keep speeds up |

> A roundabout only works if the **weaving section is long enough** to complete the merge — which is why an undersized rotary performs worse than a signal.

examTip.trick: Only **grade separation** removes crossing conflicts. A **roundabout converts** them to weaving, **signals separate** them in time, and **channelization merely guides** them. Three of the four options do not eliminate anything.
examTip.trap: A **DIAMOND** interchange is grade-separated on the main line but its **ramp terminals are still at-grade junctions** — so it is only partially conflict-free. A **trumpet** serves only three arms.
examTip.mnemonic: **A simple four-arm crossroads has 32 conflict points, 16 of them CROSSINGS** — the most dangerous kind. That number is why grade separation is worth its cost at high volumes.

questions.stem: If m₁ and m₂ are the numbers of members of two individual trusses, the combined compound truss will be determinate if:
questions.solution:
**m = m₁ + m₂ + 3.**

**Why three connecting members.** Two separate rigid trusses, considered as bodies in a plane, have **three relative degrees of freedom** between them — two translations and one rotation. To lock them into a single rigid body, exactly **three** connections are needed.

> **Three members, not concurrent and not parallel**, remove the three relative degrees of freedom and make the compound truss rigid and determinate.

**Verify it with the determinacy formula.** For a plane truss:

> **D_s = m + r − 2j**

> Two determinate trusses joined: the member count is m₁ + m₂ + 3, the joint count is j₁ + j₂ (no new joints if the connecting members span existing ones), and r = 3. Substituting confirms D_s = 0.

**The three standard ways of connecting two trusses:**

| Method | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **Three members** | Not concurrent, not parallel |
| **A hinge plus one member** | The hinge removes two freedoms, the member the third |
| Two hinges | Over-restrained unless one is a roller |

**The critical caveat**, which the arithmetic cannot supply:

> **The three connecting members must NOT be CONCURRENT and must NOT be PARALLEL.**

| Arrangement | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| **Three PARALLEL members** | The two trusses can still **slide** perpendicular to them |
| **Three CONCURRENT members** | The two trusses can still **rotate** about the common point |

> **The count checks DEGREE, not STABILITY.** A compound truss can satisfy m = m₁ + m₂ + 3 exactly and still be a mechanism if the geometry is wrong.

**The parallel with support reactions** is exact and worth noticing:

> A rigid body in a plane needs **three support reactions**, and they too must be **neither parallel nor concurrent**. Connecting two bodies to each other is the same problem as connecting one body to the ground.

**Truss classification:**

| Type | Formation |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE** | Built from a base triangle by adding **two members and one joint** at a time — hence **m = 2j − 3** |
| **COMPOUND** | **Two or more simple trusses** joined rigidly |
| **COMPLEX** | Neither — needs special methods (Henneberg's) |

> A **simple** truss can always be solved by the **method of joints** working outward from a support. A **compound** truss usually needs the **method of sections** to cut the connecting members first, after which each simple truss can be solved on its own.

examTip.trick: Count **degrees of freedom**: two rigid bodies in a plane have **three** relative freedoms (two translations, one rotation), so **three** connections lock them together. The same reasoning gives three support reactions for one body.
examTip.trap: The three members must be **neither PARALLEL nor CONCURRENT** — otherwise the trusses can still slide or rotate. The count gives D_s = 0 and the structure is still a mechanism.
examTip.mnemonic: **Simple truss: m = 2j − 3, built two members and one joint at a time. Compound: two simples plus three connections.** Solve a compound truss by **sections** first, cutting the connectors, then joints on each half.

questions.stem: The coefficient of compressibility of soil is the ratio of:
options: Rate of loading to that of settlement
questions.solution:
**Strain to stress** — the reciprocal of a modulus.

**The precise definition:**

> **a_v = −de/dσ′** — the **coefficient of compressibility**, the change in **void ratio** per unit change in **effective stress**.

> The source explanation notes candidly that **none of the four options matches this exactly**, and that **"strain to stress" is the closest** — which it is, since a change in void ratio is a measure of strain and the denominator is a stress.

**Why it is strain over stress rather than stress over strain:**

> A **modulus** is stress ÷ strain (E, G, K). A **compressibility** is its **reciprocal** — strain ÷ stress. The two names signal opposite ratios, and that is the discriminator here.

> Compare fluid mechanics: **compressibility = 1/K**, the reciprocal of the bulk modulus. The same convention applies.

**The related consolidation parameters:**

| Parameter | Definition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **a_v** — coefficient of compressibility | **−de/dσ′** | Units m²/kN |
| **m_v** — coefficient of volume compressibility | **a_v/(1 + e₀)** | **Volumetric** strain per unit stress; used directly in settlement |
| **C_c** — compression index | Slope of the **e – log σ′** virgin curve | Dimensionless |
| **c_v** — coefficient of consolidation | **k/(m_v γ_w)** | Units **m²/year** — governs the **RATE** |

> **m_v is the one used in practice** for settlement: **S = m_v Δσ H**, which is the simplest of all the settlement expressions.

**The organising distinction:**

> **a_v, m_v and C_c say HOW MUCH settlement. c_v says HOW FAST.**

> A clay may be **highly compressible yet drain quickly**, or **barely compressible yet take decades**. Keeping the two questions apart is the whole of consolidation theory — and only the second is helped by **vertical drains**.

**A caution about a_v**: it is **not a constant**. It varies with the stress level, because the e–σ′ relationship is curved. That is precisely why **C_c**, defined on the **logarithmic** plot where the virgin curve is straight, is preferred for settlement calculations over a range of stress.

**And the settlement expression that follows:**

> **S = (C_c H/(1 + e₀)) log₁₀[(σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀]** for a normally consolidated clay

> For an **over-consolidated** clay the calculation **splits at σ′_c**, using C_r below it and C_c above. Using C_c throughout can **overestimate the settlement five-fold** and buy a foundation that was never needed.

examTip.trick: A **MODULUS** is stress ÷ strain; a **COMPRESSIBILITY** is its **reciprocal**, strain ÷ stress. The name itself tells you which way the ratio runs — the same convention as compressibility = 1/K in fluids.
examTip.trap: None of the four options states the strict definition (**a_v = −de/dσ′**), so this is a "closest match" question. Recognising that the ratio must be **strain over stress** is what decides it.
examTip.mnemonic: **a_v, m_v and C_c say HOW MUCH; c_v says HOW FAST.** Use **m_v** for settlement (S = m_v Δσ H), and **split at σ′_c** for an over-consolidated clay — using C_c throughout can overestimate settlement five-fold.

questions.stem: The number of professional engineers registered by the time 2078/12/31 was approximately:
questions.solution:
**61** (in the relevant category, as recorded by the Council at that date).

**This is a pure recall question** about the Council's registration statistics — the kind that cannot be reasoned out and is either known or not. Such questions appear in every sitting and are among the cheapest marks on the paper for a candidate who has read the Council's material.

**The NEC registration categories** are the substance worth carrying, since they recur in many forms:

| Category | Who |
|---|---|
| **General Engineer** | The standard registration for a graduate engineer |
| **Professional Engineer** | A higher category, requiring further experience |
| Non-Nepali engineer | Foreign nationals practising in Nepal under prescribed conditions |

> The **Professional Engineer** category is small precisely because its experience requirement is substantial — which is why the number is in the dozens rather than the thousands.

**The Council facts most often examined**, worth holding as one block:

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulations** | **2057 BS** |
| **Total members** | **21** |
| **Chairman** | Bachelor's + **15 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Vice-Chairman** | Bachelor's + **10 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Registrar (Member Secretary)** | Bachelor's + **10 years** |
| **Members nominated by the Council itself** | **2** |
| **Members elected from the NEA** | **5** |
| **First Registrar** | Er. Bindeshwar Yadav |
| **Minimum average for institutional affiliation** | **70%** |

**And the standing distinction** that answers most institutional questions:

> **The COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION represents.**

> Registration with the **NEC is a LEGAL REQUIREMENT to practise** — practising or signing drawings without it is an offence under the Act. Membership of the **NEA is voluntary**.

**The Council's functions**, for completeness: register engineers and maintain the register, **recognise** academic institutions and programmes, **prescribe** minimum standards for engineering education and for admission, prepare policy for the profession, **regulate professional conduct** and take disciplinary action, and issue the **license to practise**.

> What it does **not** do: open or run colleges, award degrees, fix fees or salaries, or represent engineers' interests.

examTip.trick: This is **pure recall** and cannot be derived — so treat institutional facts as a memorisation block and take the free marks. Every sitting carries several.
examTip.trap: The four options are close together (41, 51, 61, 71), so there is no way to reason toward an answer. Guess if you must, but the whole block is cheap to learn.
examTip.mnemonic: **Act 2055, Regulations 2057, 21 members, chairman 15 years, VP and Registrar 10 years, 2 nominated by the Council, 5 elected from the NEA, 70% for affiliation.** Learn the block, not the isolated figures.

questions.stem: The formula for the ultimate bearing capacity of a square footing is:
questions.solution:
**q_u = 1.3 c N_c + q N_q + 0.4 γ B N_γ.**

**The shape factors** applied to Terzaghi's strip-footing equation:

| Shape | Cohesion term | Width term |
|---|---|---|
| **Strip** (the base case) | **1.0** c N_c | **0.5** γBN_γ |
| **SQUARE** | **1.3** c N_c | **0.4** γBN_γ |
| **Circular** | **1.3** c N_c | **0.3** γBN_γ |
| Rectangular | (1 + 0.2B/L) | (1 − 0.2B/L) |

> **Note that the surcharge term qN_q is UNCHANGED** for every shape — only the cohesion and width terms carry shape factors.

**The two factors move in OPPOSITE directions**, which is the substance of the question:

| Term | Square vs strip | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Cohesion** | **INCREASED** to 1.3 | A square footing's failure surface is **confined on all four sides**, so more cohesive resistance is mobilised |
| **Width** | **REDUCED** to 0.4 | The failure wedge is **smaller relative to the width**, so the self-weight contribution is less |

> **Options (b) and (c) each get one factor right and the other wrong** — which is exactly what the distractor set is designed to catch.

**Check the circular case as a memory aid**: it is **1.3 and 0.3** — the same cohesion factor as a square, but a smaller width factor still, because a circle's wedge is smaller again.

**The three terms and what each contributes:**

| Term | From | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **c N_c** | **Cohesion** | c |
| **q N_q** | **Surcharge** above founding level | **DEPTH** D_f |
| **0.4 γ B N_γ** | **Self-weight of the failure wedge** | **WIDTH** B |

**Two consequences worth carrying:**

> For **pure clay (φ = 0)**: **N_γ = 0**, so the **width term vanishes** and the bearing capacity is **INDEPENDENT of the footing width**. Widening a footing on clay carries more total load but not more pressure.

> For **sand (c = 0)**: the cohesion term vanishes and capacity depends on **depth and width** alone.

**The other corrections that apply in practice (IS 6403):**

| Correction | When |
|---|---|
| **Local shear reduction** (c′ = ⅔c, tan φ′ = ⅔tan φ) | Loose or soft soil |
| **Depth factors** | Where D_f is significant |
| **Inclination factors** | Inclined loading |
| **WATER TABLE correction** (R_w1, R_w2) | Can **HALVE** a sand's capacity |

> And the final step: **q_ns = (q_u − γD_f)/F** with **F = 2.5–3**, applied to the **NET** value — then take the **lesser** of that and the settlement-limited pressure.

examTip.trick: The two shape factors move in **OPPOSITE directions**: cohesion **up** to 1.3 (the wedge is confined on four sides), width **down** to 0.4 (the wedge is smaller relative to B). Options (b) and (c) each get one right and one wrong.
examTip.trap: The **surcharge term qN_q is UNCHANGED** for every shape — only the cohesion and width terms carry factors. An option that alters qN_q is wrong on that ground alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Strip 1.0/0.5, SQUARE 1.3/0.4, CIRCLE 1.3/0.3.** And for **pure clay N_γ = 0**, so bearing capacity is **independent of footing width** — widening carries more load, not more pressure.

questions.stem: Which type of formwork is best for repetitive use?
questions.solution:
**Steel.**

**Why steel is best for repeated use:**

| Property | Steel formwork |
|---|---|
| **Number of reuses** | **100 to 200 times** — by far the highest |
| Dimensional stability | **Does not warp, swell or shrink** with moisture |
| Surface finish produced | **Smooth and consistent**, often needing no plastering |
| Watertightness | Excellent — no grout leakage at joints |
| Strength-to-thickness | High, so thin panels carry the pressure |

**The comparison across materials:**

| Material | Reuses | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Timber** | **10 – 12** | Cheap, easily worked on site; but **warps and absorbs water** |
| **Plywood** | **20 – 30** | Larger panels, better finish than sawn timber |
| **STEEL** | **100 – 200** | **Highest initial cost, lowest cost per use** |
| Aluminium | High | Light and reusable, but **softer and more easily damaged**, and it **reacts with wet concrete** unless coated |

> **The economics turn entirely on the number of repetitions.** Steel's high first cost is spread over so many uses that its **cost per pour is the lowest** — provided the job actually has the repetition to justify it. For a single villa, timber is cheaper; for a fifteen-storey block of identical floors, steel is far cheaper.

**Why aluminium is not the answer** despite also being reusable: it is **softer**, dents more easily on a construction site, and **reacts chemically with the alkalis in wet concrete**, staining the surface and pitting the panel unless it is properly coated. Aluminium systems exist and work well, but steel is the standard answer for durability under repetition.

**Formwork's real significance on a project:**

> **Formwork is typically 30–40% of the cost of a concrete structure** — often more than the concrete and steel combined. Which is why **repetition in the design** (identical floor heights, repeating bay sizes, standard column dimensions) saves more money than almost any other decision an engineer makes.

**Striking times (IS 456)** — the other formwork fact that is regularly examined:

| Member | Ordinary Portland cement |
|---|---|
| Vertical faces of walls, columns, beam sides | **16 – 24 hours** |
| Soffit of slabs (props left under) | **3 days** |
| **Slab props, span up to 4.5 m** | **7 days** |
| **Beam soffits, props left under** | **7 days** |
| **Beam props, span up to 6 m** | **14 days** |
| **Beam props, span over 6 m** | **21 days** |

> **The props matter more than the panels.** Striking a beam's side shutters early is harmless; removing its props early is how young concrete beams fail. And **back-propping** during multi-storey construction is what stops a freshly cast floor being loaded through the props above it before it has the strength to take it.

examTip.trick: Judge by **cost per use, not first cost**. Steel costs most to buy and least per pour — **100–200 reuses** against 10–12 for timber and 20–30 for plywood.
examTip.trap: **Aluminium** is the near-miss: it is light and reusable, but it is **softer** and **reacts with wet concrete** unless coated. Steel is the durable standard.
examTip.mnemonic: **Formwork is 30–40% of a concrete structure's cost** — often more than the concrete and steel together. So designing for **repetition** saves more than almost any other decision. And **props matter more than panels**: beam props stay 14–21 days.

questions.stem: The second moment of area of a triangle about its base is:
questions.solution:
**bh³/12** about the base.

**The two triangle values, which are constantly confused:**

| Axis | Second moment |
|---|---|
| **About the CENTROIDAL axis** (parallel to the base, at h/3) | **bh³/36** |
| **About the BASE** | **bh³/12** |

> The base value is **THREE TIMES** the centroidal value, and the parallel axis theorem shows exactly why.

**Verification by the parallel axis theorem:**

> **I_base = I_centroid + A d²**
> **= bh³/36 + (½bh)(h/3)²**
> **= bh³/36 + bh³/18**
> **= bh³/36 + 2bh³/36 = 3bh³/36 = bh³/12** ✓

> The check takes ten seconds and removes any doubt about which value goes with which axis.

**Standard second moments of area:**

| Shape | About the centroid | About the base |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × h** | **bh³/12** | **bh³/3** |
| **Triangle b × h** | **bh³/36** | **bh³/12** |
| **Circle diameter d** | **πd⁴/64** | — |
| Semicircle | 0.11 r⁴ | πr⁴/8 |

> **Note the coincidence that traps candidates: bh³/12 is the RECTANGLE's CENTROIDAL value AND the TRIANGLE's BASE value.** The same expression means two different things depending on the shape, and offering it as an option here is no accident.

**The parallel axis theorem itself:**

> **I = I_centroid + A d²** — and the added term is **always positive**, so **the centroidal axis always gives the MINIMUM second moment**. If a calculation produces a smaller value about some other axis, it is wrong.

**Where these values are used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bending stress** | **σ = My/I** |
| **Section modulus** | **Z = I/y_max** |
| **Deflection** | **δ ∝ 1/EI** |
| **Buckling** | **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**, using the **MINIMUM** I |
| Composite sections | Sum the parts, each transferred by the parallel axis theorem |

> For **buckling** always use the **least** second moment — a column buckles about its **weak axis**, and using I about the strong axis is a serious and common error.

**A note on the polar second moment**: **J = I_xx + I_yy** (the perpendicular axis theorem, valid for **plane laminae only**). For a circle, **J = πd⁴/32**, which is exactly twice πd⁴/64.

examTip.trick: Check it with the **parallel axis theorem in ten seconds**: bh³/36 + (½bh)(h/3)² = bh³/36 + 2bh³/36 = **bh³/12** ✓. No recall needed.
examTip.trap: **bh³/12 is the RECTANGLE's CENTROIDAL value AND the TRIANGLE's BASE value** — the same expression with two meanings. Offering it here is deliberate.
examTip.mnemonic: **Triangle: /36 about the centroid, /12 about the base — three times.** And since I = I_c + Ad² always **adds**, the **centroidal axis gives the minimum** — a value smaller than that is arithmetic gone wrong.

questions.stem: What is the section modulus of a hollow circular section of external diameter D and internal diameter d?
questions.solution:
**Z = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32 D).**

**Derivation.**

> **I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64** for a hollow circular section
> **y_max = D/2** — the extreme fibre is at the **outside** surface
> **Z = I/y_max = [π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64] ÷ (D/2) = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32 D)** ✓

> **Dividing by D/2 doubles the expression**, turning the 64 into a 32. Forgetting that step gives option (a), which is the most-picked wrong answer.

**Check by setting d = 0** (a solid circle):

> **Z = πD⁴/(32D) = πD³/32** ✓ — the standard solid circular section modulus.

> That check works on any of these formulae and catches an algebra slip instantly.

**Note option (d) is dimensionally wrong**: a section modulus must have dimensions of **length³**, and π(D³ − d³)/32 does have them — but subtracting **cubes** rather than fourth powers is not how second moments combine. Second moments are additive as **fourth powers**, and only the final division by y_max reduces the order.

**Standard section moduli:**

| Section | Z |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × h** | **bh²/6** |
| **Solid circle** | **πd³/32** |
| **Hollow circle** | **π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D)** |
| Hollow rectangle | (BH³ − bh³)/(6H) |

**Why hollow sections are efficient**, which is the substance behind the formula:

> **Material near the neutral axis contributes almost nothing** to bending resistance, because its stress (σ = My/I) is nearly zero. Removing it costs little strength and saves a great deal of weight.

> A hollow section with d = D/2 loses only **1/16 of its second moment** (since I ∝ D⁴ and (1/2)⁴ = 1/16) while removing **1/4 of the area**. That is a very favourable exchange.

**The same logic explains the I-section**: it places material in **flanges** far from the neutral axis, where it is stressed most, and keeps only a thin **web** to carry the shear.

**A caution about buckling**: for a **column**, the relevant property is the **radius of gyration r = √(I/A)**, and a hollow section is far better again — a tube has a **large r for its area in every direction**, which is why it is the natural shape for a strut. A solid bar of the same area buckles at a fraction of the load.

examTip.trick: Set **d = 0** and check you recover the solid value **πD³/32**. Only option (b) does. That single substitution settles it without recalling anything.
examTip.trap: Option (a) keeps the **64** from I and forgets that dividing by **y = D/2 DOUBLES** it. That omission is the most common error in the whole topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Material near the neutral axis does almost nothing.** A hollow section with d = D/2 loses **1/16 of I** while shedding **1/4 of the area** — which is the whole argument for tubes, and for the I-section's flanges.

questions.stem:
Match List I with List II.

**List I:** A. Capillarity  B. Vapour pressure  C. Viscosity  D. Specific gravity

**List II:** a. Cavitation  b. Ratio of density to that of water  c. Rate of angular deformation  d. Surface tension
questions.solution:
**A-d, B-a, C-c, D-b.**

**Each pairing:**

| Property | Paired with | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Capillarity** | **d. Surface tension** | Capillary rise is caused **entirely** by surface tension acting at the meniscus: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd)** |
| **B. Vapour pressure** | **a. Cavitation** | **Cavitation occurs when the local pressure falls to the VAPOUR PRESSURE** — vapour bubbles form and then collapse violently |
| **C. Viscosity** | **c. Rate of angular deformation** | **Newton's law: τ = μ(du/dy)**, and du/dy **IS** the rate of angular deformation of a fluid element |
| **D. Specific gravity** | **b. Ratio of density to that of water** | The definition — dimensionless, water at 4 °C as the reference |

**On the viscosity–deformation pairing**, which is the one most worth understanding:

> The defining difference between a **solid** and a **fluid**: a solid's shear stress is proportional to the **AMOUNT** of deformation (**τ = Gγ**); a fluid's is proportional to the **RATE** of deformation (**τ = μ dγ/dt**).

> **A fluid cannot resist shear at rest, however small the stress** — it simply keeps deforming. That single sentence defines what a fluid is.

**On cavitation**, which is the engineering consequence in this list:

> Where the pressure drops to the vapour pressure — at a **pump suction**, on a **turbine runner's low-pressure side**, at a **valve throat**, or on a **spillway** where the nappe lifts off — **vapour bubbles form**. Carried to a higher-pressure region, they **collapse implosively**, generating local pressures high enough to **pit steel and concrete**.

| Symptom | Note |
|---|---|
| Noise like gravel in the pump | The bubbles collapsing |
| Vibration | — |
| **Pitting** of metal surfaces | The damage itself |
| **Loss of head and efficiency** | The performance cost |

> The remedy is expressed through **NPSH**: the available net positive suction head must **exceed** the pump's required NPSH — which is why pumps are set **low** and suction pipes kept **short, large and free of high points**.

> Note that **vapour pressure RISES with temperature**, so **hot water cavitates far more readily**. A pump handling hot liquid needs much more submergence than the same pump on cold water.

**And a note on specific gravity**: being a **ratio of two densities** it is **dimensionless**, which is why it is the same number in every system of units — a genuine practical convenience.

examTip.trick: On a matching question, **anchor the pair you are surest of and eliminate**. **Vapour pressure → cavitation** is unmistakable, and only one option contains it.
examTip.trap: Option (a) is the lazy "in order" answer A-a, B-b, C-c, D-d — offered on almost every matching question precisely because it needs no thought.
examTip.mnemonic: **A solid resists the AMOUNT of shear strain (τ = Gγ); a fluid resists only its RATE (τ = μdγ/dt).** That is what makes something a fluid. And vapour pressure **rises with temperature**, so hot liquids cavitate far more readily.

questions.stem: The sequent depth ratio of a hydraulic jump in a rectangular horizontal channel is 16.48. What is the Froude number of the supercritical flow?
questions.solution:
**Fr₁ = 12.**

**Working.** The sequent depth relation is:

> **y₂/y₁ = ½[√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1]**

Substituting **y₂/y₁ = 16.48** and solving for Fr₁:

> **2 × 16.48 + 1 = √(1 + 8Fr₁²)**
> **33.96 = √(1 + 8Fr₁²)**
> **1153.3 = 1 + 8Fr₁²**
> **Fr₁² = 1152.3/8 = 144.0**
> **Fr₁ = 12** ✓

**A useful shortcut for large Froude numbers:**

> When Fr is large, **8Fr² ≫ 1**, so **√(1 + 8Fr²) ≈ 2.83 Fr** and:
> **y₂/y₁ ≈ 1.41 Fr − 0.5**

> Checking: 1.41 × 12 − 0.5 = **16.4** ✓ — close enough to identify the answer at once. Rearranged, **Fr ≈ (y₂/y₁ + 0.5)/1.41 = 16.98/1.41 = 12.0**.

> That approximation is worth carrying because it turns a two-minute algebraic rearrangement into a ten-second estimate.

**What Fr₁ = 12 means physically:**

| Fr₁ | Jump type | Energy loss |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 – 1.7 | Undular | < 5% |
| 1.7 – 2.5 | Weak | 5 – 15% |
| **2.5 – 4.5** | **Oscillating — AVOID** | 15 – 45% |
| **4.5 – 9.0** | **Steady — best for a stilling basin** | 45 – 70% |
| **> 9.0** | **STRONG** | **70 – 85%** |

> **Fr₁ = 12 is a STRONG jump** — very effective at dissipating energy (over 80% lost) but with a rough, choppy surface. It occurs below high-head spillways, where the approach flow is very fast and shallow.

**The corresponding energy loss:**

> **E_L = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂)**

> With y₂ = 16.48 y₁, this gives **E_L ≈ (15.48 y₁)³/(4 × 16.48 y₁²) = 56.3 y₁** — a very large loss indeed, which is precisely the purpose of the jump.

**And the design consequence:**

> A strong jump generates **high velocities and severe turbulence** in the basin, so its floor and walls need **substantial protection** — and the basin must be long enough, roughly **6 y₂**, which for a large y₂/y₁ ratio makes it a long structure.

> The **tailwater must actually supply y₂**. If it does not, the jump **sweeps out** of the paved basin and undermines it — the failure mode that destroys spillway aprons.

examTip.trick: Rearrange rather than trial-and-error: **2(y₂/y₁) + 1 = √(1 + 8Fr²)**, so **33.96² = 1153.3**, **Fr² = 144**, **Fr = 12**. Two lines.
examTip.trap: For large Fr the shortcut **y₂/y₁ ≈ 1.41Fr − 0.5** gives 16.4 against the exact 16.48 — accurate enough to pick the option in ten seconds. Learn it; it converts a two-minute problem into a glance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fr = 12 is a STRONG jump (>9)** — over 80% of the energy destroyed, but a rough surface needing heavy floor protection and a basin about **6 y₂** long. And the **tailwater must supply y₂**, or the jump sweeps out.

questions.stem: At a section where the shear force is zero, the bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**Maximum** (strictly, a **stationary value** — a maximum or a minimum).

**Why.** The fundamental relation between shear and moment is:

> **V = dM/dx**

> So **V = 0 means dM/dx = 0**, which is the condition for a **turning point** in the bending moment diagram. Standard calculus: where the derivative vanishes, the function is stationary.

**The complete set of relations:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| The **shear is the SLOPE** of the moment diagram | dM/dx = V |
| **V = 0 marks a moment peak** | The turning point |
| The **change in M equals the AREA of the shear diagram** | ΔM = ∫V dx |
| The change in V equals the area of the load diagram | ΔV = −∫w dx |

> **The area rule is the fastest way to draw a BMD by hand** — no integration needed, only the areas of rectangles and triangles under the SFD.

**Worked check for a simply supported beam under a UDL:**

> **V(x) = wL/2 − wx**, which is zero at **x = L/2**
> **M(L/2) = wL²/8** — the maximum ✓

**The strict qualification** that makes "maximum" the intended answer here rather than the exact one:

> V = 0 gives a **stationary** value, which may be a maximum **or a minimum**. On a **continuous beam** the span moment at V = 0 is a **local maximum (sagging)** while the **support moment is a larger hogging value** — and the support moment does **not** occur where V = 0. It occurs where V **changes sign abruptly** at the reaction.

> So on a continuous beam the **greatest moment in the whole beam is usually at a support, where V is NOT zero**. Searching only for V = 0 would miss it entirely.

**The other cases where the maximum is not at V = 0:**

| Case | Maximum moment at |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | The **fixed end** — where V is greatest, not zero |
| **Continuous beam** | Often at an **interior support** |
| Beam with an applied **couple** | At the **step** in the BMD |

> **Always check the ends and the supports as well as the V = 0 points.** The design moment is the largest anywhere in the beam, not merely the largest stationary value.

**A note on the sign convention**: with sagging positive, a beam under gravity load on simple supports has a positive (sagging) moment throughout, and the maximum sagging moment governs the **bottom** steel. Where the moment is **hogging** — at a continuous support or on a cantilever — the tension is in the **TOP**, and that is where the main steel must go.

examTip.trick: **V = dM/dx**, so V = 0 is where the moment diagram turns. It is calculus, not a rule to memorise — and the same relation says **ΔM = area of the SFD**, which is the fastest way to draw a BMD by hand.
examTip.trap: V = 0 gives a **stationary** value, not necessarily the **largest** one. On a **cantilever** the maximum is at the **fixed end**, and on a **continuous beam** often at a **support** — neither of which has V = 0.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the ends and supports as well as the V = 0 points.** And remember which face the steel goes in: **sagging → bottom, hogging → top** — a continuous beam needs both.

questions.stem: The effective length of a column with both ends fixed is:
questions.solution:
**L/2** — that is, **0.5 L**.

**The effective length table** (theoretical values):

| End conditions | **L_e** | Relative buckling load |
|---|---|---|
| **Both ends FIXED** | **0.5 L** | **4 ×** the pinned case |
| **One fixed, one pinned** | **0.707 L** | 2 × |
| **Both ends PINNED** | **1.0 L** | **1 ×** (the reference) |
| **One fixed, one FREE** (cantilever) | **2.0 L** | **1/4 ×** |

> **The whole range spans a factor of SIXTEEN in buckling load** — from 4× down to ¼×. Nothing else in structural design is so sensitive to a detail as small as how the ends are held.

**Euler's formula:**

> **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**

> Since L_e is **squared**, halving it **quadruples** the critical load. That is why fixing both ends of a column is worth so much — and why an unintended **free end** is so dangerous.

**The one to fear is 2L**, the cantilever case:

> A column free at the top carries only **a quarter** of what the same column would carry pinned at both ends — and **a sixteenth** of the fixed–fixed value. Unbraced columns in a construction sequence, temporary props, and scaffold standards missing a tie are all in this category.

**Design values are more conservative than the theory:**

> **IS 456 (concrete)** and **IS 800 (steel)** give **higher** values than the theoretical ones — for instance **0.65 L** rather than 0.5 L for fixed–fixed — because **a real "fixed" end is never perfectly rigid.** The connection rotates a little, and the code allows for it.

> **Never use the theoretical value in design.** Assuming a perfect fixity that the detail does not deliver is unconservative in the one direction where the penalty is a sudden collapse.

**The slenderness ratio** and the limit of Euler's theory:

> **λ = L_e/r**, where **r = √(I/A)** is the radius of gyration, taken about the **MINIMUM** axis — a column buckles about its **weak axis**.

| Slenderness | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **λ < 12** (concrete) | **SHORT** column — fails by **crushing** |
| λ > 12 | **SLENDER** — buckling reduces the capacity |
| **λ > ~100** (steel) | Euler's elastic formula applies |
| λ moderate | **Inelastic** buckling — Euler **OVERESTIMATES**; use **Rankine** or the code curves |

> **Euler's formula is unsafe for intermediate slenderness**, because it takes no account of yielding. **Rankine's formula — 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler — bridges both ends** and is the safer general expression.

**And the practical point**: bracing a column at midheight **halves L** and therefore **quadruples** its buckling capacity — usually far cheaper than enlarging the section.

examTip.trick: The sequence is **0.5 / 0.707 / 1.0 / 2.0** as the restraint is progressively released — fixed-fixed, fixed-pinned, pinned-pinned, cantilever. Since **P_cr ∝ 1/L_e²**, that is a **sixteen-fold** range in capacity.
examTip.trap: **Codes use higher values than the theory** — IS 456 gives 0.65 L, not 0.5 L, because a real fixed end always rotates a little. Using the theoretical value in design is unconservative.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bracing at midheight halves L and QUADRUPLES the buckling load** — almost always cheaper than a bigger section. And always take **r about the MINIMUM axis**: a column buckles the weak way.

questions.stem: In risk management, mitigation means:
options: Transferring the risk to another party
Accepting the risk and its consequences
Reducing the probability or impact of the risk to an acceptable level
Eliminating the risk completely by changing the project scope
questions.solution:
**Reducing the probability or the impact of the risk to an acceptable level.**

**The four standard risk responses** for a **negative** risk (a threat):

| Response | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **AVOID** | **Eliminate** the risk by changing the plan or scope | Reroute an alignment away from an unstable slope |
| **TRANSFER** | Shift the **impact and ownership** to a third party | **Insurance**, performance bonds, a fixed-price subcontract |
| **MITIGATE** | **REDUCE the probability or the impact** to an acceptable level | Ground improvement; extra site investigation; prototyping |
| **ACCEPT** | Take no action; absorb the consequence | Set a **contingency reserve** (active) or simply monitor (passive) |

> Each of the four wrong-sounding options in this question is in fact the definition of one of the **other** three responses — which is what makes it a clean test of whether the four are distinguished or merely half-remembered.

| Option | Which response it defines |
|---|---|
| "Transferring to another party" | **TRANSFER** |
| "Accepting the risk and its consequences" | **ACCEPT** |
| "Eliminating completely by changing the scope" | **AVOID** |

**The key distinction:**

> **Mitigation REDUCES; avoidance ELIMINATES; transfer MOVES; acceptance ABSORBS.**

> Note that **transfer does not reduce the risk** — insurance does not stop the flood, it only pays for it. And **the residual risk always remains with the project**: a subcontractor who goes bankrupt returns the risk to you.

**For a POSITIVE risk (an opportunity)** the four mirror responses are **exploit, share, enhance and accept**.

**The risk management process:**

| Step | Activity |
|---|---|
| **1. Identify** | Brainstorming, checklists, expert judgement, lessons learned |
| **2. Analyse — qualitative** | **Probability × Impact matrix**; rank and prioritise |
| **3. Analyse — quantitative** | Expected monetary value, sensitivity, **Monte Carlo** |
| **4. Plan responses** | Avoid / transfer / mitigate / accept |
| **5. Monitor and control** | Track the register; watch for new risks |

> **The risk register is a living document**, not a one-off deliverable. A register written at tender and never revisited has no value.

**When risk management pays:**

> Risks are **cheapest to address EARLY**, in the **feasibility and design** phases, where the ability to influence is high and the cost of change is low. By the time a risk materialises in construction, the response options have narrowed to the expensive ones.

> **Which is exactly why risk analysis belongs at feasibility**, in the phase that spends the least and decides the most.

examTip.trick: **Each wrong option is the definition of one of the OTHER three responses** — transfer, accept, avoid. Recognising that turns the question into a straight four-way match.
examTip.trap: **Transfer does not reduce risk** — insurance does not stop the flood, it pays for it. And the **residual risk stays with the project**: a subcontractor who goes bankrupt hands it straight back.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mitigation REDUCES, avoidance ELIMINATES, transfer MOVES, acceptance ABSORBS.** Address risks in **feasibility**, where influence is high and change is cheap — by construction the options are all expensive.

questions.stem: Which type of pictorial sketch shows the front face in its true shape?
questions.solution:
**Oblique** projection.

**What distinguishes each pictorial view:**

| Projection | Front face | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **OBLIQUE** | **TRUE SHAPE and true size** | The front face is drawn as a normal orthographic view; depth is projected at an angle (usually 45°) |
| **ISOMETRIC** | **DISTORTED** | All three axes equally inclined, **120° apart**; no face is true shape |
| **Perspective** | Distorted | Converging lines to vanishing points — most realistic to the eye |
| **Axonometric** | Distorted | The family (isometric, dimetric, trimetric) of which isometric is one type |

> **Only oblique preserves one face undistorted**, and that is precisely why it is used.

**The advantage of oblique projection:**

> Place the **most complex face — the one with circles, arcs and curved detail — at the FRONT**. It can then be drawn with compasses as a normal view, instead of laboriously as an ellipse.

> **Circles in an isometric view become ELLIPSES** and are tedious to construct accurately. In oblique they stay circles, provided the face is at the front.

**The two oblique variants:**

| Variant | Depth scale |
|---|---|
| **CAVALIER** | **Full scale** — depth looks **exaggerated** |
| **CABINET** | **HALF scale** — looks far more natural |

> **Cabinet projection halves the depth** precisely because the eye finds full-scale depth in an oblique view distinctly wrong.

**Isometric details** for contrast:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Axes** | **120° apart** — the two horizontal axes at **30°** to the horizontal |
| **Isometric scale** | **≈ 0.816** (√2/√3) of the true length |
| Isometric **drawing** | Uses **true lengths** — simpler and far more common |
| Isometric **projection** | Uses the 0.816 scale — technically correct, rarely used |

> **In practice "isometric" almost always means the isometric DRAWING**, at full scale, because the 0.816 reduction adds work for no practical gain.

**Pictorial versus orthographic:**

> A **pictorial** view shows three faces at once and is immediately understandable — good for assembly instructions and for explaining an idea. But it is **not dimensionally reliable** for manufacture.

> **Orthographic projection** — front, top and side views — is what a workshop builds from, because every view is a true shape in its own plane.

**And the essential orthographic convention:**

| System | Top view |
|---|---|
| **FIRST angle** (ISO, India, Nepal) | **BELOW** the front view |
| **THIRD angle** (USA) | **ABOVE** the front view |

> Every drawing must carry the **projection symbol** in its title block, because **a drawing read in the wrong system is a mirror image of the intended part**.

examTip.trick: **Only OBLIQUE keeps a face true.** In isometric all three axes are equally inclined, so nothing is true shape — which is why isometric circles become **ellipses**.
examTip.trap: **Axonometric** is the near-miss: it is the **family** that contains isometric, dimetric and trimetric — none of which preserves a true face.
examTip.mnemonic: **Put the face with the circles at the FRONT in oblique** — they stay circles instead of becoming ellipses. And use **CABINET** (half-scale depth) rather than **cavalier** (full scale), which looks wrong to the eye.

questions.stem: The formula for calculating superelevation for hilly roads is:
questions.solution:
**e = V²/(225 R)**, with V in km/h and R in metres.

**Where the 225 comes from.** The full equilibrium relation is:

> **e + f = V²/(127 R)**

> But superelevation is designed for **75% of the design speed**, so that slow-moving vehicles are not made to slide inward on a steeply banked curve. Substituting **0.75V** and neglecting friction:

> **e = (0.75V)²/(127R) = 0.5625 V²/(127R) = V²/(225.8 R) ≈ V²/(225R)** ✓

> **The 225 is simply 127 ÷ 0.75².** Knowing that derivation means the formula never has to be memorised, and it explains **why** the design is not done at full speed.

**The design procedure (IRC), in order:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Calculate **e = V²/(225R)** ignoring friction |
| **2** | If **e ≤ e_max**, adopt it |
| **3** | If e exceeds e_max, **set e = e_max** and check that **f ≤ 0.15** at full design speed |
| **4** | If f still exceeds 0.15, **restrict the speed** or increase the radius |

**Maximum superelevation:**

| Terrain | e_max |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling** | **7%** |
| **Hilly, not snow bound** | **10%** |
| **Snow bound** | **7%** |
| Urban roads | 4% |

> **Snow-bound roads are limited to 7% even in the hills**, because a steeply banked icy road makes a **stationary or slow vehicle slide inward and off the carriageway**. The steeper bank that helps a fast vehicle endangers a slow one.

**The maximum radius beyond which superelevation is unnecessary**: where the camber alone provides the required tilt.

**The related design values:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Minimum radius** | **R = V²/(127(e + f))** |
| **Lateral friction coefficient** | **f = 0.15** for design |
| **Extra widening** | **B_e = nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** |
| **Transition curve length** | The **greatest** of three criteria |

**The transition curve** deserves its own note, since it is where superelevation is introduced:

> A **SPIRAL (clothoid)** is used, because its **radius decreases uniformly with length** — exactly matching how a driver turns the steering wheel at a steady rate. The **superelevation is attained gradually over its length**.

> The length is the **greatest** of: the **rate of change of radial acceleration** criterion (**L = 0.0215V³/CR**), the **rate of superelevation application** (1 in 150 for hills), and the **IRC empirical** value.

> **A curve without a transition forces an instantaneous change in radial acceleration** — the driver must jerk the wheel, and the superelevation must appear abruptly. Both are unsafe and uncomfortable.

examTip.trick: **225 = 127 ÷ 0.75²** — superelevation is designed for **75% of the design speed** so that slow vehicles are not made to slide inward. Knowing the derivation means never memorising the number.
examTip.trap: **v²/127R** is the full equilibrium relation for **e + f together**, not for e alone. It is the most-picked wrong answer here.
examTip.mnemonic: **e_max: 7% plain, 10% hilly, but back to 7% if SNOW BOUND** — a steeply banked icy road slides a stationary vehicle off the inside. And the **transition curve** is a spiral because its radius falls uniformly with length, matching how a driver turns the wheel.

questions.stem: In a uniform flow, if Manning's roughness coefficient is doubled while the velocity and hydraulic radius are unchanged, the bed slope becomes:
questions.solution:
**Quadruple** — four times the original slope.

**Working.** Manning's equation is:

> **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**

Rearranging for the slope:

> **S^{1/2} = Vn/R^{2/3}**, so **S = V²n²/R^{4/3}**

> With V and R held constant, **S ∝ n²**.

> **Doubling n therefore multiplies S by 2² = 4** ✓

**The physical reading is worth having:**

> A rougher channel resists the flow more, so to drive the **same velocity** through it, the slope must be **steeper**. And because the resistance goes as n², the slope penalty is **quadratic**, not linear.

> That is why **channel lining pays so handsomely**: halving n (from an earth channel's 0.025 to a concrete lining's 0.014, roughly) allows the **same discharge on about a third of the slope** — or, on the same slope, a substantially **smaller section**.

**Typical Manning's n values:**

| Surface | n |
|---|---|
| **Smooth concrete, well finished** | **0.012** |
| Ordinary concrete lining | 0.014 |
| Brickwork | 0.015 |
| **Earth channel, clean and straight** | **0.022** |
| Earth channel, weedy or winding | **0.030** |
| **Natural stream, clean** | **0.030** |
| Natural stream, stony and irregular | 0.040 – 0.070 |

> **Note the whole practical range is only about 0.012 to 0.07** — a factor of six. But since **S ∝ n²**, that becomes a factor of **36** in slope, which is why estimating n well matters so much in natural channel work.

**How the other quantities scale**, at constant slope:

| Quantity | Dependence |
|---|---|
| **V** | **∝ 1/n** and **∝ R^{2/3}** and **∝ S^{1/2}** |
| **Q = AV** | ∝ A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}/n |
| **S** (at fixed V, R) | **∝ n²** |

**The most efficient section** is worth noting alongside:

> For a given area, the section with the **least wetted perimeter** carries the most — because **R = A/P** is then greatest.

| Shape | Most efficient proportions |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **b = 2y** — width twice the depth; then **R = y/2** |
| **Trapezoidal** | A **half-hexagon**, side slope 1:√3 (60°) |
| **Any shape at all** | A **SEMICIRCLE** — the theoretical optimum |

> **For every efficient section, R = y/2** — a neat and genuinely useful result.

**A caution about Manning's equation**: it is **empirical and dimensionally inhomogeneous** — the 1/n carries hidden units and the formula as written applies **only in SI**. In foot-pound units the coefficient becomes 1.486/n.

examTip.trick: Rearrange first: **S = V²n²/R^{4/3}**, so **S ∝ n²**. Doubling n quadruples S. Working from the rearranged form removes any chance of getting the power wrong.
examTip.trap: The relation is **quadratic, not linear** — "double" is the intuitive and wrong answer, and it is deliberately offered.
examTip.mnemonic: **S ∝ n² is why LINING pays** — halving n lets the same discharge run on about a third of the slope. And for **every efficient section R = y/2**; a **semicircle** is the theoretical optimum, a **half-hexagon** the best trapezoid.

questions.stem: According to Shields, the entrainment function for the beginning of sediment motion in a turbulent boundary layer is:
questions.solution:
**0.056.**

**What the Shields parameter is:**

> **θ = τ₀/[(γ_s − γ) d]**

> a **dimensionless** ratio of the **driving bed shear stress** to the **submerged weight of a grain** — the force trying to move the particle against the force holding it down.

> **For fully turbulent flow over a rough bed, the critical value is θ_c = 0.056**, and it becomes **constant** in that regime — independent of the particle Reynolds number. That constancy is what makes the number so useful.

**The Shields diagram** plots θ_c against the **particle Reynolds number R* = u*d/ν**:

| Regime | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Low R*** (fine sediment, smooth bed) | θ_c **varies** — the grains sit within the viscous sublayer |
| **Minimum** at R* ≈ 10 | θ_c ≈ 0.03 |
| **High R* > ~400** (coarse, fully rough) | **θ_c = 0.056, CONSTANT** |

> Note that **0.03 is the minimum of the curve** and it is offered as a distractor — it is a real value on the diagram, just not the fully-turbulent one the question asks for.

**Using it — the critical shear stress:**

> **τ_c = 0.056 (γ_s − γ) d**

> With γ_s = 26 kN/m³ and γ = 9.81 kN/m³, **τ_c ≈ 0.9 d** in kN/m² for d in metres — or roughly **0.9 N/m² for each millimetre of grain size**. A handy rule for a quick check.

**And the bed shear stress in a channel:**

> **τ₀ = γ R S**

> Comparing τ₀ with τ_c decides whether the bed moves. That comparison is the **TRACTIVE FORCE method** of stable channel design — the modern successor to Kennedy's and Lacey's empirical regime theories.

**Why the tractive force approach is better:**

| Approach | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Kennedy** | A **critical VELOCITY** for non-silting, non-scouring |
| **Lacey** | A **regime** relation covering width, depth and slope together |
| **SHIELDS / tractive force** | The actual **FORCE on the grain** — a physical criterion, not an empirical fit |

> Velocity-based criteria are indirect: **it is the shear stress at the bed, not the mean velocity, that actually moves a grain.** Two channels with the same mean velocity can have very different bed shear.

**A practical refinement**: on the **SIDE SLOPES** of a channel the grain's own weight has a component down the slope helping the flow move it, so the **permissible shear on the sides is LOWER** than on the bed — typically by a factor of about 0.75. Designing the sides to the bed value is a real and common error.

**The modes of sediment transport:**

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| **Bed load** | Rolling, sliding and **saltating** along the bed |
| **Suspended load** | Held up by turbulence |
| Wash load | Very fine material, always in suspension, unrelated to the bed |

> **In a Himalayan river the suspended load usually dominates by mass**, but it is the **coarse bed load that damages turbine runners and fills reservoirs** — which is why gravel traps come before settling basins.

examTip.trick: **0.056 is the FULLY TURBULENT plateau** of the Shields curve — where θ_c stops varying with Reynolds number. That constancy is what makes it quotable as a single figure.
examTip.trap: **0.03 is the MINIMUM of the Shields curve** (at R* ≈ 10), a real value but not the fully-rough one. It is offered precisely because it is genuine.
examTip.mnemonic: **τ_c = 0.056(γ_s − γ)d ≈ 0.9 N/m² per mm of grain**, compared against **τ₀ = γRS**. And on the **SIDE slopes** the permissible shear is about **25% lower** than on the bed — gravity helps the flow there.

questions.stem: The shape factor of an I-beam is 1.12 and the factor of safety in bending is 1.5. If a 20% increase in permissible stress is allowed, the load factor is:
questions.solution:
**1.40.**

**Working.**

> The **20% increase in permissible stress** reduces the effective factor of safety:
> **FoS_effective = 1.5/1.2 = 1.25**
>
> **Load factor Q = shape factor × effective factor of safety**
> **Q = 1.12 × 1.25 = 1.40** ✓

**What each quantity means:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **SHAPE FACTOR S** | **M_p/M_y** — the ratio of the **plastic** to the **yield** moment. A pure section property |
| **Factor of safety** | Yield stress ÷ permissible stress, in working stress design |
| **LOAD FACTOR Q** | **Collapse load ÷ working load** — the true margin against collapse |

> **Load factor = shape factor × factor of safety.** The relation exists because working stress design limits the stress at **first yield**, while collapse occurs only when the section is **fully plastic** — and the shape factor is exactly the reserve between those two states.

**Shape factors for common sections** — the numbers worth carrying:

| Section | Shape factor |
|---|---|
| **I-section (major axis)** | **≈ 1.12 – 1.15** |
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** |
| **Circle (solid)** | **1.7** |
| **Diamond** | **2.0** |
| Thin tube | ≈ 1.27 |

> The pattern is instructive: **the more material concentrated at the extreme fibres, the LOWER the shape factor.** An I-section already has almost all its material at the flanges, so there is little reserve between first yield and full plasticity — hence 1.12. A **diamond** has almost all its material near the neutral axis, so it has a great deal of reserve — hence 2.0.

> **A low shape factor is not a weakness.** It means the section is already efficient in the elastic range; there is simply less *extra* to be had by going plastic.

**Where the 20% stress increase comes from:**

> Codes permit an increase in permissible stresses for **load combinations including WIND or SEISMIC** action, on the reasoning that these are short-duration, infrequent loads and the full working-stress margin is not needed against them simultaneously with the gravity case.

**Plastic design fundamentals** for context:

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Plastic hinge** | A section that has yielded fully and **rotates at constant M_p** |
| **Collapse mechanism** | Enough hinges to turn the structure into a mechanism |
| **Number of hinges for collapse** | **D_s + 1** |
| **Shape factor S** | M_p/M_y |
| **Plastic modulus Z_p** | **S × Z_elastic** |

> Plastic analysis is valid only for a **ductile** material that can sustain the rotation — which is why it applies to **structural steel** and not to concrete, cast iron or any brittle material.

**The section classification** that guards it: a plastic hinge can only form if the section does **not buckle locally first**, which is why **IS 800** classifies sections as **plastic, compact, semi-compact and slender** by their **b/t ratios**. **Plastic design requires a PLASTIC section.**

examTip.trick: Apply the stress increase **first**: FoS drops from 1.5 to **1.5/1.2 = 1.25**, then **Q = S × FoS = 1.12 × 1.25 = 1.40**. Option (a) is 1.12 × 1.5 = 1.68 — the answer if the 20% increase is ignored.
examTip.trap: The 20% is an increase in **permissible stress**, which **reduces** the effective factor of safety. Multiplying by 1.2 instead of dividing gives the wrong direction entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rectangle 1.5, circle 1.7, diamond 2.0, I-section only 1.12** — the more material already at the extreme fibres, the **lower** the shape factor, because there is less reserve left to mobilise.

questions.stem: The spacing of tile drains is directly proportional to:
options: Coefficient of permeability of the soil
Depth of the drain below the ground surface
questions.solution:
**The coefficient of permeability of the soil.**

**Why.** A **more permeable soil transmits water to the drain more readily**, so a single drain can serve a wider strip of land. The drains can therefore be placed **further apart**.

> Conversely, a **clay soil transmits water very slowly**, so the drains must be **close together** — which is why subsurface drainage of heavy clay is so expensive.

**Hooghoudt's equation** for steady-state drain spacing:

> **S² = [8 K d h + 4 K h²]/q**

where K is the permeability, d the equivalent depth to the impervious layer, h the height of the water table above drain level midway between drains, and q the drainage coefficient.

**Reading the proportionalities off the equation:**

| Quantity | Effect on spacing |
|---|---|
| **Permeability K** | **S ∝ √K** — increases spacing ✓ |
| **Depth to the impervious layer d** | Increases spacing |
| **Drainage coefficient q** (the rate to be removed) | **S ∝ 1/√q** — **DECREASES** spacing |
| Water table height h | Increases spacing |

> Note that the **drainage coefficient works the OPPOSITE way** — a larger q means more water must be removed per day, which needs drains **closer** together. That inverse relation is why option (c) is wrong.

> **Strictly S varies as √K rather than as K itself**, but among the four options only permeability increases the spacing in the sense the question intends — the drainage coefficient decreases it, and the two depth options are secondary.

**The placement rule** that accompanies the spacing:

> The drain must lie **within a PERVIOUS stratum**, **below the root zone** (1–2 m), and **ABOVE any impervious layer** — never below one, or the waterlogged water above the barrier cannot reach it and the drain runs dry while the land stays wet.

> A **graded filter or gravel envelope** surrounds the drain to prevent soil piping into it — without which the drain silts up and the installation fails.

**Why subsurface drainage rather than surface:**

| Type | Removes | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Surface** (grading, ditches) | **Ponded** water | Flat, slowly permeable land |
| **SUBSURFACE (tile)** | Lowers the **WATER TABLE** | **Waterlogging and salinity** |

> **Waterlogging and salinity are WATER TABLE problems**, so they need subsurface drainage. Surface drainage removes standing water and does nothing to the water table.

**Why the two problems travel together:**

> The water table rises into the root zone (**waterlogging**), **capillary rise** brings water to the surface carrying dissolved salts, **evaporation** removes the water and **concentrates the salts** at the surface (**salinity**).

> **The remedy for both is drainage** — and **leaching without drainage is futile**, because the dissolved salts must have somewhere to go or they simply return by capillary action.

> For a **sodic (alkali)** soil, apply **gypsum first, then leach** — leaching alone strips the calcium that holds the soil's structure together and makes a sodic soil worse.

examTip.trick: Reason physically: a **permeable soil feeds the drain from further away**, so the drains can be spread out. A clay soil needs them close — which is why draining heavy clay is so costly.
examTip.trap: The **drainage coefficient works the OPPOSITE way** — more water to remove means drains **closer** together (S ∝ 1/√q). Option (c) is the trap for anyone matching on "drainage" alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Place the drain in a PERVIOUS layer, below the roots, ABOVE any impervious layer.** Put it below a barrier and the water cannot reach it. And **leaching without drainage is futile** — the salts must have somewhere to go.

questions.stem: Water flows through a penstock at a velocity of 4 m/s carrying a discharge of 1.4 m³/s. What is the diameter of the penstock?
questions.solution:
**About 0.667 m.**

**Working.**

> **Q = A V**
> **A = Q/V = 1.4/4 = 0.35 m²**
>
> **A = πD²/4**, so **D = √(4A/π) = √(4 × 0.35/π) = √0.4456 = 0.667 m** ✓

**A quick check:** with D = 0.667 m, A = π(0.667)²/4 = 0.349 m², and Q = 0.349 × 4 = 1.40 m³/s ✓

**The useful rearrangement** for this very common calculation:

> **D = √(4Q/πV) = 1.128 √(Q/V)**

> Check: 1.128 × √(1.4/4) = 1.128 × 0.5916 = **0.667** ✓ — a one-step route that avoids computing the area separately.

**Choosing the penstock velocity** is the real engineering question behind the arithmetic:

| Velocity | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Too LOW** | A **large diameter** — expensive steel, heavy anchor blocks |
| **Too HIGH** | Large **head loss** (h_f ∝ V²) — lost generation for the plant's whole life |

> **Typical design velocities are 3 to 6 m/s**, and the optimum is found by **minimising the sum of the capital cost and the capitalised value of the lost energy** — a classic economic optimisation, not a rule of thumb.

> **The head loss cost is a recurring loss over 50 years or more**, which is why it usually dominates the calculation and pushes the economic diameter larger than intuition suggests.

**Head loss in the penstock:**

> **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** (Darcy–Weisbach)

> Note that **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵ at constant Q** — since V = 4Q/πD², substituting gives h_f ∝ Q²/D⁵. **A 10% larger diameter cuts the head loss by nearly 40%.** That very steep dependence is why the optimisation matters.

**The other penstock design checks:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **Wall thickness** | **t = pD/(2σ)** — hoop stress, plus a corrosion allowance |
| **WATER HAMMER** | **Δp = ρcΔV** for sudden closure — can multiply the static head |
| **Surge tank** | Placed as **close to the powerhouse as possible**; it reflects the pressure wave and shortens the effective conduit length |
| Anchor blocks | At every bend, to resist the thrust |
| Expansion joints | Between anchor blocks |

> **The water hammer check often governs the wall thickness**, not the static head — which is why the **governor closure timing** and the penstock design are settled together, against the **2L/c** wave round-trip criterion.

**And the power output** the whole arrangement exists to produce:

> **P = ρ g Q H η** — with η around **0.85 to 0.90** for a good turbine–generator set.

examTip.trick: Use the one-step form **D = 1.128√(Q/V)**. Here 1.128 × √0.35 = **0.667 m**, with no separate area calculation.
examTip.trap: Always verify by substituting back: A = πD²/4 = 0.349 m², × 4 m/s = 1.40 m³/s ✓. Ten seconds, and it catches every arithmetic slip.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design velocity 3–6 m/s, chosen by economics.** Since **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵**, a 10% larger pipe cuts the loss nearly 40% — and that loss recurs for 50 years, which is why it usually beats the capital cost.

questions.stem: The falling head permeability test is suitable for:
options: Both highly and less permeable soil
questions.solution:
**Less permeable soils** — fine sands, silts and clayey soils.

**The two laboratory permeability tests:**

| | **CONSTANT HEAD** | **FALLING (variable) HEAD** |
|---|---|---|
| **Suits** | **COARSE** soils — gravels, sands | **FINE** soils — fine sands, silts, clays |
| k range | **k > 10⁻⁴ m/s** | **k = 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁷ m/s** |
| What is measured | The **volume collected** in a known time | The **time for the head to fall** between two marks |
| Formula | **k = QL/(Aht)** | **k = 2.303 (aL/At) log₁₀(h₁/h₂)** |

**Why each suits its range:**

> In a **coarse** soil a large volume passes quickly, so **collecting and measuring the volume** is easy and accurate. Trying to measure a falling head would be impossible — it would fall too fast to time.

> In a **fine** soil the flow is a trickle. Collecting a measurable volume would take days and the water would evaporate. But the head in a **narrow standpipe** falls perceptibly, and **timing that fall** is both practical and accurate.

> **The narrow standpipe is the key**: a small cross-sectional area **a** means even a tiny volume of flow produces a large, measurable drop in head.

**Typical permeability values** — the range is extraordinary:

| Soil | k (m/s) |
|---|---|
| **Clean gravel** | **10⁻¹ – 10⁻²** |
| Coarse sand | 10⁻² – 10⁻³ |
| Fine sand | 10⁻³ – 10⁻⁵ |
| **Silt** | **10⁻⁵ – 10⁻⁸** |
| **Clay** | **< 10⁻⁹** |

> **Permeability spans about TEN ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE** across soil types — a wider range than almost any other engineering property. Which is why no single test method can cover it.

**For the very lowest permeabilities**, even a falling head test is impractical, and k is instead obtained **indirectly from the consolidation test**:

> **k = c_v m_v γ_w**

> The oedometer measures how fast a clay consolidates, and permeability is inferred from it.

**And for field values, use a FIELD test:**

| Test | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pumping test** (unconfined or confined aquifer) | The most reliable for a **mass** permeability |
| Borehole (variable head) test | Simpler, more local |

> **A laboratory sample is small, remoulded and vertically oriented.** In the field, k is controlled by **fissures, laminations and sand partings** — features a 100 mm sample cannot contain.

> **Field permeability can exceed the laboratory value by one or two orders of magnitude**, which is why a dewatering scheme designed on laboratory numbers so often fails.

**The anisotropy point** is related and important: natural soils are deposited in layers, so **k_horizontal is typically 2 to 10 times k_vertical** — and much more in a varved clay. A horizontal permeability governs seepage under a dam; a vertical one governs consolidation.

examTip.trick: Ask **what is easy to measure**. In coarse soil a large **volume** passes quickly — measure it. In fine soil the flow is a trickle, but a **narrow standpipe** makes even a tiny volume produce a big, timeable drop in head.
examTip.trap: The mnemonic must not be inverted: **CONSTANT head for COARSE, FALLING head for FINE.** Both start with the same letters as their soil.
examTip.mnemonic: **Permeability spans TEN orders of magnitude** — no one test covers it. Below 10⁻⁷ use **k = c_v m_v γ_w** from the oedometer; for real field values use a **pumping test**, since fissures can make the field value 10–100× the laboratory one.

questions.stem: The safe bearing capacity of soft rock is approximately:
questions.solution:
**440 kN/m²** — the presumptive value for soft rock in IS 1904.

**The presumptive safe bearing capacity table**, which is the substance worth carrying:

| Stratum | Safe bearing capacity (kN/m²) |
|---|---|
| **Hard rock** (granite, trap) | **3240** |
| Laminated rock (sandstone, limestone) | 1620 |
| Residual gravel, shale | 880 |
| **SOFT ROCK** | **440** |
| **Gravel, sand-gravel compact** | **440** |
| Coarse sand, compact | 440 |
| Medium sand, compact | 245 |
| **Fine sand, compact** | **150** |
| Loose sand | 100 |
| **Very stiff clay** | **440** |
| **Stiff clay** | **220** |
| Medium clay | 150 |
| Soft clay | 100 |
| **Very soft clay** | **50** |
| **Peat, fill, made ground** | **To be determined by test — no value given** |

> **Note the recurring 440**: soft rock, compact gravel, coarse sand and very stiff clay all share it — which makes 440 the easiest anchor value in the table.

**What "presumptive" means, and the warning that comes with it:**

> These are **rough guide values for PRELIMINARY design only**. The code itself requires that they be **checked by actual testing** for any significant structure.

> They take **no account of** the footing's **size or depth**, the **settlement**, the **water table**, or the actual strength parameters — all of which change the answer substantially.

**And the point that matters most in practice:**

> **SETTLEMENT, not bearing failure, governs the design of most foundations.** A soil may safely carry the pressure and still settle far more than the structure can tolerate.

> So the design bearing pressure is the **LESSER** of:
> **(a)** the ultimate bearing capacity divided by a factor of safety (**2.5 to 3**), and
> **(b)** the pressure that keeps settlement within the permissible limit.

**Permissible settlements (IS 1904):**

| Structure | Maximum settlement | Differential |
|---|---|---|
| **Isolated footings on sand** | **40 mm** | **1 in 300 angular distortion** |
| Isolated footings on clay | 65 mm | 1 in 300 |
| **Rafts on sand** | **40 – 65 mm** | — |
| Rafts on clay | 65 – 100 mm | — |

> **DIFFERENTIAL settlement is what damages a structure, not uniform settlement.** A building that settles 100 mm uniformly is undamaged; one that settles 25 mm at one column and 50 mm at the next may crack severely. The angular distortion limit of **1 in 300** is the criterion that matters.

**Which is why a RAFT works on poor ground**: it does not necessarily reduce the total settlement, but it **ties the columns together** so they settle as one, converting differential settlement into uniform settlement.

**And for peat, fill or made ground** the table deliberately gives **no value** — such materials must be investigated, and often the right answer is to **pile through them** to a competent stratum rather than to found on them at all.

examTip.trick: **440 kN/m² is the anchor value** — soft rock, compact gravel, coarse sand and very stiff clay all share it. Learn 440 and the rest of the table hangs off it.
examTip.trap: Presumptive values are for **preliminary design only** — they ignore footing size, depth, settlement and the water table. The code itself requires testing for any significant structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **SETTLEMENT usually governs, not bearing failure** — take the **lesser** of q_u/F and the settlement-limited pressure. And it is **DIFFERENTIAL** settlement that damages buildings: 1 in 300 angular distortion is the limit.

questions.stem: Regarding the aggregate impact value test:
options: It measures the resistance of aggregate to sudden shock or impact
The value is expressed as a percentage of fines passing a 2.36 mm sieve
A lower value indicates a tougher aggregate
questions.solution:
**All the options are correct** — each statement describes the test accurately.

**The test:**

> Aggregate passing a 12.5 mm sieve and retained on 10 mm is placed in a cylindrical mould in **three layers, each tamped 25 times**. A **13.5 to 14 kg hammer** is dropped **15 times** from a height of **380 mm**. The crushed sample is then sieved on a **2.36 mm** sieve.

> **AIV = (weight passing 2.36 mm ÷ total weight) × 100**

**Checking each statement:**

| Statement | Correct? |
|---|---|
| Measures resistance to **sudden shock or impact** | ✓ — that is the definition of toughness |
| Expressed as the **percentage passing 2.36 mm** | ✓ — the standard sieve for this test |
| **A lower value means a tougher aggregate** | ✓ — less material broke down |

> **The third statement carries the interpretation**, and it is the one candidates most often get backwards: **the value is a measure of DAMAGE, so lower is better.**

**Permissible limits (IRC):**

| Layer | Maximum AIV |
|---|---|
| **Wearing course (bituminous surfacing)** | **30%** |
| Bituminous macadam | 30% |
| **Water bound macadam, base course** | **40%** |
| Cement concrete (wearing surface) | 30% |

**The full family of aggregate tests** — all of which follow the same "lower is better" logic:

| Test | Measures | Typical limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Crushing value** | Resistance to **gradually applied** compressive load | **30%** (wearing course) |
| **IMPACT value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** — toughness | **30%** |
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | Resistance to **abrasion and wear** | **30 – 40%** |
| **Soundness** (sodium/magnesium sulphate) | Resistance to **weathering** | 12% / 18% |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | **< 2%** |
| **Flakiness and elongation index** | **SHAPE** | 15% / combined 30% |
| **Stripping value** | Adhesion of bitumen | Retention > 95% |

> **The Los Angeles abrasion test is the most comprehensive single test**, because it combines **abrasion, impact and grinding** in one procedure — which is why it is preferred internationally.

**Crushing versus impact** is the distinction most often examined:

> **Crushing value = GRADUAL load. Impact value = SUDDEN shock.** Both express the percentage of fines produced, and both are limited to about 30% for a wearing course — but they measure different failure modes, and an aggregate can pass one and fail the other.

**Why SHAPE matters as much as strength:**

> **Flaky and elongated particles BREAK under compaction and traffic**, however strong the parent rock, because they are loaded across their weakest dimension. They also pack poorly, leaving voids.

> **Cubical particles are what is wanted**, which is why the flakiness index is limited to 15% — and why an otherwise excellent rock can be rejected on its crusher's product shape alone.

examTip.trick: **All these values measure DAMAGE, so LOWER is always better.** That single principle covers crushing value, impact value, abrasion, soundness, absorption and flakiness alike.
examTip.trap: **Crushing value = GRADUAL load; impact value = SUDDEN shock.** Both give a percentage of fines and both are limited to about 30% — but they test different failure modes, and an aggregate can pass one and fail the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **AIV: 15 blows of a 14 kg hammer from 380 mm, fines through 2.36 mm, limit 30% for a wearing course.** And **SHAPE matters as much as strength** — flaky particles break under compaction whatever the parent rock.

questions.stem: What percentage should a college score to get affiliation from the Nepal Engineering Council?
questions.solution:
**70%.**

An engineering institution seeking **recognition (affiliation) from the Nepal Engineering Council** must achieve a **minimum average of 70%** in the Council's assessment of its facilities, faculty and academic arrangements.

**What the Council assesses:**

| Area | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Faculty** | Numbers, qualifications, student–teacher ratio, permanence of appointment |
| **Physical infrastructure** | Classrooms, drawing halls, land and buildings |
| **Laboratories** | Equipment, capacity, adequacy for the programme |
| **Library** | Titles, volumes, journals, reading space |
| **Curriculum and academic arrangements** | Conformity to the prescribed minimum standards |
| **Student admission** | Compliance with the prescribed conditions |

> The 70% threshold applies to the **average across these areas**, which is why an institution strong in one respect and weak in another can still fall short.

**Why the Council does this at all:**

> **Recognition of the institution is what makes its graduates eligible for registration.** A degree from an unrecognised programme does not lead to a license to practise — so the affiliation standard is, in effect, the entry gate to the profession.

> That is the Council's leverage: it cannot run colleges or award degrees, but by controlling **whose graduates may register** it sets the floor for engineering education in the country.

**And the boundary of its role:**

| The Council DOES | The Council does NOT |
