|---|---|
| **Recognise** institutions and programmes | **Open or run** colleges |
| **Prescribe** minimum standards and admission conditions | **Award** degrees |
| **Register** engineers; issue the **license** | Fix fees or salaries |
| **Regulate conduct**; take disciplinary action | **Represent** engineers' interests |

> The last row is the standing distinction: **the COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION (NEA) represents.** Registration with the NEC is a **legal requirement** to practise; NEA membership is voluntary.

**The Council facts most often examined**, worth holding as a single block:

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulations** | **2057 BS** |
| **Total members** | **21** |
| **Chairman** | Bachelor's + **15 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Vice-Chairman** | Bachelor's + **10 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Registrar (Member Secretary)** | Bachelor's + **10 years** |
| **Members nominated by the Council itself** | **2** |
| **Members elected from the NEA** | **5** |
| **Minimum for institutional affiliation** | **70%** |

> These recall questions are the **cheapest marks on the paper** for anyone who has read the Council's material once — and they appear in every sitting.

examTip.trick: This is **pure recall**, so learn the Council block as a unit rather than as isolated facts — the same block answers four or five questions across a typical paper.
examTip.trap: The Council **recognises** institutions; it does not **open** them. Questions in this area frequently test that boundary rather than the number itself.
examTip.mnemonic: **Act 2055, Regulations 2057, 21 members, chairman 15 years, VP and Registrar 10 years, 2 nominated by the Council, 5 elected from the NEA, 70% for affiliation.** Recognition is the Council's real leverage — an unrecognised degree leads to no license.

questions.stem: If the basic wind speed is 55 m/s, what is the design wind pressure?
questions.solution:
**1815 N/m².**

**Working.** The design wind pressure from the design wind speed (IS 875 Part 3):

> **p_z = 0.6 V_z²**  (p_z in N/m², V_z in m/s)
>
> **p_z = 0.6 × 55² = 0.6 × 3025 = 1815 N/m²** ✓

**Where the 0.6 comes from:**

> The dynamic pressure of a moving fluid is **½ρV²**. For air at standard conditions **ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³**, so:
> **½ × 1.2 = 0.6** ✓

> **The coefficient is not arbitrary — it is half the density of air.** Knowing that means the formula never has to be memorised, and it explains why the same expression appears in every wind code in the world.

**The relation is QUADRATIC**, which is the fact with practical consequences:

| Wind speed | Pressure |
|---|---|
| 33 m/s | 653 N/m² |
| 39 m/s | 913 |
| 44 m/s | 1162 |
| 47 m/s | 1325 |
| **50 m/s** | **1500** |
| **55 m/s** | **1815** |

> **A 10% higher wind speed gives a 21% higher pressure.** Which is why the difference between wind zones matters far more than the speeds themselves suggest, and why a small error in the basic speed is a large error in the load.

**The full design sequence** — the basic speed is only the starting point:

> **V_z = V_b × k₁ × k₂ × k₃ × k₄**

| Factor | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **V_b** | **Basic wind speed** — from the wind map, a 3-second gust at 10 m in open terrain, 50-year return period |
| **k₁** — risk coefficient | The structure's **importance and design life** |
| **k₂** — terrain, height and size | **Terrain category** (1 open to 4 city) and **height above ground** |
| **k₃** — topography | **Hills, cliffs and escarpments** — up to **1.36** |
| k₄ — importance for cyclonic regions | Coastal exposure |

> **Then p_z = 0.6 V_z², and the FORCE is F = C_f × A × p_z** — the pressure must still be multiplied by a **force coefficient** that depends on the shape.

**The topography factor k₃ deserves emphasis in a Nepali context:**

> A building on a **ridge or the crest of an escarpment** experiences accelerated flow, and **k₃ can reach 1.36**. Since pressure goes as the **square**, that is an **85% increase in load** over the same building on flat ground.

> Ignoring k₃ on a hilltop site is a serious and easily made omission.

**And the effect that damages buildings most:**

> **SUCTION on the leeward face and on the roof — not pressure on the windward face.** Roofs are lost to **UPLIFT**, and light roofs are the most vulnerable of all, because there is little dead load to hold them down.

> Which is why the **0.9 dead load combination** matters here: where the dead load **resists uplift**, it is factored **DOWN** to 0.9, not up to 1.5. Using 1.5 hides the uplift failure entirely.

examTip.trick: **p = 0.6V², and the 0.6 is just ½ρ for air (ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³).** Knowing where it comes from means never mis-remembering it — and 0.6 × 3025 = 1815.
examTip.trap: The relation is **quadratic**: a 10% higher speed gives a **21% higher pressure**. So a small error in the basic wind speed becomes a large error in the load.
examTip.mnemonic: **Roofs are lost to SUCTION and UPLIFT, not to windward pressure** — which is why the **0.9 dead load** combination governs light roofs. And on a ridge, **k₃ up to 1.36** means an 85% larger load than on flat ground.

questions.stem: In a closed traverse, the sum of the latitudes and the sum of the departures should each theoretically be:
questions.solution:
**Zero.**

**Why.** A **closed traverse returns to its starting point**. The total displacement north–south and the total displacement east–west must therefore each cancel out completely.

> **ΣL = Σ(l cos θ) = 0** and **ΣD = Σ(l sin θ) = 0**

> where **latitude L = l cos θ** (the north–south component, **+N, −S**) and **departure D = l sin θ** (the east–west component, **+E, −W**).

**In practice they never are exactly zero**, and the residuals are the **closing error**:

> **e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²]** — the magnitude of the closing error
> **Relative error = e/perimeter**, expressed as **1 in N**

**Acceptable closure:**

| Survey class | Relative closure |
|---|---|
| Rough (compass) | 1 in 300 to 1 in 1000 |
| **Ordinary theodolite** | **1 in 3000 to 1 in 5000** |
| Precise | 1 in 10 000 and better |

**Adjusting the traverse** — the two classical rules:

| Rule | Distributes the error in proportion to | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **BOWDITCH (compass) rule** | The **LENGTH** of each line | **Angles and distances are measured with EQUAL precision** — the usual case |
| **TRANSIT rule** | The **LATITUDE/DEPARTURE** of each line | **ANGLES are measured more precisely** than distances |

> **Bowditch correction to a line's latitude = ΣL × (length of that line ÷ perimeter)**, and similarly for departures.

> **Bowditch is the default** because with modern instruments angles and distances are usually of comparable accuracy. Transit is the specialist case.

**Checking the ANGLES first** is the step that must come before any of this:

| Traverse | Angle sum check |
|---|---|
| **Interior angles** | **(2n − 4) × 90°** |
| **Exterior angles** | **(2n + 4) × 90°** |

> **Adjust the angles first, then compute latitudes and departures.** Distributing a linear misclosure while an angular blunder is still present simply spreads the blunder around the whole traverse instead of exposing it.

**And the area**, once the traverse closes:

> **Area = ½|Σ(x_i y_{i+1} − x_{i+1} y_i)|** — the coordinate (shoelace) method, which is exact for a polygon and is why traverse computation ends in coordinates.

**A note on locating a blunder**: if the closing error is large, the **BEARING of the closing error** often points along the line containing a **distance** blunder, and a closing error **perpendicular** to a line suggests an **angular** blunder at its start. That diagnostic saves re-surveying the whole traverse.

examTip.trick: A closed traverse **returns to where it started**, so its net north–south and east–west displacements must both be **zero**. The reasoning is geometric, not a rule to memorise.
examTip.trap: **Adjust the ANGLES first** — check against (2n − 4) × 90° for interior angles. Distributing a linear misclosure while an angular blunder remains just smears the blunder across every line.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOWDITCH by LENGTH (equal precision — the default); TRANSIT by LATITUDE/DEPARTURE (angles more precise).** And the closing error's **direction** often identifies which line carries the blunder.

questions.stem: The initial setting time of ordinary Portland cement should not be less than:
questions.solution:
**30 minutes.**

**The two setting time limits (IS 269 / IS 4031):**

| Limit | Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **INITIAL setting time** | **NOT LESS THAN 30 minutes** | Time to **mix, transport, place and compact** before stiffening begins |
| **FINAL setting time** | **NOT MORE THAN 600 minutes (10 hours)** | So the work can proceed — formwork, curing, the next lift |

> **Note that the two limits run in OPPOSITE directions**: the initial time has a **minimum** and the final time a **maximum**. Getting that the wrong way round is the standard error, and it is exactly what the distractors probe.

**Why each direction:**

> If the cement set **too fast**, there would be no time to place and compact the concrete — it would stiffen in the mixer or the chute.
> If it set **too slowly**, the formwork could not be struck and construction would stall.

**Measured by the VICAT apparatus:**

| Setting | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Initial set** | The needle (1 mm²) **fails to penetrate to within 5–7 mm of the bottom** |
| **Final set** | The **annular attachment leaves no impression** on the surface |

> Both use a paste of **standard consistency**, which is itself defined by the Vicat plunger penetrating to **5–7 mm from the bottom** — usually around **26–33% water** by weight of cement.

**Special cements differ:**

| Cement | Initial set |
|---|---|
| **Ordinary Portland (OPC)** | **≥ 30 min** |
| Rapid hardening | ≥ 30 min (it gains **strength** faster, not sets faster) |
| **Low heat** | **≥ 60 min** |

> **Rapid hardening cement is a common misunderstanding**: it does **not** set faster. Its setting times are the same as OPC — it develops **strength** more quickly, reaching in **3 days** what OPC reaches in 7.

**The other cement tests:**

| Test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Fineness** (Blaine) | **≥ 225 m²/kg** — finer cement hydrates faster |
| **SOUNDNESS** (Le Chatelier) | **≤ 10 mm** expansion — free lime and magnesia cause **delayed expansion** |
| Soundness (autoclave) | ≤ 0.8% |
| **Compressive strength** (OPC 33 grade) | **16 / 22 / 33 MPa at 3 / 7 / 28 days** |

> **Unsoundness is the most dangerous defect**, because it appears **months after construction**. Free lime hydrates slowly and expands, cracking concrete that was sound when placed — and by then nothing can be done.

**The compound that controls setting:**

> **C₃A** hydrates almost instantly and would cause a **flash set**. **GYPSUM (2–3%) is added to retard it** — which is the entire reason gypsum is interground with cement clinker.

> **C₃S** gives **early strength** (up to 7 days) and **C₂S** the **later strength** (beyond 28 days). **Low heat cement reduces C₃A and C₃S and raises C₂S** — which is why it is slower in every respect and used for mass concrete.

examTip.trap: The two limits run in **OPPOSITE directions**: initial set has a **MINIMUM of 30 minutes**, final set a **MAXIMUM of 600 minutes**. Reversing them is the standard error, and the distractors are chosen to catch it.
examTip.trick: Reason from the site: you need **time to place** (so a minimum on the initial set) and you need to **get on with the work** (so a maximum on the final set).
examTip.mnemonic: **Rapid hardening cement does NOT set faster** — same 30 minutes; it gains **strength** faster. And **GYPSUM is added purely to retard C₃A**, which would otherwise cause a flash set. Unsoundness is the worst defect: it appears **months later**.

questions.stem: The centre of pressure on a vertical plane surface submerged in a liquid always lies:
options: Below the centroid of the surface
At the centroid of the surface
Above the centroid of the surface
questions.solution:
**Below the centroid**, always.

**Why.** The pressure on a submerged surface **increases with depth**, so the lower portion of the surface carries a larger share of the total force. The resultant therefore acts **below** the geometric centre.

> **h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄)**

> The added term **I_G/(A h̄) is always POSITIVE**, so the centre of pressure is **always deeper** than the centroid. It can never be at or above it.

**Two consequences worth reading off the formula:**

| Situation | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **The surface is DEEP** (h̄ large) | I_G/(A h̄) becomes **small** — the centre of pressure **approaches the centroid** |
| The surface is near the free surface | The offset is **largest** |

> Physically: at great depth the pressure variation across the surface is small **relative to** the absolute pressure, so the loading is nearly uniform and the resultant sits nearly at the centroid.

**The standard case — a vertical rectangle with its top edge at the free surface:**

> **h̄ = H/2**, **I_G = bH³/12**, **A = bH**
> **h_cp = H/2 + (bH³/12)/(bH × H/2) = H/2 + H/6 = 2H/3**

> **The centre of pressure is at 2H/3 from the surface — one third of the height from the base.** That is the single most useful result in hydrostatics, and it is worth knowing without derivation.

**The total force:**

> **F = γ h̄ A** — the pressure at the **CENTROID** times the area.

> **Note the split: the FORCE uses the centroid, but its LINE OF ACTION does not.** Confusing the two is the classic error in this topic.

**Where it matters:**

| Application | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Dam and retaining wall design** | The **overturning moment** depends on where the force acts, not just its size |
| **Sluice gates and stop logs** | The hinge and the hoisting force |
| **Lock gates** | — |
| Tank walls | — |

> **Using the centroid for the line of action underestimates the overturning moment** — a real and dangerous error for a dam or a retaining wall.

**A note on the pressure prism**: for a vertical rectangle the pressure distribution is a **triangle**, and the resultant of a triangular distribution acts at its **centroid — one third from the base**. That gives 2H/3 from the surface directly, with no formula at all.

**And for a curved surface**: resolve into a **horizontal component** (the force on the vertical projection) and a **vertical component** (the **weight of the fluid above** the surface, real or imaginary). The resultant passes through the **centre of curvature** for a circular surface — which is why a radial gate exerts no moment on its trunnion.

examTip.trick: Pressure grows with depth, so the **bottom of the surface carries more** — the resultant must sit **below** the centroid. The term **I_G/(Ah̄) is always positive**, so it can never be otherwise.
examTip.trap: **The FORCE uses the centroid (F = γh̄A) but its LINE OF ACTION does not.** Using the centroid for both underestimates the overturning moment — a dangerous error for a dam or retaining wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vertical rectangle from the surface: h_cp = 2H/3 — one third up from the base.** It follows from the triangular pressure prism with no formula at all. And the offset **shrinks as the surface goes deeper**.

questions.stem: According to IS 456, the partial safety factor for the load combination of dead load and live load at the limit state of collapse is:
questions.solution:
**1.5 DL + 1.5 LL.**

**The IS 456 load combinations at the limit state of COLLAPSE:**

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** |
| **DL + WL/EL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 WL** — or **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** when DL **stabilises** |
| **DL + LL + WL/EL** | **1.2 (DL + LL + WL)** |

> Note the **1.2** in the three-load case: it is **less than 1.5** because the simultaneous occurrence of full live load **and** full wind at their design values is improbable. Codes reduce the factor to reflect that.

**The 0.9 DL case is the one most often forgotten:**

> Where the dead load **RESISTS** — against **overturning, sliding or uplift** — it is factored **DOWN to 0.9**, because relying on a load that might turn out smaller than estimated is unsafe.

> **Applying 1.5 to a stabilising dead load conceals overturning and uplift failures entirely.** Cantilever canopies, light roofs under wind uplift, retaining walls and empty basements are all governed by this combination.

**At the limit state of SERVICEABILITY** the factors are quite different:

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| DL + LL | **1.0 DL + 1.0 LL** |
| DL + WL | 1.0 DL + 1.0 WL |
| DL + LL + WL | 1.0 DL + **0.8** LL + **0.8** WL |

> **Serviceability uses UNFACTORED loads** — because deflection and cracking are checked against what the structure will actually experience, not against a hypothetical overload.

**Material partial safety factors:**

| Material | γ_m | Design strength |
|---|---|---|
| **Concrete** | **1.5** | **0.67 f_ck/1.5 = 0.447 f_ck** |
| **Steel** | **1.15** | **0.87 f_y** |

> **Concrete carries the larger factor because its strength is far more variable** — it is made on site, cured by whoever is there, and its strength depends on workmanship. Steel is manufactured under factory control, so 1.15 suffices.

> The **0.67** applied to concrete separately accounts for the difference between the cube strength and the strength of concrete in a real flexural member under sustained load.

**The philosophy behind partial factors:**

> **Loads are factored UP and strengths factored DOWN**, and each is factored **according to how well it is known**. That is the whole of limit state design in one sentence — and it is more rational than working stress design's single global factor, which treated every uncertainty alike.

**The two limit states:**

| Limit state | Concerns | Loads |
|---|---|---|
| **COLLAPSE (ultimate)** | Flexure, shear, torsion, compression | **Factored** |
| **SERVICEABILITY** | **Deflection, cracking, vibration** | **Unfactored** |

> A structure must satisfy **both**. A beam can be perfectly safe against collapse and still be unusable because it deflects visibly or cracks unacceptably.

examTip.trick: **Loads up, strengths down — each by how well it is known.** Dead and live both take 1.5; the three-load case drops to 1.2 because full LL and full WL together is improbable.
examTip.trap: **0.9 DL is the combination most often forgotten.** Where dead load **resists** overturning or uplift, it is factored **DOWN**, not up. Using 1.5 there hides the failure completely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Concrete γ_m = 1.5, steel 1.15** — concrete is site-made and variable, steel is factory-controlled. And **serviceability uses UNFACTORED loads**, because deflection is checked against what will really happen.

questions.stem: The characteristic strength of concrete is defined as the strength below which not more than what percentage of test results are expected to fall?
questions.solution:
**5%.**

**The definition (IS 456 cl. 6.1.1):**

> The **characteristic strength** is the value below which **not more than 5% of test results** are expected to fall.

> It is therefore the **5th percentile** of the strength distribution — not the mean, and not the minimum.

**The relation to the target mean strength for mix design:**

> **f_target = f_ck + 1.65 s**

> where **s** is the standard deviation and **1.65** is the standard normal deviate for a **5% exceedance probability**.

| Grade | Assumed s (IS 10262) | Target mean |
|---|---|---|
| **M20** | **4.0** | **26.6 MPa** |
| **M25** | **4.0** | **31.6 MPa** |
| M30–M35 | 5.0 | 38.25 / 43.25 |
| M40–M50 | 6.0 | 49.9 / 59.9 |

> **The concrete must be designed for a mean strength well ABOVE its grade** — about 33% above for M20. Designing a mix to produce exactly 20 MPa on average would mean **half the results fell below grade**.

**The critical consequence, which is the real substance of the idea:**

> **The margin (1.65 s) depends entirely on the CONSISTENCY of production, not on the cement content.**

| Producer | s | Target for M25 |
|---|---|---|
| **Well-controlled plant** | **3 MPa** | **29.95 MPa** |
| Poor site control | 6 MPa | 34.9 MPa |

> **The poorly-controlled producer must aim nearly 5 MPa higher** — and pay for the extra cement — **to achieve the same characteristic strength**. Consistency is worth money, quite literally.

> That is the argument for **quality control**: it is not merely a guard against failure, it is a direct saving in materials.

**Acceptance criteria (IS 456)** are a separate matter and often confused with the definition:

> For a group of **four consecutive** test results:
> **Mean ≥ f_ck + 0.825 s** (or f_ck + 3 for M15–M20, f_ck + 4 for M25 and above), **AND**
> **Every individual result ≥ f_ck − 3** (M15–M20) or **f_ck − 4** (M25 and above)

> **Both conditions must be satisfied** — a good average does not excuse one bad result, and no individual result may fall more than 3 or 4 MPa below grade.

**A note on the test itself**: the characteristic strength refers to the **28-day cube strength** of 150 mm cubes. A **cylinder** (150 × 300 mm) gives about **0.8 times** the cube value — which matters when reading international literature, where cylinders are the norm.

**And the grade designation**: **M25 means Mix, 25 N/mm² characteristic cube strength at 28 days.** The M is for mix, not for anything else.

examTip.trick: **5% below → the 5th percentile → 1.65 standard deviations below the mean.** The 1.65 in the mix design formula and the 5% in the definition are the **same fact** stated two ways.
examTip.trap: Characteristic strength is **not the mean and not the minimum**. A mix designed to average exactly 20 MPa would have **half** its results below M20.
examTip.mnemonic: **The margin depends on CONSISTENCY, not cement.** A well-controlled plant (s = 3) targets 30 MPa for M25; a poor site (s = 6) must target 35 and pay for the extra cement. Quality control is a material saving, not just a safeguard.

questions.stem: In the limit state design of a singly reinforced beam, the maximum depth of the neutral axis for Fe 415 steel is:
questions.solution:
**0.48 d.**

**The limiting neutral axis depths (IS 456):**

| Steel grade | **x_u,max/d** | Limiting moment M_u,lim |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.53** | **0.148 f_ck b d²** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** | **0.138 f_ck b d²** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.46** | **0.133 f_ck b d²** |

> **Note that HIGHER grade steel gives a SMALLER limiting depth**, and therefore a **smaller limiting moment** for the same section. That reads backwards to many candidates and is worth understanding rather than memorising.

**Where the values come from:**

> **x_u,max/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + ε_y)** where **ε_y = 0.87f_y/E_s + 0.002**

> For Fe 415: ε_y = 0.87 × 415/200000 + 0.002 = 0.0018 + 0.002 = 0.0038
> **x_u,max/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + 0.0038) = 0.0035/0.0073 = 0.48** ✓

> The 0.0035 is the **limiting compressive strain in concrete**, fixed by the code; ε_y is the steel's strain at design yield. **Higher grade steel yields at a higher strain**, so the neutral axis must be **shallower** for the steel to reach yield before the concrete crushes.

**What the limit is FOR — ensuring a ductile failure:**

| Section type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **UNDER-reinforced (x_u < x_u,max)** | **STEEL yields FIRST** — large deflections and wide cracks give **warning** before collapse. **DESIRABLE** |
| **Balanced (x_u = x_u,max)** | Both reach their limits together |
| **OVER-reinforced (x_u > x_u,max)** | **CONCRETE crushes first** — **sudden, brittle failure with no warning**. **NOT PERMITTED** |

> **IS 456 does not permit over-reinforced sections.** If the required moment exceeds M_u,lim, the answer is **not** more tension steel — it is a **doubly reinforced** section (adding compression steel) or a **deeper** section.

> **Adding more tension steel to an over-stressed beam makes it MORE brittle, not stronger** — a genuinely dangerous misunderstanding.

**The stress block** the values rest on:

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| Shape | **Parabolic to 0.002 strain, then rectangular** |
| **Compressive force C** | **0.36 f_ck b x_u** |
| **Centroid of the block** | **0.42 x_u** from the extreme fibre |
| **Tensile force T** | **0.87 f_y A_st** |
| **Lever arm** | **d − 0.42 x_u** |

> **Equating C = T gives x_u**, and **M_u = T × lever arm = 0.87 f_y A_st (d − 0.42 x_u)**. Those few numbers — **0.36, 0.42, 0.87** — carry the whole of singly reinforced beam design.

**And the minimum and maximum steel:**

> **A_st,min/bd = 0.85/f_y** and **A_st,max = 4% of the gross area** — the maximum being a practical limit on congestion, not a strength criterion.

examTip.trick: The sequence **0.53 / 0.48 / 0.46** for Fe 250 / 415 / 500 **falls as the grade rises** — because higher-grade steel yields at a **higher strain**, so the neutral axis must be shallower for it to yield before the concrete crushes at 0.0035.
examTip.trap: **If M exceeds M_u,lim, adding more tension steel makes the beam MORE BRITTLE, not stronger.** The answer is a doubly reinforced section or a deeper one. This is a genuinely dangerous misunderstanding.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.36, 0.42, 0.87** — compressive force 0.36f_ck·b·x_u, its centroid at 0.42x_u, steel at 0.87f_y. Those three numbers carry the whole of singly reinforced design.

questions.stem: The critical section for two-way (punching) shear in a footing is taken at a distance from the face of the column of:
questions.solution:
**d/2 from the face of the column**, where d is the effective depth.

**The two shear checks in a footing**, and their different critical sections:

| Shear type | Critical section | Failure surface |
|---|---|---|
| **ONE-WAY (wide beam) shear** | **At distance d from the column face** | A **plane** across the full footing width |
| **TWO-WAY (punching) shear** | **At d/2 from the column face**, all round | A **PERIMETER** around the column |

> **The perimeter for punching shear is therefore (column dimension + d) on each side** — that is, d/2 added on both sides of the column.

**For a square column of side c**: the punching perimeter is **b₀ = 4(c + d)**.

**Why d/2 and not d?** The assumed failure surface is a **truncated pyramid** sloping outward from the column at roughly 45° through the depth. Taking the check at **half the depth out** represents the average of that inclined surface.

**The permissible punching shear stress:**

> **τ_c = k_s × 0.25 √f_ck**

> where **k_s = 0.5 + β_c** (subject to a maximum of 1.0) and **β_c** is the ratio of the **short to long side** of the column.

> For a **square** column β_c = 1, so k_s = 1.0 and **τ_c = 0.25√f_ck**.

**Punching shear is the failure mode that matters most in flat slabs and footings:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sudden and brittle** | The column punches straight through — no warning |
| **PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE risk** | The slab drops onto the floor below, which punches in turn |
| Hard to detect beforehand | Little cracking to observe |

> **Punching shear failures in flat slabs have caused some of the worst progressive collapses on record** — because each failed floor loads the one beneath it dynamically, and the failure runs down the whole building.

**The remedies**, in order of preference:

| Remedy | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increase the DEPTH** | Most effective — it increases both b₀ and d |
| **Drop panel / column head** | Thickens the slab locally, exactly where it is needed |
| **Shear reinforcement** (studs, stirrups) | Effective but congested and detail-sensitive |
| Higher concrete grade | Only a √f_ck gain — weak leverage |

> **Depth is the strongest lever** because the punching resistance is **τ_c × b₀ × d**, and increasing d increases **both** b₀ (= 4(c + d)) **and** d — a roughly quadratic gain.

**A footing's design sequence** for completeness:

> **1.** Size the base from the **safe bearing capacity** using **service** loads (never factored ones — the SBC already contains its own factor of safety).
> **2.** Compute the **factored** soil pressure for the structural design.
> **3.** Check **one-way shear at d**, and **two-way shear at d/2** — punching usually governs the depth.
> **4.** Design the **flexural** steel at the column face.
> **5.** Check **development length** from the critical section.

> **Using factored loads for the bearing check is a common and expensive error** — it applies the factor of safety twice and produces a footing far larger than necessary.

examTip.trick: **One-way shear at d, two-way at d/2** — the plane check is further out, the perimeter check nearer. The punching perimeter is therefore **(column + d)** on each side.
examTip.trap: **Size the base from SERVICE loads against the safe bearing capacity**, then use **factored** pressure for the structural design. Using factored loads for the bearing check applies the safety factor twice.
examTip.mnemonic: **Punching is SUDDEN and can run as PROGRESSIVE COLLAPSE** down a building. The strongest remedy is **DEPTH**, because resistance is τ_c·b₀·d and increasing d raises both b₀ and d.

questions.stem: In a fillet weld, the throat thickness is related to the size of the weld 's' by:
questions.solution:
**0.7 s** — strictly **0.707 s** for the usual 90° fillet.

**Where the factor comes from.** A standard fillet weld between two plates at right angles has a **triangular** cross-section with equal legs of size s. The **throat** is the **shortest dimension through the weld** — the perpendicular from the root to the hypotenuse:

> **t = s cos 45° = s/√2 = 0.707 s** ✓

> **IS 800 tabulates this as a factor K depending on the angle between the fusion faces:**

| Angle between fusion faces | K |
|---|---|
| **60° – 90°** | **0.70** |
| 91° – 100° | 0.65 |
| 101° – 106° | 0.60 |
| 107° – 113° | 0.55 |
| 114° – 120° | 0.50 |

> The factor **falls as the angle opens out**, because a flatter weld has a shorter throat for the same leg length.

**Why the throat matters:**

> **A fillet weld is ALWAYS designed in SHEAR on the throat area**, regardless of the direction of the applied load — whether the weld is loaded along its length or across it.

> **Effective area = throat thickness × effective length = 0.7 s × l_eff**

> **Design strength = f_u/(√3 γ_mw)**, with **γ_mw = 1.25** for shop welding and **1.5** for site welding.

> Note the **site welding penalty**: the same weld is worth **17% less** if made on site, because conditions are harder to control. That is a genuine design consideration in deciding what to weld in the shop.

**Effective length:**

> **l_eff = actual length − 2s**, deducting for the start and stop craters where the weld is not full size.

> **Minimum effective length = 4s.** A shorter weld is not counted at all.

**Minimum weld size** depends on the **thicker** part being joined:

| Thicker part | Minimum fillet size |
|---|---|
| Up to 10 mm | 3 mm |
| 10 – 20 mm | 5 mm |
| 20 – 32 mm | 6 mm |
| Over 32 mm | 8 – 10 mm |

> **The minimum exists to prevent rapid cooling.** A small weld on a thick plate loses its heat into the parent metal too quickly, hardening the heat-affected zone and causing cracking.

**Maximum size along an edge**: **t − 1.5 mm** for a plate of thickness t, so the edge is not melted away.

**Fillet versus butt welds:**

| | **FILLET** | **BUTT (groove)** |
|---|---|---|
| Preparation | **None** — plates simply overlap or meet | **Edge preparation** required (V, U, bevel) |
| Cost | Lower | Higher |
| Strength | Designed in **shear** | **Full strength of the parent metal** if full penetration |
| Use | The great majority of connections | Where full strength is needed |

> **A full-penetration butt weld is as strong as the parent plate**, so no calculation is needed — the plate governs. That is why butt welds are specified for the most heavily stressed joints despite their cost.

examTip.trick: The throat is the **perpendicular from the root to the hypotenuse** of a right-angled triangle with equal legs — **s cos 45° = 0.707 s**. It is geometry, not a code table to memorise.
examTip.trap: **A fillet weld is designed in SHEAR on the throat whatever the load direction** — along or across. And **effective length = actual − 2s**, deducting the start and stop craters.
examTip.mnemonic: **Site welding costs 17% of the strength** (γ_mw 1.5 against 1.25 in the shop). And the **minimum weld size** exists to stop a small weld cooling too fast into thick plate and cracking the heat-affected zone.

questions.stem: The slenderness ratio of a load-bearing masonry wall is defined as the ratio of the effective height (or effective length) to:
questions.solution:
**The effective thickness.**

> **Slenderness ratio (SR) = effective height ÷ effective thickness**, or **effective length ÷ effective thickness**, whichever is **less**.

**Note that masonry uses THICKNESS, not the radius of gyration:**

| Material | Slenderness defined by |
|---|---|
| **Steel and concrete columns** | **λ = L_e/r**, r = radius of gyration |
| **MASONRY walls** | **SR = h_e/t_e**, effective **thickness** |

> **Option (d) is the trap**, because "slenderness ratio" in every other structural context means L/r. Masonry is the exception — it uses thickness directly, because a wall's behaviour is governed by its thin dimension and the simpler definition is adequate.

**Permissible slenderness ratios (IS 1905):**

| Construction | Maximum SR |
|---|---|
| **Load-bearing masonry, cement mortar** | **27** |
| Lime mortar | 20 |
| **Load-bearing wall in an earthquake zone** | Reduced further |

**Effective height** depends on the restraint at top and bottom:

| Restraint | h_e |
|---|---|
| **Both ends restrained** (lateral support at floor and roof) | **0.75 H** |
| One end restrained | 1.0 H |
| **Free at the top** (parapet, boundary wall) | **1.5 H or more** |

**Effective thickness:**

| Wall | t_e |
|---|---|
| **Solid wall** | The **actual thickness** t |
| **Wall with PIERS** | t × a **stiffening coefficient** (> 1) |
| **Cavity wall** | **⅔(t₁ + t₂)** — or the thicker leaf, whichever is greater |

> **Piers and cross walls increase the effective thickness**, which is why a long unstiffened wall is so much more slender than the same wall with buttresses — and why traditional masonry buildings have cross walls at regular intervals.

**The stress reduction factor:**

> The permissible compressive stress in masonry is reduced by a **stress reduction factor** that depends on **both the slenderness ratio and the eccentricity** of the load. At SR = 6 with axial load it is 1.0; at SR = 27 with eccentricity it can fall below 0.4.

> **So a slender wall may carry less than half the stress a stocky one can** — the same material, differently proportioned.

**Why masonry is limited so tightly:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **No tensile strength** | Masonry cannot carry the bending that accompanies buckling |
| **Brittle failure** | Little warning |
| **Poor out-of-plane behaviour in earthquakes** | The commonest failure in Nepali masonry buildings |

> **In an earthquake, unreinforced masonry walls fail OUT OF PLANE** — they topple away from the building. The remedy is **horizontal bands (plinth, sill, lintel, roof) and vertical reinforcement at corners and openings**, which tie the walls to the diaphragms and to each other.

> **NBC 109 and NBC 202** set these requirements for Nepal, and they are the single most important provision for the safety of the country's building stock.

examTip.trap: **Radius of gyration is the trap** — that is how slenderness is defined for **steel and concrete columns**. Masonry is the exception and uses **effective THICKNESS** directly.
examTip.trick: **Piers, buttresses and cross walls increase the EFFECTIVE thickness**, which is why traditional masonry buildings place cross walls at regular intervals rather than running long unstiffened walls.
examTip.mnemonic: **SR ≤ 27 in cement mortar; h_e = 0.75H when both ends are restrained.** And in an earthquake unreinforced masonry fails **OUT OF PLANE** — the cure is horizontal **bands** at plinth, sill, lintel and roof, plus vertical bars at corners.

questions.stem: The permissible limit of turbidity in drinking water as per the WHO/Nepal drinking water quality standard is:
questions.solution:
**5 NTU** (Nepal's National Drinking Water Quality Standard; the WHO guideline is stricter still, aiming below 1 NTU where disinfection is practised).

**Why turbidity matters far more than its appearance suggests:**

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **SHIELDS pathogens from disinfection** | Micro-organisms hide **inside** suspended particles, where chlorine cannot reach them |
| Consumes chlorine | The organic fraction exerts a demand, reducing the residual |
| Indicates treatment failure | A rise in turbidity is the fastest warning that a filter has broken through |
| Aesthetically objectionable | People reject cloudy water and turn to unsafe sources |

> **The shielding effect is the decisive one: chlorination of turbid water does not work reliably, however large the dose.** Which is why the treatment sequence is always **clarify FIRST, disinfect LAST**.

**Key Nepali standard values** worth carrying as a block:

| Parameter | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Turbidity** | **5 NTU** |
| **pH** | **6.5 – 8.5** |
| **Total hardness** | **500 mg/l** (as CaCO₃) |
| **Iron** | **0.3 mg/l** |
| Manganese | 0.2 mg/l |
| **Chloride** | **250 mg/l** |
| **Nitrate (as NO₃)** | **50 mg/l** |
| **Fluoride** | **0.5 – 1.5 mg/l** |
| **ARSENIC** | **0.05 mg/l** (Nepal); WHO 0.01 |
| **E. coli / total coliform** | **0 per 100 ml** |
| Residual chlorine | 0.1 – 0.2 mg/l |

**Three of these are worth singling out:**

> **ARSENIC** — a major public health problem in the **Terai**, where tubewell water in parts of the region exceeds the limit. It causes skin lesions and cancers after years of exposure, with **no taste, odour or colour** to warn anyone.

> **FLUORIDE has a RANGE, not just a maximum** — too little causes dental caries, too much causes **fluorosis**. It is one of the few parameters where a deficiency is also a defect.

> **NITRATE** above 50 mg/l causes **methaemoglobinaemia ("blue baby syndrome")** in infants, and it is a marker of sewage or fertiliser contamination of groundwater.

**The bacteriological standard is absolute:**

> **Zero E. coli in 100 ml.** There is no permissible level, because the presence of any faecal indicator means faecal contamination has occurred and pathogens may be present.

> **E. coli is used as an INDICATOR** rather than testing for each pathogen, because it is abundant in faeces, easy to detect, survives about as long as the pathogens, and does not multiply in water.

**The conventional treatment train** and what each stage removes:

> **Screening → aeration → coagulation/flocculation → sedimentation → FILTRATION → DISINFECTION**

| Stage | Removes |
|---|---|
| Coagulation and sedimentation | The bulk of the **turbidity** |
| **Rapid sand filtration** | The remainder — down to about 1 NTU |
| **Disinfection** | **Pathogens** — but only if the water is already clear |

> **Filtration is what makes disinfection work.** Reversing the order, or skipping the clarification, is the commonest reason a treatment plant fails to deliver safe water.

examTip.trick: Turbidity's real significance is that it **SHIELDS pathogens from chlorine** — micro-organisms hide inside particles. Hence the rule: **clarify FIRST, disinfect LAST**.
examTip.trap: **Fluoride has a RANGE (0.5–1.5 mg/l), not just a maximum** — too little causes caries, too much causes fluorosis. It is one of the few parameters where deficiency is also a defect.
examTip.mnemonic: **Turbidity 5 NTU, pH 6.5–8.5, arsenic 0.05, nitrate 50, E. coli ZERO.** Arsenic in the **Terai** is the serious one — tasteless, odourless and colourless, so nothing warns the user.

questions.stem: In the Hardy Cross method of analysing a water distribution network, the correction to the assumed flow in a loop is applied:
options: Only to the pipe with the largest head loss
Equally to every pipe in the loop, with the sign of the assumed flow direction
Only to the pipes carrying flow in the clockwise direction
In proportion to each pipe's diameter
questions.solution:
**Equally to every pipe in the loop**, added with regard to the assumed direction of flow.

**The method.** Hardy Cross is an **iterative** solution of a looped network. Flows are assumed in every pipe, satisfying continuity at each junction, and then corrected loop by loop until the head losses balance.

> **ΔQ = − Σh_f / (n Σ|h_f/Q|)**

> where **n = 2** for Darcy–Weisbach and **n = 1.85** for Hazen–Williams.

**The two conditions the solution must satisfy:**

| Condition | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Continuity** at every junction | **Inflow = outflow** — satisfied by the initial assumption and preserved by the correction |
| **Energy** around every loop | **Σh_f = 0** — the condition the iteration drives toward |

> **Applying ΔQ equally to every pipe in the loop is exactly what PRESERVES continuity.** Adding the same amount to every pipe going one way round the loop adds nothing net at any junction — whatever enters a node through one loop pipe leaves through the other.

> That is the whole reason the correction must be uniform. Applying it to one pipe, or in proportion to diameter, would **destroy continuity** at the junctions and the method would not converge to a valid solution.

**The sign convention:**

> Take **clockwise flows and their head losses as positive**, anticlockwise as negative. The correction ΔQ then has a sign, and it is **added algebraically to every pipe** in the loop.

> **A pipe shared between two loops receives BOTH corrections** — which is what couples the loops together and makes the iteration converge across the whole network.

**Convergence:**

> The method converges when **Σh_f in every loop is acceptably close to zero** — typically within a small fraction of a metre.

> **A good initial guess speeds it greatly**, but the method converges from almost any reasonable starting assumption, which is why it survived as a hand method for decades before computers.

**Why looped networks are used at all**, despite being harder to analyse:

| | **BRANCHED (dead-end)** | **LOOPED (grid)** |
|---|---|---|
| Analysis | **Simple** — flows are determinate | **Iterative** — indeterminate |
| Cost | Lower | Higher |
| **Reliability** | A break cuts off everything downstream | **Water reaches any point by MORE THAN ONE ROUTE** |
| **Water quality** | **STAGNATION at dead ends** | Continuous circulation |
| Fire fighting | Limited | Better — flow from several directions |

> **The stagnation problem is the decisive one for water quality.** Dead ends lose their chlorine residual, accumulate sediment, and become the places where contamination shows up first — which is why they need **regular flushing** through a scour valve.

**Distribution system design values:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Design flow** | **Peak hourly demand** (≈ 2.7 × average) |
| **Minimum residual pressure** | **7 m** at the consumer (single storey); more for taller buildings |
| **Velocity** | 0.6 – 3.0 m/s |
| Minimum main size | 100 mm (150 mm where fire demand applies) |

> **The distribution system is usually the largest single cost in a water supply scheme** — often more than the source and treatment works combined.

examTip.trick: The correction must be **uniform around the loop precisely because that PRESERVES CONTINUITY** — the same ΔQ entering a node through one loop pipe leaves through the other, so nothing changes at any junction.
examTip.trap: **A pipe shared between two loops receives BOTH corrections.** That coupling is what propagates the balance across the whole network, and forgetting it stalls the iteration.
examTip.mnemonic: **ΔQ = −Σh_f/(nΣ|h_f/Q|), with n = 2 for Darcy and 1.85 for Hazen–Williams.** Looped networks cost more but avoid **dead-end stagnation** — where the chlorine residual dies and contamination shows first.

questions.stem: In a rapid sand filter, backwashing is carried out when:
options: The filter has been in service for exactly 24 hours
The effluent turbidity falls below 1 NTU
The head loss across the filter reaches the permissible limit or the effluent quality deteriorates
questions.solution:
**When the head loss reaches its permissible limit, or the effluent quality deteriorates** — whichever occurs first.

**The two triggers for backwashing:**

| Trigger | What it means |
|---|---|
| **HEAD LOSS reaches the limit** (typically **2.5 – 3 m**) | The bed has clogged; the filter can no longer pass its design rate |
| **Effluent turbidity rises (BREAKTHROUGH)** | Trapped material is being **pushed through** the bed and into the supply |

> **Breakthrough is the more serious of the two**, because it means contaminated water is reaching the clear water tank. **A well-designed filter reaches its head loss limit BEFORE it breaks through** — that ordering is a design objective, not an accident.

**Rapid sand filter details:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Filtration rate** | **3000 – 6000 l/m²/hr** (about 5 m/hr) |
| **Sand effective size** | **0.35 – 0.6 mm** |
| Uniformity coefficient | 1.3 – 1.7 |
| **Bed depth** | **0.6 – 0.75 m** |
| **Backwash rate** | **~15 l/m²/s**, expanding the bed **30 – 50%** |
| **Backwash duration** | **10 – 15 minutes** |
| **Run length** | **24 – 48 hours** typically |
| Water used in backwashing | **2 – 5%** of the filtered output |

**Rapid versus slow sand filters** — the comparison that is always examined:

| | **RAPID sand** | **SLOW sand** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rate** | **~5 m/hr** | **~0.1 – 0.2 m/hr** — about **30× slower** |
| **Land required** | Small | **Very large** |
| **Pre-treatment** | **Coagulation essential** | Usually none needed |
| **Cleaning** | **BACKWASHING**, 24–48 hours | **SCRAPING** the top 2 cm, every 1–3 months |
| **Bacterial removal** | **Poor (~80–90%)** | **Excellent (98–99%)** |
| **Mechanism** | Mainly **physical** straining and adsorption | **BIOLOGICAL** — the **schmutzdecke** |

> **The slow sand filter's advantage is biological.** A living mat — the **schmutzdecke** — forms on its surface and removes bacteria far more effectively than any physical process. That is why it needs no coagulation and why it must **never be allowed to dry out**: killing the mat destroys the filter's effectiveness until it re-forms over several days.

> The trade-off is **land and rate**. A slow sand filter needs perhaps thirty times the area for the same output — which is why rapid filters dominate in cities and slow filters remain excellent for small rural schemes where land is available and skilled operation is not.

**Why coagulation must precede rapid filtration:**

> Rapid filters strain **flocs**, not individual colloidal particles. Colloids are far too small to be caught by 0.5 mm sand. **Coagulation with alum destabilises them so they aggregate into flocs large enough to be removed** — first by sedimentation, then by the filter.

> **A rapid sand filter without coagulation is close to useless**, which is why the two are always specified together.

**Backwash troubles worth knowing:**

| Problem | Cause |
|---|---|
| **MUD BALLS** | Inadequate backwash — floc and sand agglomerate into lumps that sink |
| **Air binding** | Negative pressure in the bed releases dissolved air, blocking the pores |
| Media loss | Excessive backwash rate carries sand out over the troughs |
| **Cracking** of the bed | Short-circuiting straight through |

> **Air binding is a sign of excessive head loss** and is itself a reason to backwash — the negative pressure it implies can also draw contamination in through any defect in the underdrains.

examTip.trick: Two triggers, and their order matters: **head loss limit (2.5–3 m)** or **breakthrough**. A well-designed filter should reach the head loss limit **first** — breakthrough means contaminated water is already reaching the supply.
examTip.trap: A fixed 24-hour schedule is not the criterion. Run length **varies with raw water quality** — a turbid monsoon inflow clogs a filter in hours, a clear winter one in two days.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rapid: 5 m/hr, backwash, needs coagulation, 80–90% bacteria. Slow: 0.1 m/hr, scraped, no coagulation, 98–99% — thanks to the living SCHMUTZDECKE**, which must never be allowed to dry out.

questions.stem: A separate sewerage system is preferred over a combined system because:
options: It requires only one set of pipes
Storm water can be discharged directly to a watercourse without treatment
The treatment plant is smaller and its loading is more uniform, and storm water needs no treatment
questions.solution:
**The treatment plant is smaller and its loading more uniform, and the storm water needs no treatment.**

> Option (c) is **true but incomplete** — it states one benefit while missing the decisive one, which is what the separate system does for the **treatment works**.

**Separate versus combined:**

| | **SEPARATE** | **COMBINED** |
|---|---|---|
| Pipes | **TWO systems** — foul and storm | **ONE** system carrying both |
| **Construction cost** | **HIGHER** — two sets of pipes | Lower |
| **Treatment plant size** | **SMALL** — sized for sewage only | **VERY LARGE** — must take storm flow too |
| **Loading on the works** | **UNIFORM** — biological processes work well | **Hugely variable** — shock dilution upsets the process |
| Storm water | **Discharged direct** to a watercourse | Must pass through, or be spilled |
| **Self-cleansing in dry weather** | Good — the foul sewer is small and always flowing | **POOR** — a large sewer carrying only sewage silts up |
| **Pollution risk** | Cross-connections only | **CSO — combined sewer overflows** discharge raw sewage in storms |

**The decisive argument is the treatment works:**

> Storm flow can be **50 to 100 times** the dry weather flow. Sizing a treatment plant for that is impossible, so a combined system must **spill** the excess — and what spills is **diluted raw sewage** going straight into the river.

> **Combined sewer overflows are a major and well-documented pollution source** in cities with old combined systems, and retrofitting them is enormously expensive.

**And the biological process argument:**

> Biological treatment depends on a **stable microbial population**. A sudden hundredfold dilution **washes out the biomass** and the process takes days to recover — during which the effluent is poor.

> **Uniform loading is worth a great deal to a treatment plant**, and the separate system delivers it.

**The honest disadvantages of the separate system:**

| Disadvantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Two sets of pipes** | Higher capital cost, more excavation, more congestion under the road |
| **Cross-connections** | A foul connection wrongly made into the storm sewer discharges **raw sewage direct to the river**, undetected |
| First flush pollution | The initial storm runoff is dirty and goes untreated |

> **Cross-connections are the practical weakness**, and they are common where connections are made without supervision. A single wrong connection can pollute a watercourse continuously for years before anyone traces it.

**Design flows:**

| System | Design flow |
|---|---|
| **Foul sewer** | **Peak dry weather flow** (≈ 3 × average) plus **infiltration** |
| **Storm sewer** | The **rational method: Q = CIA/360** (Q in m³/s, I in mm/hr, A in hectares) |
| Combined | The sum, plus provision for overflows |

> **Sewage flow is usually taken as 80% of the water supply**, the remainder being consumed, evaporated or used for irrigation.

**And the self-cleansing point** deserves emphasis:

> A **combined sewer is large**, so in dry weather the sewage forms a shallow trickle at the bottom with a **low velocity** — well below the **0.6 m/s** needed to keep solids moving. **Silting follows, then blockage, then flooding.**

> That is the everyday operational cost of a combined system, quite apart from its pollution record.

examTip.trap: Option (c) is **true but incomplete** — it names one benefit and misses the decisive one. On a question with a partly-right option, look for the fuller statement rather than stopping at the first true thing you read.
examTip.trick: The separate system is **more expensive to build and cheaper to operate**. Storm flow can be **50–100× dry weather flow**, which no treatment plant can be sized for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Combined systems SPILL raw sewage (CSOs) and SILT UP in dry weather** — a large pipe carrying a trickle never reaches the 0.6 m/s self-cleansing velocity. The separate system's own weakness is **cross-connections**, which pollute undetected for years.

questions.stem: The BOD₅ test is conducted at a standard temperature and duration of:
questions.solution:
**20 °C for 5 days.**

**What BOD measures:**

> **Biochemical Oxygen Demand** is the **oxygen consumed by micro-organisms** in decomposing the organic matter in a sample, under standard conditions. It is the standard measure of the **organic strength** of a wastewater.

**Why 5 days and 20 °C:**

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| **20 °C** | A representative **temperate river temperature**, and the conventional standard |
| **5 days** | Historically the **longest time a British river takes to reach the sea** — a genuinely arbitrary but universally adopted convention |

> **The 5-day BOD captures only about 68% of the ultimate BOD.** The remainder continues to be exerted for weeks.

**The first-order relation:**

> **BOD_t = L₀(1 − 10^{−kt})** or **L₀(1 − e^{−k′t})**

> with **k ≈ 0.1/day** (base 10) at 20 °C. At t = 5: **1 − 10^{−0.5} = 1 − 0.316 = 0.684** ✓ — the 68% figure.

**Temperature correction:**

> **k_T = k₂₀ × 1.047^{(T−20)}**

> Note that **BOD exertion is faster at higher temperature but the ULTIMATE BOD is unchanged** — temperature changes the **rate**, not the total oxygen demand. That distinction is regularly examined.

**BOD versus COD:**

| | **BOD** | **COD** |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | **BIODEGRADABLE** organics | **ALL** oxidisable matter |
| Time | **5 days** | **3 hours** |
| Value | Lower | **Always HIGHER** |
| Uses | Process design; discharge standards | Rapid process control |

> **COD is always greater than BOD**, because it oxidises material that bacteria cannot. **A ratio BOD/COD above about 0.5 indicates readily biodegradable waste** suitable for biological treatment; a low ratio suggests an industrial waste needing physico-chemical treatment instead.

**Typical values:**

| Wastewater | BOD₅ |
|---|---|
| **Weak domestic sewage** | **~110 mg/l** |
| **Medium domestic sewage** | **~220 mg/l** |
| Strong domestic sewage | ~400 mg/l |
| **Effluent discharge standard (Nepal)** | **50 mg/l** commonly |

**Why BOD matters — the receiving water:**

> Organic matter discharged to a river **consumes its dissolved oxygen**. If the DO falls too far, **fish die and the river turns septic**.

> The **oxygen sag curve (Streeter–Phelps)** describes the balance between **deoxygenation** (the BOD being exerted) and **reoxygenation** (atmospheric reaeration):

> **The critical point is where the two rates are EQUAL** — the minimum DO in the river, and the point at which the discharge must be judged.

> **Self-purification** is real but limited. It depends on **dilution, temperature, turbulence and time of travel** — and a slow, warm, sluggish river in the dry season has very little of it, which is exactly when discharge standards matter most.

**A caution about the test itself**: the sample must usually be **diluted with aerated dilution water and seeded**, because raw sewage contains far more BOD than the ~9 mg/l of oxygen that saturated water can supply. **A test where the DO falls to zero is invalid**, not a very high result.

examTip.trick: **20 °C for 5 days** — and the 5 days captures only about **68% of the ultimate BOD**, from 1 − 10^{−0.1×5}. That figure is worth knowing because questions often ask for the ultimate value.
examTip.trap: Temperature changes the **RATE** of BOD exertion, not the **ultimate** demand. A warmer sample exerts its BOD faster; the total oxygen required is the same.
examTip.mnemonic: **COD is always higher than BOD** (3 hours, everything oxidisable). A **BOD/COD ratio above 0.5** means biological treatment will work; below it, suspect an industrial waste needing physico-chemical treatment.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower plant, the design discharge is usually selected from the flow duration curve at an exceedance probability of about:
questions.solution:
**About 40%** — commonly in the range **30–50%**, depending on the economics of the particular scheme.

**What the flow duration curve shows:**

> The **percentage of time** a given discharge is **equalled or exceeded**. **Q40** means the flow available **40% of the time**.

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Q10** | A **high** flow, available only 10% of the time |
| **Q40** | The typical **design discharge** for a run-of-river plant |
| **Q90 – Q95** | **Dependable / firm** flow — available almost always |
| **Q100** | The absolute minimum |

> **Note the counter-intuitive direction: a HIGHER percentage means a LOWER flow**, because it is available a greater proportion of the time. Reading the curve backwards is the standard error.

**Why 40% and not 90%:**

| Design at | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Q90** (the firm flow) | The plant runs at **full capacity almost always** — but the machine is **small** and **spills most of the monsoon flow**, generating far less energy than the river could provide |
| **Q40** | Full output about 40% of the time, **part load the rest** — **maximises total annual ENERGY per rupee invested** |
| **Q10** | A huge, expensive machine idle most of the year |

> **The optimum is an ECONOMIC choice, not a hydrological one.** It maximises the net present value of energy sold against the capital cost of the plant, and it lands around Q40 for most Nepali schemes.

**Reading energy off the curve:**

> **The AREA under the flow duration curve is the total volume of water available.** The area under the curve **up to the design discharge** is what the plant can actually use; everything above it is **spilled**.

> That picture explains the trade-off immediately: raising the design flow captures more of the area but costs more machine, and the added area shrinks as you go higher up the curve.

**The distinction that matters for a Nepali scheme:**

| Plant type | Design flow basis |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river** | **Q40** — energy maximisation |
| **Peaking run-of-river (PROR)** | Q40 plus a **pondage** for daily peaking |
| **Storage** | The **firm flow after regulation** — the reservoir converts monsoon surplus into dry season supply |

> **Nepal's problem is not annual water but its DISTRIBUTION**: about 80% of the flow arrives in four monsoon months. A run-of-river plant therefore generates far less in the dry season, exactly when demand peaks — which is the argument for storage schemes and for the pondage in a PROR.

**The power equation:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η** — with η around **0.85–0.90** overall.

> **Q comes from the flow duration curve; H from the topography.** The two together, times the efficiency, give the installed capacity — and the **annual energy** follows from integrating the usable area under the curve.

**Other planning studies** in a hydropower project: **head and discharge assessment**, geological investigation, **sediment** studies (critical in the Himalaya), **environmental and social impact assessment**, transmission access, and the **economic and financial analysis** that decides whether any of it proceeds.

examTip.trap: **A HIGHER percentage means a LOWER flow** — Q90 is a small, dependable discharge and Q10 a large, rare one. Reading the curve the wrong way round is the standard error in this topic.
examTip.trick: The choice is **economic, not hydrological**: design at Q90 and you spill the whole monsoon; design at Q10 and the machine idles. **Q40 maximises energy per rupee invested.**
examTip.mnemonic: **The AREA under the FDC up to the design discharge is the usable water; everything above is spilled.** Nepal's problem is not annual volume but **distribution** — 80% arrives in four monsoon months, which is the case for storage.

questions.stem: The plant load factor of a hydropower plant is defined as the ratio of:
options: Average load to the installed (rated) capacity
questions.solution:
**Average load ÷ installed (rated) capacity.**

> **Plant load factor = actual energy generated in a period ÷ (installed capacity × hours in the period)**

**The family of power-system factors**, which are constantly confused with one another:

| Factor | Definition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PLANT LOAD FACTOR (capacity factor)** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED capacity** | How fully the **plant** is used |
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **Average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND** | How steady the **demand** is |
| **PLANT USE (utilisation) FACTOR** | Energy produced ÷ (capacity × hours **in service**) | Excludes shutdown time |
| **DEMAND FACTOR** | Maximum demand ÷ connected load | Not everything runs at once |
| **DIVERSITY FACTOR** | Σ individual maximum demands ÷ system maximum demand | **Always > 1** |
| **UTILISATION FACTOR** | Maximum demand ÷ rated capacity | — |

> **The discriminator between the first two is the DENOMINATOR**: the plant load factor divides by the **installed capacity**; the load factor divides by the **maximum demand**. Option (b) states the load factor, which is why it is the most-picked wrong answer.

**Typical plant load factors:**

| Plant | PLF |
|---|---|
| **Base load thermal** | **60 – 80%** |
| **Run-of-river hydro (Nepal)** | **~40 – 60%** — limited by dry-season flow |
| **Peaking plant** | **10 – 20%** |
| Solar PV | 15 – 20% |

> **A low plant load factor is not necessarily bad.** A **peaking plant** is *meant* to run rarely — its value is being available at the daily peak, not in the energy it produces. Judging it by its PLF misunderstands its purpose entirely.

**Why the load factor (the demand one) matters commercially:**

> **A high load factor means steady demand**, which allows cheaper generation — plant runs continuously at its efficient point instead of cycling.

> **A low load factor means peaky demand**, requiring expensive peaking capacity that sits idle most of the time. That is why **industrial tariffs reward a high load factor** and why **time-of-day tariffs** exist at all.

**Nepal's particular position:**

> The country's run-of-river plants have a **low PLF in the dry season** — exactly when demand peaks. The result is a **seasonal surplus in the monsoon and a deficit in winter**, which is the structural problem of the Nepali power system.

> The answers are **storage projects** (converting monsoon surplus into dry-season supply), **peaking run-of-river with pondage**, and **cross-border trade** — exporting the monsoon surplus and importing in the dry season.

**The diversity factor** deserves a note because it is why systems work at all:

> **Not everyone's maximum demand occurs at the same instant.** The sum of individual peaks always exceeds the system peak, so the diversity factor is **always greater than 1** — and the whole system can be built smaller than the sum of its consumers' demands.

> **Diversity is what makes electricity supply economically possible.**

examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the LOAD FACTOR** (average ÷ maximum demand), not the plant load factor (average ÷ installed capacity). The **denominator** is the whole discriminator, and the two are swapped constantly.
examTip.trick: **Load factor judges the DEMAND's steadiness; plant load factor judges the PLANT's utilisation.** Ask which one the question is about, then pick the matching denominator.
examTip.mnemonic: **A low PLF is not necessarily bad** — a peaking plant is meant to run rarely. And the **diversity factor is always > 1**, because peaks do not coincide — which is what makes electricity supply economically possible at all.

questions.stem: In a gravity dam, the resultant of all forces (reservoir full) must pass through the middle third of the base primarily to ensure that:
options: The dam does not slide on its foundation
The dam is economical in concrete
No tension develops at the heel of the dam
questions.solution:
**No tension develops at the heel.**

**Why tension at the heel is intolerable in a gravity dam:**

> **Concrete and masonry have negligible reliable tensile strength.** If tension develops at the heel, a **crack opens** there.

> But the crack is not the end of it — it is the **beginning of a progressive failure**:

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1** | A crack opens at the **heel** |
| **2** | **FULL RESERVOIR PRESSURE enters the crack** |
| **3** | The **UPLIFT force increases** dramatically |
| **4** | The resultant moves **further downstream** |
| **5** | The crack **propagates further**, admitting more water |

> **The process is self-accelerating.** A crack that admits water makes the conditions that opened it worse — which is why the no-tension criterion is treated as absolute rather than as a stress limit to be traded against a factor of safety.

**The middle third rule:**

> **e ≤ B/6** from the centre of the base, for a rectangular base of width B. Beyond that the minimum base pressure **p = (ΣV/B)(1 − 6e/B)** becomes negative.

**The gravity dam's stability requirements:**

| Check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **No tension** | Resultant in the **middle third** |
| **Sliding (shear friction factor)** | **≥ 3 to 5** |
| **Overturning** | FoS ≥ 1.5 |
| **Compressive stress** | Within the allowable for concrete and foundation |

**The forces on a gravity dam:**

| Force | Note |
|---|---|
| **Self weight W** | The **stabilising** force — a gravity dam resists by weight alone |
| **Water pressure P** | **γH²/2 per metre**, acting at **H/3 from the base** |
| **UPLIFT U** | Acts **upward** on the base — reduces the effective weight |
| Silt pressure | Behind the dam |
| Earthquake forces | Inertia plus **hydrodynamic** pressure |
| Ice, wave, wind | Usually minor |

**UPLIFT is the force that most often decides the section:**

> Water penetrating the foundation and the dam–rock contact exerts an **upward pressure** over the base, **reducing the effective weight** — and weight is the only thing holding a gravity dam in place.

> **Uplift was not understood in early dam engineering, and several nineteenth-century failures are attributed to it.**

**The remedies, and why the drainage gallery matters more than the grout curtain:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **GROUT CURTAIN** near the heel | **Reduces seepage** by sealing the rock |
| **DRAINAGE GALLERY with relief holes** | **RELIEVES the uplift pressure** by giving the water a low-pressure escape |

> **The drainage gallery is typically more effective at reducing uplift than the grout curtain is** — it does not try to stop the water, it gives it somewhere to go at atmospheric pressure. A well-drained foundation can reduce the uplift diagram to a fraction of the undrained value.

> **Grouting reduces flow; drainage reduces PRESSURE.** It is pressure that threatens the dam.

**And the elementary profile** for context:

> The theoretical minimum section is a **triangle with its apex at the reservoir level**, base width **B = H/√(S_c − c)** where S_c is the specific gravity of the material and c the uplift coefficient. With uplift ignored (c = 0) and S_c = 2.4, **B ≈ 0.65H**; with full uplift (c = 1), **B ≈ 0.85H** — a **30% larger dam**, which is a direct measure of what uplift costs.

examTip.trick: The no-tension rule is not a stress limit but a guard against a **self-accelerating failure**: a crack at the heel **admits full reservoir pressure**, which raises uplift, which moves the resultant further downstream, which extends the crack.
examTip.trap: Sliding and uplift are both genuine stability concerns, but the **middle third rule** addresses **tension** specifically. Sliding is checked separately by the shear friction factor (3–5).
examTip.mnemonic: **GROUT reduces FLOW; DRAINAGE reduces PRESSURE** — and it is pressure that threatens the dam, so the drainage gallery usually matters more than the grout curtain. Full uplift makes the section about **30% wider**.

questions.stem: A Pelton turbine is most suitable for:
options: Very low head and very high discharge
questions.solution:
**High head and low discharge.**

**Turbine selection by head:**

| Turbine | Head | Discharge | Type | Specific speed N_s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **HIGH — above ~250 m** | **LOW** | **IMPULSE** | **10 – 35** |
| **Turgo / Crossflow** | Medium | Medium | Impulse | — |
| **FRANCIS** | **Medium — 30 to 250 m** | Medium | **REACTION** | **60 – 300** |
| **KAPLAN** | **LOW — below ~30 m** | **HIGH** | **REACTION** | **300 – 1000** |

> **Specific speed rises as head falls** — and it is the parameter that actually selects the machine, since it combines head, discharge and speed into one number:

> **N_s = N√P/H^{5/4}**

**Impulse versus reaction — the fundamental distinction:**

| | **IMPULSE (Pelton)** | **REACTION (Francis, Kaplan)** |
|---|---|---|
| Energy at the runner | **All KINETIC** — converted in the nozzle | **Kinetic AND pressure** |
| Pressure at the runner | **ATMOSPHERIC** throughout | **Above atmospheric**, falling through the runner |
| Runner | **Runs in AIR**, partially filled casing | **Runs FULL of water** |
| **Draft tube** | **NOT used** | **ESSENTIAL** |
| Flow control | **Spear valve** in the nozzle | **Guide vanes** |

**Why the draft tube is essential to a reaction turbine** — and pointless on a Pelton:

> The **draft tube recovers the kinetic energy of the water leaving the runner** and, by creating **suction**, allows the turbine to be set **above the tailwater** without losing that head.

> A Pelton discharges to atmosphere into the tailrace, so there is no pressure to recover — and **the head between the runner and the tailwater is simply LOST**, which is why a Pelton is set as close above the tailwater as flooding allows.

**Pelton design relations:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Jet velocity** | **V = C_v √(2gH)**, with C_v ≈ 0.98 |
| **Optimum bucket speed** | **u = 0.46 V** — very close to **half** the jet velocity |
| **Speed ratio** | 0.43 – 0.48 |
| **Jet ratio D/d** | **11 – 14** |
| **Number of buckets** | **15 + D/2d**, typically 18–25 |
| Deflection angle | 165° (not 180°, so the water clears the following bucket) |

> **The bucket travels at half the jet speed** because that is what leaves the water with **zero absolute velocity** — all its kinetic energy transferred. It is the same result as an elastic collision, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising.

> The **deflection is 165° rather than a theoretical 180°** because water turned completely back would strike the following bucket. That 15° costs a little efficiency and is unavoidable.

**CAVITATION** affects reaction turbines but not Pelton:

> A Pelton runs at **atmospheric pressure**, so the pressure never falls to the vapour pressure and cavitation cannot occur. A **Francis or Kaplan runs below atmospheric on its downstream side**, and the setting relative to tailwater must satisfy **Thoma's cavitation parameter σ**.

**And in Nepal specifically:**

> The steep terrain gives **high heads with modest flows** over much of the country, which is exactly Pelton territory — and Pelton runners are also the easiest to manufacture and repair locally, which matters for small schemes.

> But **sediment erosion is severe**: quartz sand at high jet velocity **cuts the needle and buckets**, and a runner can lose its profile in a single monsoon without an effective settling basin.

examTip.trick: **Head falls, specific speed rises: Pelton (high head) → Francis (medium) → Kaplan (low).** Specific speed **N_s = N√P/H^{5/4}** is what actually selects the machine.
examTip.trap: **A Pelton has NO draft tube** and cannot cavitate — it runs at atmospheric pressure in air. Reaction turbines need the draft tube to recover exit energy and must satisfy Thoma's σ.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bucket speed u = 0.46V, about HALF the jet** — which leaves the water with zero absolute velocity, transferring all its energy. And the deflection is **165°, not 180°**, so the water clears the following bucket.

questions.stem: In highway alignment surveys, the correct sequence of surveys is:
options: Preliminary survey, map study, reconnaissance, detailed survey
Reconnaissance, map study, detailed survey, preliminary survey
Map study, detailed survey, reconnaissance, preliminary survey
Map study, reconnaissance, preliminary survey, detailed survey
questions.solution:
**Map study → Reconnaissance → Preliminary survey → Detailed survey.**

**The logic is a steady narrowing**, from the widest and cheapest investigation to the narrowest and most expensive:

| Stage | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **1. MAP STUDY** | Desk work on **topographic maps** — identify possible corridors, obstacles, gradients, river crossings | **Cheapest** — no field work at all |
| **2. RECONNAISSANCE** | **Rapid field inspection** of the corridors identified; eliminate the unworkable ones | Low |
| **3. PRELIMINARY survey** | **Instrument survey along the surviving alternatives**; compare them on cost, gradient, curvature, land and drainage | Moderate |
| **4. DETAILED survey** | **Full survey of the ONE chosen alignment** — levels, cross-sections, soil and material investigation, drainage design | **Most expensive** |

> **Each stage costs more per kilometre and covers less ground than the one before.** That is the organising principle, and it is why the sequence cannot be rearranged: doing detailed work on a corridor that a map study would have eliminated wastes the most expensive effort on the least promising ground.

**What each stage produces:**

| Stage | Output |
|---|---|
| Map study | A shortlist of **feasible corridors** |
| **Reconnaissance** | Elimination of corridors with **fatal obstacles** — unstable slopes, unbridgeable crossings, protected areas |
| **Preliminary** | A **comparison of alternatives** on measurable criteria |
| **Detailed** | The **working drawings and estimate** |

**The requirements of a good alignment**, which are the criteria applied throughout:

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **SHORT** | Directly reduces cost and travel time |
| **EASY** | To construct, and to traverse — gradients and curves within limits |
| **SAFE** | Adequate sight distances; stable slopes |
| **ECONOMICAL** | Construction **plus maintenance plus vehicle operating cost** over the life |

> **The four often conflict.** The shortest route is frequently the steepest and the most expensive to build; the easiest gradient is usually the longest. **Alignment design is the resolution of that conflict**, not the satisfaction of any one criterion.

**Special considerations in HILL roads**, which is the Nepali case:

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stability of the hillside** | The **first** consideration — a road on an unstable slope will not survive whatever else is right about it |
| **Drainage** | On a hill road **water does more damage than traffic** |
| **Geometric standards** | Relaxed, but hairpins need **grade compensation** |
| **Resisting length** | The total rise, which governs the ruling gradient |
| Avoid | Landslide zones, unstable talus, springs, deep cuts |

> **Choosing a stable alignment is worth more than any amount of retaining wall.** A road placed on a moving slope needs rebuilding every monsoon; one placed on sound ground needs almost nothing.

**The obligatory points** that constrain the alignment:

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Points the road MUST pass through** | Towns to be served, an intermediate bridge site, a mountain pass |
| **Points the road MUST avoid** | Unstable slopes, protected forest, religious sites, expensive land, marshy ground |

> The alignment is threaded between these, and identifying them correctly at the **map study** stage is what makes all the later work efficient.

examTip.trick: The sequence narrows: **each stage costs more per kilometre and covers less ground**. Map study is free desk work; the detailed survey covers one alignment only. That principle fixes the order without memorising it.
examTip.trap: **Reconnaissance and preliminary survey** are the pair most often swapped. Reconnaissance is a **rapid field walk-over to eliminate** corridors; the preliminary survey is an **instrument survey to compare** the survivors.
examTip.mnemonic: **Short, easy, safe, economical — and they conflict.** On a hill road, **slope stability comes first**: a road on moving ground needs rebuilding every monsoon, whatever else is right about it.

questions.stem: The main difference between a flexible pavement and a rigid pavement is that:
options: A flexible pavement is thicker than a rigid pavement
A rigid pavement requires no subgrade preparation
A flexible pavement is made of concrete and a rigid pavement of bitumen
A flexible pavement transmits load to the subgrade through grain-to-grain contact
questions.solution:
**A flexible pavement transmits the load through grain-to-grain contact; a rigid pavement distributes it by slab action.**

**The fundamental difference:**

| | **FLEXIBLE** | **RIGID** |
|---|---|---|
| Material | **Bituminous** layers over granular base | **Cement concrete** slab |
| **Load transfer** | **GRAIN-TO-GRAIN contact**, spreading through successive layers | **SLAB ACTION** — the slab bends and spreads the load over a wide area |
| **Flexural strength** | Negligible | **High — it is the design property** |
| **Design based on** | **CBR of the subgrade** | **Modulus of subgrade reaction k** and **flexural strength f_cr** |
| **Load distribution** | Through a **cone** widening with depth | Over a **wide area** by bending |
| **Subgrade quality** | **Critical** — the pavement is only as good as what is under it | **Less critical** — the slab bridges over weak spots |
| Initial cost | Lower | Higher |
| **Life** | **10 – 15 years** | **30 – 40 years** |
| **Maintenance** | Frequent | **Minimal** |
| Joints | None | **Required** — contraction, expansion, construction |
| Riding quality when new | Excellent | Good |
| Night visibility | Poorer (dark surface) | **Better** (light surface) |

**The consequence of the load transfer mechanism:**

> In a **flexible** pavement, each layer distributes the load to a wider area of the layer below. **Stress reduces with depth**, so the strongest and most expensive material goes on **top** and progressively cheaper material below.

> **The subgrade is therefore critical**, because it ultimately carries everything. A weak subgrade means a thicker pavement — and the relationship is steep.

> In a **rigid** pavement the slab's own **flexural strength** carries most of the load and spreads it widely, so **the subgrade matters much less**. A rigid pavement can bridge over a soft patch that would fail a flexible one.

**Design methods:**

| Pavement | Method |
|---|---|
| **Flexible** | **CBR method** (IRC 37), using **msa** — million standard axles of 8160 kg |
| **Rigid** | **Westergaard's** analysis for the three critical load positions |

**Westergaard's three load positions** in a rigid pavement:

| Position | Note |
|---|---|
| **Interior** | Load in the middle of the slab |
| **EDGE** | **Usually the most critical** for load stress |
| **CORNER** | Critical when **warping** stresses combine |

> **The corner is the weakest point of a concrete slab**, having support on only two sides — which is why dowel bars are provided at transverse joints to transfer load across.

**Temperature stresses** are unique to rigid pavements and often exceed the load stresses:

| Effect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **WARPING** | A **temperature GRADIENT** through the slab depth — the top expands more than the bottom by day, less by night |
| **Frictional** | **Uniform** temperature change resisted by subgrade friction |

> **The critical combination is the worst load position combined with the worst warping condition** — and it is often warping, not traffic, that cracks a concrete pavement.

**And the joints, each with its own purpose:**

| Joint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Contraction** | Allows **shrinkage**; controls where cracks form |

> **Dowel bars TRANSFER load across a transverse joint** (smooth, allowing movement along the axis); **TIE BARS HOLD slabs together at a longitudinal joint** (deformed, resisting separation). **They are not interchangeable** — using a deformed bar as a dowel locks the joint and causes the cracking it was meant to prevent.

examTip.trick: The difference is the **load transfer mechanism**, and everything else follows from it: grain-to-grain contact makes the **subgrade critical** for flexible pavements; slab action lets a rigid pavement **bridge over** a weak patch.
